articles.title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
articles.context: Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he...
articles.full_text:
Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries.

In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset.

The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual.

Need to buy time

“For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post. “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.”

But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said.

He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug.

Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out.

“We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said.

Making the infrastructure secure from the start

Shirudo combines Cisco’s infrastructure with OpenAI’s frontier models and AI research. It is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which supports the running of small, sandboxed programs inside a Linux kernel without changing source code or loading additional modules.

“This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems,” OpenAI explained in its blog post announcing the project.

Speaking in their own language, guardian agents investigate and detect flaws and build shields, then test whether they stop the attack, all without disrupting the targeted service. The shields are cryptographically signed and only loaded when verified and deemed safe. Linux’s eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against safety rules, and kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Shirudo also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being added or removed.

All this takes place even if attackers have already gained access to a system.

Further, self-defending agents can monitor for false positives, performance, and overall system health, and incorporate red-team findings and other feedback as well as signals for continuous improvement. Evidence backing every control travels across the system.

The idea, according to Cisco and OpenAI, is to make the infrastructure itself secure by default. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer,” OpenAI wrote in its post.

Shirudo in the wild

Shirudo has its roots in Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform developed and open-sourced by Isovalent, which was acquired by Cisco in 2024. It is already incorporated into Cisco’s Live Protect capability.

But Tetragon has been rewritten for the agentic era; its previous iteration pointed AI to human-oriented consoles, configuration files, and policy languages. In that workflow, the agent thought in machine code, which was then decoded for humans and processed, then translated back again into machine code. With Shirudo, agents interact in their natural language, which is code.

“Agents are different,” Isovalent co-founder Thomas Graf and its chief open source officer Liz Rice noted in a blog post: They are very good at generating code, can absorb huge amounts of context quickly, and “[don’t] mind reverse engineering several million lines of assembly code.”

In one controlled testing environment, researchers fed information about the Java4Shell vulnerability into Shirudo, which automatically created a shield against exploitation, generating a mitigation in Java bytecode which was injected into any Java app and added validation on the base64 input to guard against exploit attempts by threat actors.

Graf and Rice explained that agent loops can either be tasked to actively search for new vulnerabilities on their own, or work off external sources like newly-available security disclosures. Agents can generate mitigation code, reproduce and validate exploits, and determine the most effective patching measures. This step is repeated until the agent identifies a successful path. The shield is then signed and securely rolled out to vulnerable nodes; it retires when a patch is installed.

“This step is continuously monitored and repeated to achieve the highest possible security score while closely monitoring the health of applications,” Graf and Rice explained. It can be designed to be “more or less autonomous.”

Once mitigation shields are deployed, the system employs a “hit” count of active exploitation attempts, so that exploits can be investigated on demand.

Ultimately, the Shirudo project is only the beginning, Graf and Rice noted, but it already shows “true potential” and the hope is it will continue to evolve in the open source ecosystem. “We believe that building secure infrastructure for the AI era is an industry-scale problem,” they said.

Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, a permissive open-source software license approved by the Open Source Initiative. This allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute software, including in proprietary or commercial products, with minimal restrictions. Its BPF programs are dual licensed under GPL and BSD.

Developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators are encouraged to inspect the code, test outcomes, and contribute to the project’s development.

This article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

articles.title: VMware patches critical vCenter authentication bypass and ESX flaws
articles.context: The rapid succession of critical vCenter disclosures, including a vulnerability already exploited in targeted attacks, makes patch management and restricting network access to...
articles.full_text:
Broadcom patches 23 VMware flaws, including a critical vCenter authentication bypass and three flaws allowing code execution on ESX hosts.

Broadcom has released security updates to address 23 vulnerabilities affecting multiple VMware products, including vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. The security advisory includes four critical-severity flaws, with the most serious tracked as CVE-2026-123903 (CVSS score of 9.8).

This vulnerability affects the VMware Directory Service (vmdir) in vCenter. An attacker with network access to a vulnerable server could exploit the flaw to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access.

Broadcom published the issue in its security advisory VMSA-2026-0011. The company credited researchers from Qianxin, depthfirst, and ThreatBook for independently reporting the vulnerability.

The new flaw is distinct from CVE-2026-123890, the authentication bypass disclosed on November 19. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that the suspected Chinese espionage group tracked as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) had exploited the earlier vulnerability since September 2026.

According to Mandiant, the attackers used a custom tool called BONESAW to exploit vCenter, obtain an administrator session, steal sensitive data, and create a new SSO administrator account. They subsequently used additional tools to forge authentication tokens and maintain access to compromised environments.

Broadcom’s latest advisory also addresses several other vCenter vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-123904 (CVSS score of 7.5) is an arbitrary file write flaw affecting archive processing. An attacker with access to the backup repository could write files to arbitrary locations with root privileges, potentially leading to code execution on the appliance.

Three other vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, could allow attackers with network access to disrupt the VMware Directory Service and make it unavailable.

The ESX updates fix several other serious flaws. Two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911, both have a CVSS score of 9.8 and affect the I/O filter service. One can cause an out-of-bounds write in the heap, while the other is a use-after-free flaw. An attacker with network access could exploit either vulnerability to execute code on the ESX host.

Another critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-123912 (CVSS 9.3), affects the XHCI USB controller in ESX, VMware Workstation, and Fusion. Exploiting it requires local administrator privileges inside a virtual machine and could allow an attacker to run code as the VMX process. On ESX, this code remains restricted to the VMX sandbox. On Workstation and Fusion, however, it could lead to code execution on the host machine.

The advisory also covers eight vulnerabilities in Avi Load Balancer and a denial-of-service issue in VMware Tools.

Broadcom has released patches for the affected products. The fixes for vCenter are available in version 9.1.2 for the 9.1 branch, 9.0.2.0300 for the 9.0 branch, and 8.0 U3m for vCenter 8.0. Organizations running vCenter 7.0 should contact Broadcom Support if they have an extended support contract.

The company also published fixes for ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. Administrators should consult the official Broadcom advisory for the complete list of affected versions and corresponding updates.

The rapid succession of critical vCenter disclosures, including a vulnerability already exploited in targeted attacks, makes patch management and restricting network access to management interfaces particularly important for organizations relying on VMware infrastructure.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, VMware)

articles.title: NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-123633
articles.context: Related Unit 42 Topics HTTP, DNS, Threat Detection Background While researching NGINX, I independently found the HTTP/2 connection-state defect now tracked as CVE-2026-123633
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free vulnerability in NGINX HTTP/2 that may let an unauthenticated attacker cause a denial of service. In the CVE record, F5 says code execution may be possible when address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed.

CVE-2026-123633 affects NGINX servers that accept HTTP/2 client connections and proxy requests to a backend when free worker connections run low. A fragmented request can leave an active connection marked reusable. Under connection pressure, NGINX can close that connection and free memory the active request still uses.

F5's CVE record scores the issue 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0. The NGINX security advisories page labels the issue medium and lists versions 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected. F5 credits memN0ps (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42) among the reporters.

NGINX 1.30.7 on the stable branch and 1.31.9 on the mainline branch contain the fix. F5 also lists affected NGINX Plus releases.

Administrators should review HTTP/2 reverse-proxy exposure and upgrade to a fixed NGINX release or a vendor package containing the CVE-2026-123633 fix.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

HTTP, DNS, Threat Detection

Background

While researching NGINX, I independently found the HTTP/2 connection-state defect now tracked as CVE-2026-123633.

An unauthenticated client can send a fragmented HTTP/2 request that leaves an active connection marked as reusable. When the server resolves a hostname during the request and free connection slots run low, NGINX can reclaim that connection mid-request and free memory its DNS resolver is still using.

I reproduced the use-after-free with AddressSanitizer (ASan) on builds of unmodified NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 source. The NGINX security advisories page lists 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected and 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 as fixed releases.

I reported the HTTP/2 use-after-free privately to F5. F5's CVE record scores it 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0 and 8.1 High under CVSS 3.1. The NGINX security advisories page labels it Medium.

In my ASan test on a Debian guest, ASan stopped NGINX at the first read from freed DNS lookup memory.

The resolver path in my test stems from the HTTP/2 connection bug tracked as CVE-2026-123633. CVE-2026-123634 is a separate DNS resolver vulnerability fixed in the same release.

I also found a memory disclosure vulnerability that leaked a libc pointer. I used the address to calculate the libc base and work around ASLR when chaining the disclosure with CVE-2026-123633. I reported this additional bug to F5 as a separate issue. From an attacker VM, I achieved pre-authentication remote code execution on a target VM as the non-root NGINX worker. The chain required a non-default NGINX configuration, and some attempts did not open a shell.

F5 assessed the memory disclosure as a behavior limited to a non-typical configuration and has not assigned it a CVE at the time of writing, so I am leaving out its details and the exploit steps.

How the Connection State Defect Works

NGINX marks a connection reusable when it can close that connection under pressure. Stream creation should clear the reusable mark once a request starts, but ngx_http_v2_create_stream() leaves it set in affected releases.

When a client sends only part of an HTTP/2 HEADERS frame header, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection reusable and returns early. The code below shows that decision:

ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1); if (h2c->state.incomplete) { return; }

}

The reusable mark lets NGINX reclaim connections stalled on partial frames before they exhaust the worker's slots.

The client then sends the remaining header bytes. ngx_http_v2_create_stream() builds a live stream and increments the active stream counter, but returns with the reusable mark still set:

h2c->processing++; if (h2c->connection->read->timer_set) { ngx_del_timer(h2c->connection->read); } return stream;

1

2

ngx_del_timer(h2c->connection->read);

}

return stream;

NGINX now has a live request on a connection that its cleanup logic still considers reusable.

The 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 fixes clear the reusable mark at stream creation with ngx_reusable_connection(h2c->connection, 0). Figure 1 shows the sequence in affected releases:

A partial frame header marks the connection reusable

NGINX creates a stream with the mark still set

A later socket allocation drains the live connection

Reaching the Resolver Use-After-Free

The stale reusable mark lets NGINX reclaim a live connection when it needs a free slot. In my test, a request-time DNS lookup opened a new socket and triggered the drain.

My test used an HTTP/2 proxy route with a variable upstream. The variable evaluated to a hostname that was neither a literal IP address nor a configured upstream group, so NGINX looked it up during the request. The lookup also had to open a new resolver UDP socket.

The worker opens a new UDP socket only if it has none for the selected nameserver. Cached answers and in-flight lookups also skip the socket-allocation drain I tested.

Opening the DNS socket needs a connection slot, so ngx_get_connection() runs a drain check first. ngx_drain_connections() acts once free slots fall to one sixteenth of worker_connections or below while at least one reusable connection exists. The drain function then selects entries from the tail of the reusable queue, sets each connection's close flag, and calls its read handler:

c->close = 1; c->read->handler(c->read);

1

2

c->close = 1;

c->read->handler(c->read);

My test client closed its socket with zero linger after completing the frame, leaving NGINX with an active request on a reset connection. When connection pressure triggered the drain, the HTTP/2 read handler tried to send GOAWAY on that socket.

A successful write would have left the request running, but the write failed with Connection reset by peer, so NGINX finalized the connection and request. The ASan free stack passes through ngx_http_upstream_check_broken_connection().

Request cleanup reaches ngx_resolve_name_done(), which frees the resolver state while the original lookup still holds a pointer to it.

In ngx_resolve_name_locked(), the DNS send runs before timeout setup. The send can drain the connection and free ctx. When the send returns, timeout setup uses the stale pointer, as the code below shows:

if (ngx_resolver_send_query(r, rn) != NGX_OK) { /* immediately retry once on failure */ rn->last_connection++; if (rn->last_connection == r->connections.nelts) { rn->last_connection = 0; } (void) ngx_resolver_send_query(r, rn); } if (ngx_resolver_set_timeout(r, ctx) != NGX_OK) { goto failed; }

ASan reported that NGINX read memory from a freed DNS lookup context. The free path ran through ngx_drain_connections(), ngx_http_v2_finalize_connection(), ngx_http_upstream_finalize_request() and ngx_resolve_name_done(). Source review showed that, if execution continues past the reported read, ngx_resolver_set_timeout() can also write ctx->event and ctx->ident through that stale pointer.

In the run where ASan reported the read, I split the 9-byte HEADERS frame header after 5 bytes. For the control, I sent the full frame header first and then the HPACK block. NGINX sent a DNS query and kept running. Figure 2 follows the calls from socket allocation to the use-after-free.

Test Setup and Limits

I ran the ASan test in an isolated Debian 13 guest. NGINX was built from official 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 source with Clang 19.1.7, HTTP/2, ASan and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. I sent the HTTP/2 requests over the guest's loopback interface.

For the 1.31.8 run, I set worker_connections to 16 and opened 13 filler connections that NGINX had not marked reusable. Table 1 shows the sanitizer results alongside the released-source review.

Test

Builds

Result

ASan

1.31.7, 1.31.8 (tested before the HTTP/2 fix)

Read from freed resolver state during request-time DNS setup

Source review

Released NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 source

Clears the reusable mark when NGINX creates an HTTP/2 stream

Table 1. HTTP/2 use-after-free tests and source review.

Tested Conditions

Table 2 lists the conditions I used in the 1.31.8 ASan test.

Tested Path

Key Conditions

Resolver socket

Split HEADERS frame header, worker_connections set to 16, 13 filler connections, a variable upstream hostname, a new resolver UDP socket and an abortive client close

Table 2. Conditions used in the 1.31.8 ASan test.

Limits

A source build includes the HTTP/2 module only when configured with --with-http_v2_module. Distribution packages commonly enable it.

The ASan evidence in this article comes from builds of 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 over loopback. The 1.31.8 test configuration set worker_connections to 16 instead of the documented default of 512, and ran NGINX with master_process off. The sanitizer aborted that single process. The public fix commit also names upstream connection setup as a drain trigger.

Two-VM Demonstration

The two-VM demonstration combined CVE-2026-123633 with the separate memory disclosure mentioned in the Background section. The target ran NGINX 1.31.8 with a root master and a www-data worker under a non-default configuration. Figure 3 records the running processes, version, loaded configuration path and listener.

The first attempt from the attacker VM recovered a libc address but did not open a shell; the second opened an interactive shell as www-data. The shell's hostname, IP address and boot ID match the target screenshot. Figure 4 previews the accompanying recording, which shows the same session with waiting periods sped up.

Video 1 shows the session:

Video 1. Demonstration of the attacker VM session and the interactive shell opened on the target.

Detection and Hunting

In the ASan test, NGINX logged a connection-drain warning before the sanitizer aborted the process. The warning can also appear under ordinary connection pressure, while a worker exit can have unrelated causes. A release build may keep running after reading freed memory. Table 3 lists investigation leads for HTTP/2 reverse proxies.

Signal

What I Saw in Testing

What to Check

Unexpected NGINX process exit

ASan aborted the single-process NGINX test after NGINX read freed memory.

Investigate unexpected worker exits in production near HTTP/2 requests and connection pressure. A worker exit on its own is weak evidence of exploitation.

Connection pressure with request-time DNS

NGINX logged "16 worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections" at warn level during the ASan test.

Correlate the warning with resolver traffic and connection pressure on routes that resolve at request time. The warning and DNS traffic can also occur under ordinary load.

Table 3. Signals to use in detection and hunting.

The warning in Table 3 is logged at most once per second per worker, so one line can cover several drain calls. Because NGINX defaults to the error log level (which omits warnings), configure error_log at the warn level (or a level that captures more detail, such as notice or info), then correlate the warning with traffic and worker state.

Exposure Review

CVE-2026-123633 describes a use-after-free in HTTP/2 reverse proxies that are running low on worker connections. The path I reproduced used a variable proxy_pass hostname, a configured resolver and a new UDP socket. F5's CVE description covers a broader set of HTTP/2 reverse proxies.

Check the running configuration. A master process can select another file with -c, so check its command line before assuming that the packaged path is the live one. The command nginx -T prints the on-disk configuration, which can still differ from what the running workers loaded.

I only tested proxy_pass. Operators should also review variable targets in:

grpc_pass

fastcgi_pass

uwsgi_pass

scgi_pass

For a matching route, check the running build and how close the worker gets to its connection limit. I tested one DNS socket route, but upstream connection setup also allocates through ngx_get_connection(), so static upstream routes still need review.

Mitigations

NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 fix the HTTP/2 issue. No workaround is listed in the CVE-2026-123633 record. If an upgrade must wait, the following changes could reduce exposure:

Where the service allows it, disable HTTP/2 on exposed listeners. Check every relevant listen ... http2 parameter and, on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, any http2 on; setting in the http or server context. Either setting can keep HTTP/2 enabled. Disabling HTTP/2 can break gRPC clients and may increase connection use if other traffic falls back to HTTP/1.1. If HTTP/2 stays enabled on other listeners, the extra HTTP/1.1 connections can push the same worker closer to its worker_connections limit.

Raising worker_connections gives the worker more headroom under the same traffic, but an attacker can still exhaust the extra slots and the connection-state bug remains.

Test each change before deployment. After upgrading, confirm the running worker uses a binary containing the CVE-2026-123633 fix. A configuration reload (nginx -s reload) keeps the old binary running in memory, so perform a full restart or live binary upgrade.

Conclusion

The defect starts when an HTTP/2 connection stays marked reusable after a request begins. In my test, opening a DNS socket under connection pressure drained that live connection and freed resolver state that the request still used. ASan reported that NGINX read memory after it had been freed.

Defenders should identify affected HTTP/2 reverse proxies, look for worker exits around connection pressure, and install a fixed NGINX release or vendor backport. My resolver test shows one way to reach the use-after-free. F5's description covers HTTP/2 reverse proxies more broadly.

Palo Alto Networks Protection and Mitigation

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products:

Cortex XDR and XSIAM are designed to detect and block post-exploitation activity, including server and process exploitation, by leveraging Behavioral Threat Protection, machine learning-driven Local Analysis, and cloud-based malware inspection to prevent the execution of both known and unknown threats.

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security is designed to help discover every AI artifact and AI agent's activity across the agentic endpoint, assess its risk, enforce prevention and runtime controls and remediate violations.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

Research dates in the timeline come from my notes; release dates come from the NGINX changelog.

Vendor impact statement for CVE-2026-123633: F5 says the HTTP/2 use-after-free may cause a denial of service on an affected NGINX system when connection slots run low. F5 also says code execution may be possible if ASLR is disabled or bypassed. The CVE-2026-123633 record has the full vendor description.

Indicators of Compromise

This research produced no confirmed indicators of compromise. Treat the items below as leads for investigating CVE-2026-123633 alongside the running build and HTTP/2 traffic.

Unexpected shell processes running as the NGINX worker account when investigating suspected code execution

Unexpected NGINX process termination near HTTP/2 traffic and connection pressure

Connection-drain warnings containing "worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections"; check the running worker_connections value when interpreting them

articles.title: 'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc
Socket Releases Free Patches for 100% of Critical CVEs in RubyGems
articles.context: Earlier this month, we released a free security fix for a critical Rails Active Storage vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9
articles.full_text:
We've completed security patches for 100% of patchable critical-severity CVEs in the RubyGems ecosystem, and we're making those fixes available to everyone for free. Developers can now remediate these vulnerabilities without upgrading their existing dependency versions, even when an upstream fix requires a breaking change.

The milestone follows an intensive engineering sprint focused on expanding RubyGems patch coverage. During the effort, our team also made substantial improvements to the systems used to generate, test, validate, and publish security fixes.

Socket identifies six critical vulnerabilities with available patches in a sample Ruby project.

Fixing Vulnerabilities Without Dependency Upgrades #

Upgrading to a secure upstream version is generally the simplest way to address a vulnerability. But upgrades aren't always straightforward, particularly for applications that depend on older versions of libraries.

Some Ruby applications have been running for a decade or longer and still serve important functions. Their dependencies may have been abandoned, or upgrading to a supported version may require substantial changes to the application itself. In some cases, a compatible upstream fix simply doesn't exist.

Socket Certified Patches provide another option. We develop targeted security fixes for the dependency versions developers already use, often by backporting fixes from newer releases. These changes address the vulnerable code while preserving the package version and minimizing changes to its existing behavior.

For applications that depend on abandoned libraries, this can extend the useful life of software that might otherwise need to be replaced or extensively rewritten. For actively maintained applications, patches allow teams to remediate known vulnerabilities without having to coordinate an immediate dependency upgrade. They can continue upgrading on their own schedule, with time to test compatibility and address breaking changes.

Security patches don't replace the benefits of ongoing dependency maintenance. Upstream releases still provide bug fixes, new features, and compatibility improvements. But a vulnerability doesn't necessarily have to dictate when an application undergoes a larger upgrade, and in some cases, a targeted patch may be the most practical long-term solution.

Earlier this month, we released a free security fix for a critical Rails Active Storage vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9.8). The vulnerability could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files through specially crafted uploads and, under certain configurations, potentially achieve remote code execution.

Our patch gives applications affected by the vulnerability an alternative to immediately upgrading Rails. Developers can apply the security fix to their existing dependency while planning and testing a broader upgrade separately.

The RubyGems coverage milestone extends this approach across the ecosystem's patchable critical vulnerabilities.

New Hosted and Vendored Delivery Options #

We've also expanded the ways developers can install remediated packages. Previously, Socket's patching workflow primarily involved modifying dependency files after installation. Our new hosted and vendored modes integrate directly with existing package management workflows.

Hosted mode lets developers install remediated gems through Bundler. The socket-patch CLI updates the lockfile to reference patched packages served through patch.socket.dev and, when necessary, adds source: settings to the affected gem declarations in Gemfile. The dependency versions remain unchanged, and Bundler installs the patched gems through its normal installation process.

Vendored mode stores the remediated packages directly in the application's repository under .socket/vendor/. Subsequent installations use those local packages without contacting Socket's infrastructure.

Vendored patches are yours to keep. They stay in your repository and go wherever your application goes, even if you stop using Socket.

Neither mode requires an installation hook or the Socket CLI on build machines. Once the dependency changes are committed, developers can continue installing their dependencies normally.

Both options preserve the existing dependency version. They also eliminate the need to run a separate patching step after every dependency installation. Developers can continue using the original in-place patching mode if they prefer that workflow.

These delivery options are particularly useful for organizations that need to control how dependencies enter their build environments or cannot introduce a new step into existing CI/CD pipelines.

We recently expanded support for Ruby gems containing native extensions as well. With socket-patch CLI 5.1.0, native extensions are rebuilt after patching, allowing us to remediate vulnerabilities in packages such as nokogiri, where a source-level change alone would not update the compiled code that applications execute.

Socket's dashboard provides instructions for obtaining a security patch for a critical Nokogiri vulnerability without upgrading the dependency.

Testing Security Fixes Against Existing Package Behavior #

A successful security patch needs to eliminate the vulnerability without introducing regressions elsewhere in the package.

Our validation process includes reproducing the vulnerability against the original dependency and verifying that the same exploit fails after patching. We also run regression tests, differential tests comparing the original and patched versions, compatibility checks against supported runtimes, and performance benchmarks.

We've expanded this testing to include downstream dependents, allowing us to exercise patches against software that actually relies on the affected library. This helps identify compatibility problems that may not be exposed by the package's own test suite.

Developers can inspect individual patches and their verification results on Socket, including test outcomes, exploit validation, performance measurements, and the code changes made.

These checks are especially important when backporting fixes into older library versions. A change that works correctly in the latest upstream release may depend on other changes introduced in the intervening years. Those differences must be accounted for before publishing a patch for an older release.

Some Vulnerabilities Require Different Remediation #

Our 100% critical-CVE coverage applies to vulnerabilities that can be safely patched. We generally consider three types of vulnerabilities unpatchable:

Malicious packages: The correct remediation is to remove the malicious dependency, not attempt to repair it.

Misattributed vulnerabilities: An advisory may identify a package that doesn't contain the vulnerable code because the vulnerability actually exists in another dependency. In those cases, we focus on fixing the package that contains the vulnerability.

Breaking changes: Some vulnerabilities are inherent to a package's design or public interface. Fixing them would require incompatible changes, potentially making dependency replacement or reachability analysis necessary.

We evaluate these cases individually and can make exceptions for particularly serious vulnerabilities where a breaking change may be warranted. Our current assessment is that roughly 95% of RubyGems CVEs are patchable under these criteria.

Free Critical CVE Patches Are Available Now #

All Socket patches for critical-severity CVEs are free, including for developers and organizations without a Socket account or paid subscription.

To get started, install the standalone socket-patch CLI:

curl -fsSL https://install.socket.dev/patch | sh

From a Ruby project's root directory, preview the available fixes without modifying any files:

socket-patch scan --dry-run

To apply patches in the default hosted mode and install the remediated gems:

socket-patch scan bundle install

Alternatively, use vendored mode to store the patched packages in the repository:

socket-patch scan --mode vendored bundle install

The CLI identifies available security fixes for the specific dependency versions in the project and reports which vulnerabilities they address. Patches for high-, medium-, and low-severity vulnerabilities are available through Socket's Enterprise plan.

For more information about patch validation, delivery options, and supported package managers, see our Certified Patches documentation and installation guide.

We're continuing to expand RubyGems coverage across all severity levels while improving our ability to generate, validate, and distribute security fixes. The free critical patches are available now.

articles.title: VMware Updates Patch Critical ESX, vCenter Vulnerabilities
articles.context: Broadcom on Tuesday announced the release of patches for 23 vulnerabilities across multiple VMware products, including critical-severity flaws in ESX and vCenter
articles.full_text:
Broadcom on Tuesday announced the release of patches for 23 vulnerabilities across multiple VMware products, including critical-severity flaws in ESX and vCenter.

The vCenter patches resolve seven bugs, including a critical authentication bypass issue in the VMware Directory Service tracked as CVE-2026-123903 (CVSS score of 9.8).

Additionally, the fixes target three denial-of-service (DoS) issues in the VMware Directory Service, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS).

The ESX updates resolve seven security issues as well, including three critical-severity weaknesses leading to code execution on the host.

CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911 (CVSS score of 9.8) are heap out-of-bounds write and use-after-free flaws in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123912 (CVSS score of 9.3) is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the XHCI USB controller that requires local administrative privileges on a virtual machine.

An attacker “may exploit this issue to execute code as the virtual machine’s VMX process running on the host. On ESX, the exploitation is contained within the VMX sandbox whereas, on Workstation and Fusion, this may lead to code execution on the machine where Workstation or Fusion is installed,” Broadcom explains.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The remaining four include a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a DoS vulnerability in guest RPC, a security bypass in the host configuration store, and a signature verification bypass.

Broadcom also patched eight flaws in Avi Load Balancer that could lead to code execution with root privileges, privilege escalation to root, command execution, password hash leaks, access to the routing management interface and other resources, and unintended file access, and one in VMware Tools leading to DoS.

According to Broadcom, some of the issues were resolved with the vCenter updates released last week. vCenter version 8.0 U3m contained the fixes, and customers who applied it do not need to update again. vCenter 9.1.x deployments, however, as well as ESX, VMware Tools, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer instances, need to be updated.

“Patches are cumulative, so the updates listed in this advisory also contain the fixes from VMSA-2026-0009 when they are newer than the fixed versions listed in VMSA-2026-0009. However, this advisory does not mention the SDDC Manager updates from VMSA-2026-0009; please ensure you are handling those,” the company notes.

Broadcom makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, but it’s not uncommon for the company to not warn about exploitation in its public advisories.

On Tuesday, Broadcom also updated its advisory on Node2Shell to add VMware Cloud Foundation version 9.1.2 to the list of fixed releases.

articles.title: From Vulnerability Noise to Resilience: Rethinking Security in the AI Era
articles.context: A high or critical Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score can command attention, but the business question is whether the vulnerable code is relevant and exploitable...
articles.full_text:
Written by: George Manuelian, Chief Strategy Officer, RapidFort

The modern software stack has become an iceberg. The application code customers and security teams see at the surface is only a small portion of what is being shipped. Beneath it sit operating systems, frameworks, libraries, packages, and transitive dependencies, with much of it drawn from open source or third parties.

As AI accelerates software development, that hidden complexity has become an even more critical security challenge.

For business and technology leaders, the question is no longer simply how many vulnerabilities exist. It is where does meaningful risk live, which vulnerabilities can be exploited in our environment, and how we can reduce that risk without turning developers into full-time vulnerability managers.

The answer requires a fundamental shift from vulnerability accumulation to continuous software resilience.

First step: Recognizing composition of modern software

The typical containerized stack is layers of base operating system software, packages, libraries, language frameworks and dependencies, and the application itself. The application a company writes may represent only a small portion of what it ultimately ships.

That is important because vulnerabilities multiply. A vulnerable package in a base image is not necessarily one vulnerability in practice; it can be replicated across every application and container that uses that image.

In light of this, executives should ask a different question of their security programs: How much of the reported risk is relevant to the way our software operates? Traditional scanning frequently identifies the presence of a vulnerable component without establishing whether that component is loaded, executing, reachable or exposed.

A software bill of materials (SBOM) identifies what exists; a runtime bill of materials (RBOM) can pinpoint what is actually being used. That distinction can dramatically reduce noise.

For example, in the real world from a customer, an NGINX image containing 152 packages and 48 CVEs had only 47 packages actually running in the application. More than 80% of the software was not being exercised. The lesson is not that every unused package is harmless, but that security teams need operational context before assigning remediation urgency.

This is also why severity alone has become an inadequate basis for prioritization. A high or critical Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score can command attention, but the business question is whether the vulnerable code is relevant and exploitable in the environment.

There are four contextual factors increasingly shaping remediation decisions: Whether a vulnerability is exposed, whether it is a known exploited vulnerability, whether exploitation is automatable, and whether exploitation would have meaningful technical impact.

The shift from severity to exploitability and reachability is important because it changes the operating model. Instead of asking engineering teams to chase the largest number on a scanner dashboard, leaders should ask whether the organization has enough visibility to determine what is running, what is reachable, and what is exposed.

As a result, security becomes a business-risk exercise rather than a race to close tickets.

Eliminate Up to 99.9% of Container CVEs Without Code Changes

RapidFort Curated Images give your team 35,000+ near-zero CVE container images, rebuilt and hardened every 24 hours.

Swap in a hardened base image and remove exploitable vulnerabilities at the source, with no code, OS or pipeline changes.

Learn More

Hardening is the important next step

Hardening should not mean merely passing a configuration benchmark. It should also mean removing software and functionality that the application does not need

. Every unnecessary library, shell, package manager, build utility, or default component increases the amount of software that must be maintained and potentially gives an attacker additional tools if a container is compromised.

Runtime profiling is a proven approach for identifying these unused components and removing them systematically.

AI makes this discipline more important

AI-assisted development can rapidly generate code and pull in packages, but developers may not always know which dependencies were introduced or whether they remain necessary as the application evolves.

For example, a development environment in which developers may have to ask the AI system which Python version or packages were used because the model generated much of the implementation is a warning sign for governance.

Speed of development cannot come at the expense of knowing what is being shipped.

No one is going to slow AI development. The answer is to put security controls into the pipeline so developers do not have to perform every security task manually. Clean, curated base images; runtime profiling; removal of unused components; vulnerability context; and automated rebuilding can become repeatable parts of CI/CD.

The objective is to make the secure path the default path.

Introducing Zero Trust software architecture

Zero Trust has traditionally been associated with network access and identity. But when organizations continuously ingest open source and third-party software, they also need to question the software entering their environments.

Software should be verified, trusted components should be maintained in controlled registries, and the software should be continuously evaluated as it moves through development, testing and production – following the common principles of Zero Trust.

This represents a meaningful change in how software supply chain security should be managed. The goal should not be a perfect vulnerability dashboard.

The goal should be a development system that continuously produces software with less unnecessary code, fewer meaningful vulnerabilities, and a smaller attack surface.

For example, one customer reduced an initial 5,286 findings to three unresolved vulnerabilities within 48 hours by combining profiling, curated images, and removal of unused components.

The strategic lesson learned

Vulnerability remediation should become a manufacturing process, not a recurring emergency. If organizations wait until a scanner produces a massive backlog, they have already allowed complexity to become technical debt.

If instead they control what enters the software supply chain, understand what actually runs, prioritize based on reachability and impact, remove what is unnecessary, and continuously rebuild from cleaner components, security becomes part of software production itself.

This approach also changes the conversation between security and engineering. Developers should not be expected to fix every finding simply because a scanner found it. They need context, automation and a clear understanding of which risks require action.

Security leaders need visibility into runtime behavior and the ability to distinguish a theoretical exposure from a vulnerability that can actually affect the business.

The future of software security in the AI era

The future of software security belongs to organizations that manage complexity continuously. AI will accelerate development, it’s a given. Open source will remain foundational, that’s understood. Neither trend is going away, nor should it of course.

But both make it more important to establish disciplined software intake, strong supply-chain controls, runtime visibility, effective hardening, and automated remediation.

Ultimately, the objective is not simply to reduce the number of CVEs on a report. It is to build software that contains less unnecessary functionality, relies on cleaner components, exposes fewer opportunities to attackers, and can be continuously refreshed without overwhelming those responsible for delivering it

. Software supply chain security works best when profiling, verification, clean images, and removal of unused components are built directly into the pipeline.

The executive mandate for the AI era must stop treating vulnerability management as a downstream cleanup exercise. Build security into the way software is assembled, tested and deployed.

When continuous remediation becomes part of the normal development life cycle, organizations can move faster without accepting vulnerability volume as an unavoidable cost of innovation.

Eliminate Attack Vectors at the Source. Contact us today to find out more.

articles.title: Astelia blocks attack paths to vulnerabilities without waiting for patches
articles.context: Astelia has announced autonomous network mitigation, a new capability that defends against AI-driven exploits by blocking attack paths to reachable vulnerabilities at the...
articles.full_text:
Astelia has announced autonomous network mitigation, a new capability that defends against AI-driven exploits by blocking attack paths to reachable vulnerabilities at the network level. Organizations can now eliminate the 1% of vulnerabilities attackers can reach without waiting for a patch.

The mitigation workflow · 6 steps, 1 approval branch (Source: Astelia)

Frontier AI models have cut the time to exploit to almost zero. Manual triage and remediation can’t keep up, so organizations need to automate how they respond. Autonomous remediation has become the industry’s latest buzzword, but it isn’t a viable option for large enterprises, where every patch needs a change window so it doesn’t break important business processes. Often, there is no patch to apply at all because the vendor hasn’t released a fix yet, or, for older and end-of-life systems, never will.

Blocking threats at the network level avoids both problems and keeps pace with AI-driven exploits. Instead of changing the vulnerable system, Astelia blocks the path an attacker would use to reach it, automatically and within policies the organization sets, without waiting for a ticket or a change window. Nothing on the asset changes, so business-critical systems, including OT, stay online. It works whether or not a patch exists.

This approach is built on Astelia’s reachability analysis. Astelia maps the organization’s real network topology and uses agentic AI to analyze what each exploit requires. By correlating those exploit conditions with the topology, it determines which vulnerabilities attackers can reach, and through which paths. In one enterprise deployment, approximately 40 million vulnerabilities came down to fewer than 2,000 that were reachable.

For each reachable vulnerability, Astelia uses the same topology to find the most effective choke point on the attack path, then drives the mitigation there through the organization’s WAF or IPS/IDS. A single rule at that point protects every vulnerable server behind it, where patching would take one change per server. Because Astelia only mitigates paths it has proven reachable, it doesn’t add rules for exposure that doesn’t exist. Initial support covers WAF and IPS/IDS rules, with firewall rules planned.

Unlike a patch, which can break a system and can’t always be undone, every mitigation Astelia applies can be rolled back, so teams can act quickly without putting business operations at risk.

Each organization sets the guardrails. Through Astelia Agents, teams set up a dedicated autonomous network mitigation agent that applies mitigations on its own within the policies they define, and connect it to their other agents to respond to urgent threats such as zero-days and critical disclosures like the PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws of October 2026, which left end-of-life PHP servers with no official fix.

Teams can require human approval for specific environments or actions, and every action is logged and auditable. Astelia’s analysis continues to run on read-only integrations, and mitigation actions use scoped permissions that each organization enables and controls.

“For years, security teams have been told to patch faster,” said Alon Noy, CEO of Astelia. “That advice stops working when the exploit arrives before the change window does. The same network data that tells us a vulnerability is reachable tells us where to cut it off, so we block it there automatically and the exposure is closed before an attacker can use it.”

articles.title: New Shirudo tool uses AI to shield unpatched Linux systems from exploits
articles.context: OpenAI and Cisco launched an open-source Linux security tool named Shirudo that deploys temporary runtime protections to block vulnerability exploitation while administrators...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI and Cisco launched an open-source Linux security tool named Shirudo that deploys temporary runtime protections to block vulnerability exploitation while administrators prepare and roll out patches, without restarting services.

Shirudo leverages the eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) mechanism in Linux to monitor for suspicious activity and deploy targeted protections called "shields."

eBPF is a Linux technology that lets programs run in a controlled environment within the operating system's kernel without modifying its source code or requiring a restart.

It enables real-time monitoring of system and network activity, performance analysis, and enforcement of targeted security protections, making it an ideal operational basis for Shirudo.

Shirudo’s shields aim to block malicious behavior in a targeted way, leaving legitimate application operations undisturbed. OpenAI highlights four core capabilities for the tool:

Live protection: Blocks vulnerable code paths without restarting systems, letting operators assess shield impact before enforcing them.

AI-assisted defense: Enables agents to investigate vulnerabilities, develop shields, and validate their effectiveness, with deployment remaining under human control.

Trusted deployment: Uses cryptographic signatures, Linux's eBPF verifier, and kernel security controls to prevent unauthorized modifications.

Hardware-backed verification: Uses Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) to provide verifiable records of shields being loaded or removed.

OpenAI and Cisco researchers tested custom-generated shields and demonstrated that they could successfully block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without interrupting its operation.

Marcus Hutchins, principal threat researcher at managed detection and response company Expel, says that while there is "genuinely so much runtime exploit mitigation potential with eBPF," it may not be a good idea to let AI agents write rules that could impact the kernel.

He also noted that the tool's "capabilities are limited to Linux because Mac/Windows haven't implement the components needed to be effective."

Researchers at Isovalent, a cloud networking and security company acquired by Cisco in 2024, explain that "Shirudo is a rewrite of Tetragon," an open-source eBPF-based runtime security platform the company introduced in 2022, which also serves as the foundation for Cisco's existing Live Protect technology.

Shirudo is designed for agentic control plane, and a configurable degree of autonomy when it comes to deploying mitigations. Isovalent says the tool isn’t limited to eBPF and can also modify application or userspace runtime bytecode to extend protection where needed.

When a shield is deployed, they also provide operators with hit counts, giving them insight into attempted exploits and where defenses need strengthening.

The two companies plan to provide “ready-to-use” mitigations in the form of tested shields, along with vulnerability disclosures, until patching is possible. Shields will be distributed as cryptographically signed ‘.bee’ packages through an OCI registry.

Isovalent says that Shirudo can be activated through a command-line interface and doesn’t require a daemon to run permanently on the machine.

"The Shirudo project is only the beginning, but it already shows the true potential of combining agents as a workforce with machine interfaces to let agents output what they are best at: code," the researchers say.

They expect the tool to evolve and other projects to emerge around it, to the point of building self-defending that can run applications and agents side by side.

Shirudo is open-source (BSD + GPL) and comes with a quick-start guide as well as "getting started" documentation from Isovalent.

In a deep-dive webinar on December 15, OpenAI will provide a technical rundown of how the tool works and how it combines eBPF and artificial intelligence to detect and counter new attacks.
