articles.title: Attackers exploited an Azure API Management flaw to steal secrets, Microsoft warns
articles.context: Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised.

Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer.

The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.”

The potentially exposed information includes secrets stored in Named Values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs, the report added.

Microsoft warned that its mitigation does not invalidate previously compromised credentials and that affected customers must rotate potentially exposed secrets and investigate suspicious activity. The advisory said only the Classic tiers of the service are affected, not Azure API Management v2, the report added.

The potential exposure was not limited to a theoretical security risk. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an operational environment.

Norway tells customers to assume exposure

In a security advisory published November 20 and updated November 23, NSM said an unidentified actor had actively targeted access tokens, secrets, and Named Values stored in Azure API Management.

“Earlier this week, NSM became aware of a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) that affects several Norwegian businesses,” NSM said in the advisory, translated from Norwegian.

It said the vulnerability should now be closed, but asked organizations to take measures anyway.

“Anyone with Azure API Manager must assume that their secrets and named values ​​are out of whack,” the advisory added. “This means that the business must roll back all tokens and secrets.”

In the advisory, NSM’s director of operational cybersecurity, Martin Albert-Hoff, said the vulnerability was first discovered by Norway’s energy sector. The agency identified Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations and said the vulnerability had also affected organizations in other countries and sectors.

Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems on November 17. In an update published November 20, the company said the attack had been stopped, production was running normally, and there was no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

A day later, Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or production and that there was no indication that information had been compromised.

NSM warned that public disclosure of the vulnerability could encourage additional threat actors to attempt exploitation.

“When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors may attempt to exploit it,” the agency said in its advisory (translated from Norwegian), adding that the rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence was affecting the threat environment.

Neither Microsoft’s advisory nor NSM’s notice includes a CVE identifier for the flaw.

Urgent need to rotate credentials

Microsoft’s mitigation closed the unauthorized management-plane access path, but it advised customers to investigate whether their APIM instances were accessed before the fix and whether stored credentials could have been exposed, the report added.

In a November 21 post on its Azure Integration Services blog, Microsoft published guidance on identifying and rotating credentials configured in Azure API Management.

The guidance covers subscription keys, Named Values containing secrets, backend credentials, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect client secrets, connection strings, and credentials written directly into API policies.

Microsoft recommended that organizations rotate credentials at the systems where they were originally issued, rather than simply updating their values in APIM.

“Updating the value in API Management alone does not invalidate the old credential,” the company said in the blog post, as per the report.

NSM has issued more extensive recommendations, advising organizations using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and Named Values may have been exposed and to rotate all associated tokens and secrets.

The agency also published a patch check. According to NSM, instances on the 0.52.x branch are patched from build 31936, and those on 0.53.x are from build 31938. V2 and Consumption tier instances are not vulnerable, the agency said.

Organizations with unpatched instances should contact Microsoft directly, and those that see signs of compromise should contact NSM, the advisory said.

Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen, who published detection and hunting guidance after the advisories, said patching alone is not enough.

“If you run APIM, patching isn’t the end of it,” Kristiansen wrote in a blog post.

His rotation list includes backend credentials, app registration secrets, subscription keys, the Key Vault secrets the service references, and tenant access keys. Microsoft did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Azure API Management Classic Flaw as Actor Targets Customer Secrets
articles.context: "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been
articles.full_text:
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

"An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said. "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been."

The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses.

According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected.

"On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory.

"Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."

As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include -

Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers

Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers

Subscription keys

Tokens used to call direct management APIs

As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."

NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

articles.title: Elecbrakes Bluetooth Vulnerabilities Expose Trailers to Forced Braking
articles.context: Researchers from Australian IT and cybersecurity consultancy Element Digital — with help from AI — discovered three vulnerabilities in the braking controllers, including two...
articles.full_text:
Vulnerabilities discovered in Bluetooth-enabled brake controllers made by Australian firm Elecbrakes could allow hackers to manipulate trailer brakes, potentially causing accidents, researchers warned.

The affected products include the EB2, VM1 and ELBC 2000 brake controllers from Elecbrakes. According to the cybersecurity agency CISA, which last week published an advisory on the vulnerabilities, the affected brake controllers are mainly used in Australia and New Zealand.

The controllers regulate the braking force applied to trailers, with the EB2 unit mounted on the trailer and the VM1 unit on the towing vehicle. The devices can be controlled remotely via a special remote or a smartphone app.

Researchers from Australian IT and cybersecurity consultancy Element Digital — with help from AI — discovered three vulnerabilities in the braking controllers, including two critical missing authentication and insufficient replay-attack protection issues.

They demonstrated that an unauthenticated attacker who is within Bluetooth range of the targeted vehicle (up to 100 meters or 328 feet) can use a laptop or phone to engage or release a trailer’s brakes or adjust the braking force, without any interaction required from the victim.

“Your trailer’s brakes slamming to maximum while your tow vehicle keeps going is the exact recipe for a jackknife – one of the more reliably fatal things a vehicle combination can do,” the researchers warned.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The third vulnerability is a medium-severity issue related to the firmware update mechanism. Unauthorized firmware changes could enable persistent compromise of the controller, allowing an attacker to interfere with braking, brake lights, and other safety functions. However, the researchers noted that this risk is theoretical, as they did not demonstrate the full impact or attempt to install malicious firmware during their tests.

Elecbrakes was notified about the findings in mid-May and released firmware updates with patches in early July for its EB2 and VM1 products. Element Digital disclosed technical details last week.

Once the firmware patches are installed, an attacker can no longer access the brake controllers remotely without an initial pairing that requires physical access to the device and cannot be performed over Bluetooth.

The vendor is still working on a remediation plan for the older ELBC 2000 product. In a customer advisory published on Monday, Elecbrakes advised owners of the older ELBC controllers to maintain an active connection between the controller and their smartphone or wireless remote whenever the device is in use.

Elecbrakes told iTnews that nearly 40,000 app users had initially been alerted to the availability of the update, and that it had been installed on 60-70% of controllers used to connect to the system daily.

There is no evidence of malicious exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

While the researchers praised Elecbrakes for quickly developing patches, they criticized the company over the lengthy disclosure process and its failure to initially identify the older ELBC 2000 as being affected.

articles.title: WHMCS SQL Injection Could Expose Customer Data and Admin Password Hashes without Login
articles.context: Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8
articles.full_text:
A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed.

The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three.

Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet.

The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline.

The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time.

Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release.

Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation.

The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says.

The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700, lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says.

It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails.

All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon.

For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to:

Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu.

Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache.

Update to a fixed release.

The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough.

This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory, and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory.

articles.title: Patching vCenter Zero-Day Is Only Step One
articles.context: 20, 2026 ThreatDefence, VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 Zero-Day: Patching and Hunting The Cyber Sec Guru, How ARMORY CASTLE Used a vCenter Zero-Day to Reach ESXi Rescana, VMware...
articles.full_text:
CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter's directory service, rated 9.8 out of 10. An attacker who can reach vCenter on the network can become administrator@vsphere.local without a password. A suspected China-nexus espionage group, ARMORY CASTLE, exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. Broadcom patched it on Nov. 19, and CISA gave U.S. federal agencies until Nov. 23 to fix it.

Install the patch today. Then plan for the harder job. If anything that could reach your vCenter was compromised at any point since September, the patch closes the door but doesn't take back what went through it. In the intrusion researchers investigated, that included vCenter's SAML signing key, its master encryption key and Active Directory credentials copied straight out of virtual machine disks.

Let's see how the attackers used this flaw, which builds fix it, and the hunting and credential rotation that should follow the patch.

What Is CVE-2026-123890

Broadcom disclosed the flaw last week, in advisory VMSA-2026-0009, which fixes five vulnerabilities across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows. CVE-2026-123890 is the critical one. An authentication bypass using an alternate path (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service, the component behind vCenter's single sign-on. Mandiant found it and reported it privately.

The bug lives in a remote procedure call interface that vCenter's directory service exposes on TCP port 2012. Its Secure Remote Password login generates predictable identifiers based on timestamps, and according to researchers, an attacker can use that to recover the shared session key without knowing any password. The result is an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, the most powerful account in a vSphere environment.

From there, an attacker can run commands and copy files through the directory service, including data.mdb, the database that holds the SSO domain's accounts and the private key vCenter uses to sign SAML login tokens. It is not a virtual machine escape. It's worse in a different way - it hands over the console that manages every host and VM.

Two things make it easy to get wrong:

It's a different bug from CVE-2026-59309, the vCenter authentication bypass Broadcom fixed in July. Mandiant observed attackers using CVE-2026-123890 against a vCenter that was already patched for the July flaw.

There is no workaround. Broadcom's only fix is the update, which its own FAQ treats as an emergency change.

How ARMORY CASTLE used it from a support box to domain credentials

Mandiant's write-up shows why vCenter being reachable only from the internal network didn't protect it. The attackers never touched vCenter from the internet. They worked their way to it from the inside.

ARMORY CASTLE's path from a remote-support appliance to Active Directory credentials

Break in at the edge. The group, formerly tracked as UNC5221, first exploited a separate zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support, CVE-2026-102764.

Find the VMware estate. From the support appliance, it scanned the internal network for VMware ports, including 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080, then moved to internal Linux appliances that had no endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. It dropped two web shells and became root by setting the SUID bit on /bin/env with the gdb debugger.

Take vCenter. A custom Go tool Mandiant calls BONESAW exploited CVE-2026-123890 over port 2012, created a new SSO administrator account, copied the directory database and extracted the token-signing key.

Forge logins. A second tool, SAWSNAKE, used the stolen key to sign SAML tokens as the administrator, a "Golden SAML" attack that bypasses passwords and MFA.

Drop into the appliance. The group switched on SSH through vCenter's appliance management API, logged in with its new account, stole vCenter's master encryption key and its PostgreSQL database password, then switched SSH off again.

Reach the hosts and the domain. It logged in to ESXi hosts as vpxuser and root, added its own SSH key, and used a Python tool to extract the Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) and registry hives straight from a virtual machine's disk. The files left through the original support appliance.

Two backdoors kept the door open: BEARBONES, a modified Dropbear SSH server that accepts a hardcoded password, and LAZYBONES, which takes commands through Slack. The timing matters too. BONESAW's build timestamp is July 13, 2026, and the attackers used it in early September. Go build timestamps can be faked, but Mandiant reads it as a tool built for broader operations, not a one-off.

Which vCenter versions fix CVE-2026-123890?

Product line

Affected

Fixed in

vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.1

9.1.x

9.1.1.0200

vCenter in VCF / vSphere Foundation 9.0

9.0.x

9.0.2.0200

vCenter Server 8.0

8.0

8.0 U3m

VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x

5.x

5.2.5

vCenter Server 7.0

7.0

No public fix; extended-support customers go through Broadcom

Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure

Listed versions

See Broadcom KB463116

A few details that trip people up:

Patched in July doesn't mean patched now. Every vCenter below the builds in the table needs this update, including systems that already have the CVE-2026-59309 fix.

vCenter 7.0 is the hard case. vSphere 7.0 reached the end of general support on Oct. 2, 2025, so there's no public fix. Broadcom's supplemental FAQ also says to presume versions 6.5 and 6.7 are affected. If you're on any of these, restricting network access to port 2012 is your main protection until you can upgrade or obtain a fix.

ESXi isn't in the advisory. The flaw is in vCenter. ESXi hosts still matter for the cleanup, because the attackers used vCenter to reach them.

Don't run the GitHub "proof of concept." A repository that appeared on Nov. 20 claiming exploit code describes the wrong advisory and fixed versions. As of Nov. 21, Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module titled as an authentication bypass to root, so expect working public exploit code soon, if it isn't out already.

Why patching isn't enough

The patch fixes the login flaw. It does nothing about what an attacker took while the flaw was open, and in this case the stolen items are exactly the kind that keep working:

The token-signing key. Anyone holding vCenter's SAML signing key can mint valid administrator logins until that certificate is replaced. A patched vCenter will accept them.

New accounts. The attackers created an SSO administrator named sps- followed by random characters in vsphere.local. BONESAW can also add a machine account and grant Global Administrator rights on the vCenter root folder.

Appliance secrets. vCenter's master encryption key and PostgreSQL password were copied over SSH.

Host access. An SSH key was added to the ESXi root account.

Active Directory. A copy of NTDS.dit plus the SYSTEM hive is enough to recover the password hashes of every account in the domain, offline.

The exposure window also runs further back than most patch plans assume. Exploitation started in early September, more than 10 weeks before the fix. If any system that could reach your vCenter's management ports was compromised in that time, treat vCenter as possibly compromised too until you've checked.

After the patch: what to hunt for

Search logs back to at least early September 2026. These come from Mandiant's analysis; ARMORY CASTLE deletes its tools after use, so absence of files doesn't prove absence of compromise.

On the network

Connections to TCP 2012 on vCenter from anything other than your documented management hosts, especially Linux appliances or remote-support servers.

Internal scans for VMware ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080.

Servers calling the Slack API, and SSH services announcing the banner SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345, often on high, non-standard ports.

Traffic to the 11 suspected obfuscation-network IPs in GTIG's report, such as 103.147.251[.]5 and 176.9.89[.]66.

On vCenter

SSO accounts you didn't create, especially names starting with sps- in vsphere.local, and unexpected members of the Administrators group.

A PUT /rest/appliance/access/ssh call to the appliance management API, particularly SSH being enabled and disabled again shortly after.

SSH logins to the appliance, and reads of the master key or PostgreSQL password files.

On ESXi hosts

ESXi Host Client logins as vpxuser and root SSH sessions you can't explain.

New entries in root's authorized_keys.

Hidden directories such as .a on VMFS volumes, and the files vmfs-pydist.tar.gz or vmfs_browser.py.

On internal Linux appliances

The files /tmp/123 (BONESAW), /tmp/sss (SAWSNAKE), /tmp/dbr (BEARBONES), /tmp/123.key and /tmp/gdb_file.

/usr/bin/vmtoolscs (LAZYBONES) running as a systemd service that restarts every 50 minutes.

Web shells named ActiveSer.jsp or u.jsp, and the SUID bit set on /bin/env.

GTIG has published YARA rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES and both web shells in the same report.

After the patch: what to rotate and reset

If you find signs of compromise, or can't rule it out because logs don't reach back to September, work through this in order. Patch and lock down access first, or the attacker can simply take the new secrets too. These steps reflect the consensus among incident responders building on Mandiant's findings; follow Broadcom's knowledge base procedures for each vCenter task.

Patch, then close the paths in. Install the fixed build, patch BeyondTrust Remote Support if you run it, and restrict ports 2012, 443, 5480 and 22 on vCenter to named management hosts.

Rebuild what you can't trust. Where compromise is confirmed, rebuild vCenter and the affected Linux appliances rather than cleaning them. The attackers had root and deleted their tools as they went.

Replace the STS signing certificate. This is the step that kills forged SAML tokens, and no other step does. Plan for the knock-on effect: products that trust vCenter single sign-on may need to be re-registered. Afterwards, confirm that sessions created with the old key fail.

Reset vSphere identities. Reset administrator@vsphere.local and every other SSO and local account, remove accounts and Administrators-group members you didn't create, and rotate solution-user certificates, service-account passwords and third-party integration tokens tied to vsphere.local.

Clean up the hosts. Reset ESXi root passwords and remove any SSH keys you didn't add to authorized_keys.

Treat Active Directory as exposed if a domain controller ran there. If a domain controller's virtual disk sat on a host the attackers reached, assume every domain password hash was taken. That means resetting privileged and service accounts and resetting the krbtgt account twice, with time for replication in between, the standard response to a stolen NTDS.dit.

Step 6 is the one that turns a VMware incident into a company-wide one, so decide early whether it applies to you.

Harden the vCenter control plane

This is ARMORY CASTLE's second zero-day in one intrusion, and Mandiant's point is that patching alone can't keep up with that. Its hardening advice centers on making vCenter hard to reach and noisy when someone tries.

Don't rely on the built-in appliance firewall. Mandiant notes that the firewall managed through vCenter's appliance management interface can't restrict access port by port, so trusting a backup server for the API trusts it for SSH and management too. It's managed from the same interface an attacker would take over, it doesn't log blocked connections remotely, and it doesn't control outbound traffic.

Enforce rules below the application. Mandiant recommends its VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool, which applies default-deny iptables rules at the operating-system level, filters outbound traffic and forwards blocked connections and shell commands to a SIEM. By Mandiant's analysis, those rules would have blocked the exploit on port 2012, the forged logins on 443, the SSH pivot and the Slack command channel. Test any such rules under change control before production.

Close the visibility gaps. The attackers chose Linux appliances with no EDR as their staging ground. Inventory every appliance that can reach vCenter or ESXi, and get logs off them if you can't run an agent. Manage vSphere only from privileged access workstations, as set out in Mandiant's vSphere defender's guide.

Frequently asked questions

What is CVE-2026-123890?

CVE-2026-123890 is a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter Server. An attacker with network access to vCenter's TCP port 2012 can obtain an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local without a password. Broadcom fixed it on Nov. 19, 2026, in VMSA-2026-0009.

Is CVE-2026-123890 being exploited?

Yes. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE exploited it as a zero-day from early September 2026. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 20, 2026, with a Nov. 23 remediation deadline for federal agencies.

Which vCenter versions fix CVE-2026-123890?

vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m, and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5. vCenter 7.0 has no public fix; extended-support customers must go through Broadcom. There is no workaround.

I installed the July fix for CVE-2026-59309. Am I protected?

No. CVE-2026-123890 is a separate flaw, and Mandiant observed it being exploited against a vCenter already patched for CVE-2026-59309. You need the November builds.

Is there a public exploit for CVE-2026-123890?

As of Nov. 21, 2026, the attackers' tool hadn't been released, and a GitHub repository claiming a proof of concept was fake. Rapid7 had opened a Metasploit module, so working public exploit code is expected soon.

Is CVE-2026-123890 a VM escape? Do I need to patch ESXi?

No on both counts. The flaw is in vCenter, and ESXi isn't listed in the advisory. But an attacker who controls vCenter can reach every ESXi host it manages, so check your hosts during cleanup.

Know which flaws are being used before the advisory lands

CVE-2026-123890 was exploited for more than 10 weeks before it was disclosed, and it was reached through a second zero-day in a remote-support appliance. Defenders can't patch what hasn't been disclosed, but they can know which of their exposed systems sit in an attacker's path and act within hours when exploitation becomes public.

Cyble tracks vulnerability exploitation, threat-actor activity and exposed assets across the open, deep and dark web, so security teams can rank patching by what attackers are actually using, not just by CVSS score.

Talk to Cyble about vulnerability intelligence and see which of your assets are exposed to flaws under active exploitation.

Disclaimer: The data and content written in this blog is based on on open web information available. Analysts and researchers are advised to confirm once again from original sources.

articles.title: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
articles.context: The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software
articles.full_text:
OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime.

"It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X.

The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption.

The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software.

Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service.

The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation.

To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it.

"eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said. "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)."

Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations.

Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded.

"Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands."

This involves the following steps -

An agent is tasked with finding new vulnerabilities in an application, or working off external sources of new vulnerability disclosures.

Shirudo on the operator machine builds a security shield consisting of eBPF or application bytecode after reproducing and validating the exploit.

The shield is delivered as signed .bee packages via an OCI-compliant registry.

The Shirudo layer on each target pulls these .bee packages, validating each signature using TPMs to establish trust and safety.

In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said.

OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed.

"We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before."

"Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative."

articles.title: Hackers Exploit N-able MailAssure Flaw While AI Agents Exploit MONAI Label Zero-Day
articles.context: 8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory,...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The critical vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.

CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026.

As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored.

"N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity."

CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN, an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement.

The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China.

"In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step."

Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server.

"In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root."

Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network.

The attacks are part of a broader cluster of attacks involving the use of AI-driven frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, and AntiFox, and CyberStrikeAI in recent months. A subset of these activities is estimated to have breached over 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja. The end goals, per NorForge, revolve around establishing persistent access and financial theft -

AIA0001, which has targeted organizations, mainly in the U.S., Japan, and Australia, to deploy web shells and gain access to e-commerce and payment infrastructure for subsequent monetization.

AIA0002, which has targeted merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites, pharmaceutical sites, and a criminal carding site for financial gain.

AIA0003, which has targeted smaller e-commerce sites and very large U.S.-based commercial platforms to obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access.

In a report published last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) also revealed that its MadPot sensor network captured requests from AI agents linked to two offensive campaigns running on ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework.

"The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting," AWS said. "Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection."

According to Datadog Security Labs, ARTEX also appears under other names like ScopeWeaver, LUCK — 自主资产控制台 (LUCK — Autonomous Asset Console), and 观澜SEC渗透测试平台 (Guanlan SEC Penetration Testing Platform).

In-the-wild activity involving ARTEX has also targeted several AWS environments with an aim to access financial data. Initial access vectors used in these attacks include compromised long-term AWS access keys and public Cognito user pools, with the latter being used to register an account, collect tokens, and enumerate AWS accounts.

"In one instance using a valid long-term access key, ARTEX's most frequent action was FilterLogEvents," security researcher Julie Agnes Sparks said. "The most common searches were various naming conventions of cryptocurrency companies, hedge funds, and related financial institutions. The terms combine a company name with words like fund, invoice, billing, and LLC."

Telemetry data gathered by Previdian from its sensors has recorded 52 HTTP requests containing explicit ARTEX markers between October 18 and November 15, 2026, from 10 source IP addresses.

"Further investigation of these sources identified 3,651 related HTTP records involving application discovery, authentication probing, remote code execution attempts, path traversal and attempts to retrieve sensitive configuration data," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, said.

"The most significant activity targeted Oracle WebLogic, Langflow, and Flowise, with additional payloads associated with Apache Struts, Log4j, and PHPUnit."

Interestingly, one of the IP addresses associated with ARTEX activity, 31.22.91[.]156, overlaps with the AWS-documented campaign targeting AI infrastructure, including Langflow exploitation attempts consistent with CVE-2025-3248.

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the latest fixes for the two flaws by November 26, 2026.

articles.title: ZDI-26-1159: X.Org Server PCF Font Parsing Out-Of-Bounds Read Information Disclosure Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of X.Org Server. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the BufFileRawSkip function. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a read past the end of an allocated data structure. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of root.

Additional Details

X.Org has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/xorg/lib/libxfont/-/commit/dc6c313071c8b2929b1bc165e40c8ba62737b576

articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of NVIDIA Megatron Bridge
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of NVIDIA Megatron Bridge. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of model metadata. The process does not properly restrict a user-supplied argument before using it to import a module. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code within the application container.

Additional Details

NVIDIA has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://nvidia.custhelp.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/5868

Disclosure Timeline

2026-06-03 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

articles.title: ZDI-26-1103: (Pwn2Own) NVIDIA GPU Display Drivers Video Encoder Improper Update of Reference Count Local Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system, even if only within a container, in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of NVIDIA GPU Display Drivers. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system, even if only within a container, in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of memory buffers in encode pipelines. A crafted IOCTL request can force the NVIDIA GPU driver to incorrectly update a reference count. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel on the target host system.

Additional Details

NVIDIA has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://nvidia.custhelp.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/5861

articles.title: ZDI-26-1046: (0Day) Texas Instruments Smart Amplifier Driver for Speakers Stack-based Buffer Overflow Local Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
articles.context: An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of Texas Instruments Smart Amplifier Driver for Speakers. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of IOCTL 0x00220450. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel.

articles.title: Microsoft Azure flaw exploited to steal customers' API credentials
articles.context: Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian authorities linking the flaw to cyberattacks against energy companies.

Azure API Management is a cloud service that lets organizations publish, secure, monitor, and manage APIs that connect applications, services, and data.

In an Azure Service Health security advisory (Tracking ID: MZK9-GH0) sent to customers and shared with BleepingComputer, Microsoft said it identified the vulnerability on November 18, 2026, and deployed a mitigation the following day.

"Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue," Microsoft said in the advisory.

According to Microsoft, the vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to certain management functionality when APIM Classic instances were not configured according to recommended security best practices.

This access could have allowed attackers to perform administrative operations, including accessing secrets stored in the service.

Microsoft said the following information may have been exposed:

Secrets stored in Named Values

Client secrets associated with identity providers

Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers

Subscription keys

Tokens used to call direct management APIs

These credentials could potentially allow attackers to access additional applications, services, or backend systems, depending on their permissions.

Microsoft said it closed the unauthorized access path on November 19 and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate.

However, the company warned that its remediation would not invalidate customer credentials that may have been compromised before the fix was deployed.

"This remediation blocks the unauthorized management-plane access path that could allow an actor to perform administrative operations, including secrets management, against Azure API Management services," Microsoft warned.

"However, it does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed."

The vulnerability affects Azure API Management Classic tiers, while Microsoft said APIM v2 tiers are not impacted.

Microsoft urged affected customers to immediately rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious activity in systems accessible through those credentials, and review available logs for signs of unauthorized access.

In a Reddit post, an administrator claimed their organization discovered the vulnerability after detecting unauthorized access to Azure Key Vault using a valid administrator token.

"Our company has been fighting this for days, after discovering that someone logged into our keyvaults using a valid administrator token and not following the normal access pattern," the administrator claimed.

The administrator alleged that attackers exploited a zero-day authentication bypass in a deprecated legacy API to gain access to a privileged system account on APIM instances.

According to the administrator, the legacy API did not generate logs that customers could use to detect the unauthorized access. They also alleged that Microsoft initially attributed the suspicious activity to leaked customer credentials before deploying a global fix.

BleepingComputer has not independently verified these allegations.

The vulnerability has also been linked to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

In a security advisory, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said an unknown threat actor targeted access tokens, secrets, and named values stored in Azure API Management.

The agency said Norway's energy sector first discovered the vulnerability and that organizations in other countries and industries were also affected.

Equinor disclosed an ongoing cyberattack on November 17, a day before Microsoft says it identified the APIM vulnerability. The company later announced that it had stopped the attack and found no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

Skagerak Energi also reported an attempted cyberattack but said it had no impact on its operations and no evidence that information was compromised.

While Microsoft says it deployed a remediation on November 19 that required no customer action, NSM's advisory warns organizations to verify that their APIM instances have received the security update.

The agency warns that instances running below specific runtime versions remain vulnerable and advises customers to contact their "service provider" if they have not received the update.

It is unclear whether the runtime updates are separate from Microsoft's initial mitigation.

Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen shared threat-hunting queries to help organizations investigate potential exploitation and identify credentials stored in their APIM instances.

BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the attacks but has not received a reply yet.

This Azure API Management incident comes just days after Microsoft confirmed another security breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, where attackers exploited a vulnerability to steal tenant configuration information and administrator email addresses.

articles.title: Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
articles.context: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any...
articles.full_text: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers. CVE-2026-76466, which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services. The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments. “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.” At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability. That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information. The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6. The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices. A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday. Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®

articles.title: Azure Flaw Exploited to Target Secrets at Norwegian Energy Firms
articles.context: The vulnerability may have allowed threat actors to gain access to secrets stored in some APIM instances
articles.full_text:
A security issue discovered in Microsoft’s Azure API Management (APIM) service appears to have been responsible for the security incidents reported last week by two Norwegian energy firms, with impact extending beyond Norway.

Microsoft is notifying customers about the issue in Azure APIM, which is designed for publishing, securing and managing APIs. The vulnerability may have allowed threat actors to gain access to secrets stored in some APIM instances.

According to a private notification shared on Reddit by one customer, the tech giant discovered the issue on November 18 and closed the access path the next day.

“Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue,” Microsoft said.

Exposed data can include secrets stored as named values, client secrets for identity providers, subscription keys, and tokens for APIM’s direct management APIs.

Microsoft noted that APIM Classic tiers that don’t follow its documented security guidance are affected. Instances on v2 tiers are not impacted.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said on November 20 that the vulnerability had affected several organizations in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi, which independently disclosed cybersecurity incidents last week.

Equinor reported the attack on November 17, one day before Microsoft identified the APIM flaw. The company said it found no evidence that data was stolen or altered. Skagerak Energi disclosed the incident on November 18, saying it did not impact operations or production, and it found no evidence of information compromise.

NSM said an unknown threat actor targeted tokens, secrets and named values stored in APIM. It’s unclear how widely the weakness has been exploited, but the organization noted that several sectors in Norway and abroad are impacted.

APIM users have been advised by NSM to treat their secrets and named values as compromised and replace them. They should also verify that their instances have been updated and identify the data accessible through the service.

Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that credentials lifted from APIM could be used against outside services. The extent of the exposure depends on each credential’s permissions.

articles.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: VMware 0-Day, Java4Shell, NGINX2Root, Ruby2Shell, and a Whole Lot of Shell Trouble
articles.context: ⚡ Threat of the Week Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been...
articles.full_text:
A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open.

This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need.

The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week.

⚡ Threat of the Week

Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines.

Is Your Workforce Secured from AI Threats?

Attackers now weaponize AI to launch personalized phishing attacks faster than employees can react. Fight AI with AI, using realistic simulations to train employees to spot and stop threats. Stop phishing before it becomes a breach.

Book a Demo ➝

🔔 Top News

Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks.

Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue.

New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.

GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser).

🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars

6,000 Social Engineering Attacks Reveal Why MFA Still Fails to Stop Account Takeovers → AI-powered phishing and voice scams are evolving, while attackers exploit weaker authentication and recovery paths to bypass MFA. Join this webinar to uncover real attack techniques and learn how to prevent account takeovers.

8 Million Security Events Reveal Why Attackers Can Hide Behind Tools You Already Trust → Attackers abuse legitimate IT tools to evade detection, but only about 12 in a million uses are malicious. Join this webinar to learn how to distinguish real threats from normal activity without drowning in alerts.

Your GitHub Actions Are SHA-Pinned. But Are They Actually Secure? → SHA pinning locks code to a commit, but doesn't verify its author or origin. Attackers can exploit this trust gap to sneak malicious code past security checks. Join this webinar to learn how impostor commits threaten CI/CD pipelines and how to defend against them.

📰 Around the Cyber World

Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities. Users are advised to log out of sessions when not required and avoid signing in using public computers.

A large-scale malvertising operation dubbed MoldyRoost that's leveraging advertising infrastructure to deliver iPhone exploit chain kits like Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath (iOS 17.2.2 to 18.3), and GhostWave (iOS 18.7.3 to 26) with an aim to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases, iCloud Keychain data, messages, and photos. "Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected," Confidant said. "The exploit runs while the landing page loads, with no decoy download or ClickFix-style command to paste. What MoldyRoost adds is expertise in distributing the exploit kits through malvertising." Only an iOS device running Safari is offered an exploit chain. Other devices are served a working decoy website, an empty frame, or a harmless landing page. More than 480 domains have been linked to the operation between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The activity has targeted over 47 countries, mainly Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, the U.S., South Korea, the U.K., and India.

The average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes in some cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Labs.

Unknown threat actors have siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire the funds to other banks, from where it was potentially converted into cryptocurrency. "The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms," the bank said, adding the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries.

Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's Attorney General puts the number of victims at 149,346. The access data includes images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.

Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the LAPSUS$ group, pleaded guilty in a U.K. court to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, BT, and Revolut, after being released from a secure hospital after he was deemed fit to stand trial. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to the severity of his autism.

Browser extensions associated with Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have been found to be rife with critical vulnerabilities rated 9.6 on the CVSS scoring system. These digital signing extensions are used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals. "All five make the same mistake, they let the website choose which DLL the vendor's native host loads," Bay Area Labs said. "Loading a DLL runs its code and the software built to verify signatures never checked the signature on the code it loaded and on Web PKI and CertiSign WebSigner, a malicious page or iframe, such as an ad, was enough, with no click. On Softplan Web Signer, opening a link was enough. On CertiPlugin and BRy, visiting the page was enough, and the page downloaded the payload automatically." The bug class has been codenamed Sign2Shell. The flaws could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names and potentially breach major organizations. The issues have since been fixed.

Anthropic has become the latest company to cut its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, as AI collapses bug discovery timelines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027.

Recovery from a ransomware attack takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims require more than six weeks. "Only 32% were recovered within two weeks and 28% took longer than six weeks," Rubrik said. "The full case, measured until the customer was content to close it, had a median of 26 days and 45% of cases stayed open for more than 30 days."

Fortra said it's tracking targeted, large-scale "mail bombing" attacks, followed immediately by IT support impersonation on Microsoft Teams. "In the attacks, individual users are being flooded with email, then contacted by the threat actor through Teams as the volume peaks," Fortra said. "In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both."

Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years in prison in the U.S. for his role in conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies' computer systems via smishing attacks and steal over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individual victims throughout the U.S. A member of the Scattered Spider group, Buchanan pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft in April 2026. He was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the U.S. in April 2025.

Igor Andreevich D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted in the U.S. for allegedly acting as a spy of a foreign government to "conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company." Although the name of the company was not disclosed, it's understood to be Palantir Technologies. D'iu was arrested on October 30, 2026. "The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. He is said to have entered the U.S. illegally through Mexico in June 2026 and was instructed by co-conspirators on Telegram to "identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked," as well as "include surveillance of company employees and their residences."

At least $247 million of the stolen funds from the record-breaking Binance hack has now gone into coinjoins coordinated by Kruw to obscure the financial trail, Elliptic has revealed. "Almost all of these coinjoins were coordinated by Kruw, the most widely used coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users," the company said. "A coordinator organizes each coinjoin round, bringing together the users taking part, but never takes custody of their funds." Last week, blockchain investigator ZachXBT accused Kruw of knowingly helping the Lazarus Group launder stolen cryptocurrency assets, calling the threat actor their "largest" user. Arkham Intelligence has also identified 2,173.76 BTC, roughly $154.45 million, flowing into CoinJoin from wallets connected to the $387 million Bitget hack of September 2025, also linked to North Korea. Kruw.io was also the subject of an advisory issued by the U.S. Secret Service in May 2025. "Numerous illicit actors use Kruw.io to launder funds including the Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking collective also known as АPТ38 and TraderTraitor which is subject to U.S. and international sanctions," the advisory said. "The Lazarus Group has previously used Kruw.io to mix approximately $14.3 million in cryptocurrency stolen by the North Korean regime. The Lazarus Group is currently laundering some proceeds of the $1.5 billion Bybit hack through the Kruw.io service."

Conclusion

The tricky part isn't always finding the problem. It's knowing how far it has already spread. A stolen login can lead to another company. A fixed bug can leave infected devices behind. And a tool that worked fine yesterday might be the reason someone gets in tomorrow. There isn't always a clean ending once the damage is done.

That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

[R1] Stand-alone Security Patch Available for Tenable Enclave Security Versions 1.7.1, 1.8.2, 1.9.2 Arnie Cabral Mon, 11/23/2026 - 09:06

Tenable Enclave Security leverages third-party software to help provide underlying functionality. Several of the third-party components (simpleSAMLphp, libcurl, OpenSSL, Apache HTTP Server, libssh2) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Out of caution and in line with best practice, Tenable has opted to upgrade these components to address the potential impact of the issues. This patch updates simpleSAMLphp to version 2.4.11, libcurl to version 8.23.0, OpenSSL to version 3.5.9, libssh2 to version 1.11.1, and Apache HTTP Server to version 2.4.69 to address the identified vulnerabilities.
