articles.title: Critical binary-parser Flaw Enables JavaScript Injection via Malicious Parser Definitions
articles.context: A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code
articles.full_text:
A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS score: 9.2 / 8.1), is a case of code injection impacting binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1.

"Binary-parser before 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject JavaScript through string-typed options passed unvalidated by Context.generateOption()," according to a description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

"Attackers can supply crafted length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, or namely() alias values to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when the parser is compiled."

According to an advisory released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026, the problem arose from the fact that some user-controlled string options were inserted directly into the generated JavaScript code without adequate validation.

The parser options include -

length

lengthInBytes

key

tag

offset, and

the alias passed to namely()

"Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected," Keichi Takahashi, who maintains the library, said. "These options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g. foo, $parent.len). Expressions such as 'len - 1' are rejected; use a function instead."

CVE-2026-134814 can also be viewed as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS score: 6.5), another code injection vulnerability that was fixed back in January 2026 and resulted from insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters.

"[The flaw] allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript within the host Node.js process upon parser compilation," Upwind Security said in an X post. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the library for optimal protection.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning
articles.context: Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers.

The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host.

"On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said.

The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine.

The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames.

In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload.

What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder.

It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation.

The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed.

Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online.

"Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said.

"As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026."

Organizations are advised to ensure that technicians' ScreenConnect host clients are updated to 26.6.5 or later, hunt for signs of exposure, isolate affected workstations, and rotate all credentials reachable from that workstation. If immediate patching is not feasible, it's recommended to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups.

"An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target," Huntress said. "When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs."

"A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."

articles.title: Norway links energy firm cyberattacks to critical Azure API Management flaw
articles.context: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations
articles.full_text: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations. According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register, Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies, only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2. It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault. Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration. The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs. Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets. The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise. NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations. The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation. "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said. "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. "When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses." Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear. Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day. The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied. NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched. Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

articles.title: N-able Discloses Critical Mail Assure Vulnerability Found During Breach Investigation
articles.context: N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for...
articles.full_text:
N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for managed service providers.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw. It allowed a user with high-level API access to open connections to internal systems of the user's choosing on the platform's servers.

The company fixed the flaw and restored access to the dashboard and APIs late on Saturday, closing an outage that began last Monday. Email delivery and spam filtering kept working throughout, according to the company. It has not said whether the flaw was the attackers' way in.

The bug sat in a connection check that Mail Assure runs for LDAP synchronization when a relay is configured. Before the fixed build, nothing restricted that check's destination, so the server could be pointed at any internal host and port to see which ones answered.

"An authenticated API user can cause the server to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.," the vendor's security advisory says.

The advisory gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3, and lists builds earlier than 20261121.1943 as affected, with that same build as the fix. It does not claim code execution.

N-able informed customers of a service disruption last Monday and initially traced it to platform configuration and service dependencies, according to its incident timeline.

Last Wednesday, the company said the outage was, in fact, a security incident: an unauthorized party had accessed one of the Hosted Cloud servers. The dashboard and APIs were kept offline as a precaution while it investigated.

It responded by taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' existing API tokens, invalidating OAuth tokens, and resetting local users' passwords.

The company says it has found no evidence that customer data was compromised, including tenants' mailboxes, and no sign of exploitation beyond that one server since the fix was implemented.

The investigation is still open, and the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident, according to the company. In that earlier incident, it took its hosted remote-monitoring platform offline on November 9 after a researcher published 33 unpatched flaws.

For hosted customers, the work now is reconnecting. Scripts and integrations that used the revoked API tokens or OAuth tokens will need new credentials. The exact steps differ by setup: each partner has been emailed guidance specific to its environment, and anyone who has not received it is asked to contact support.

The hosted platform itself is already patched, according to yesterday's incident update, so there is nothing for Hosted Cloud users to install.

SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware, with software updates applied on a weekly schedule, according to the product's update documentation. The incident statements describe the Hosted Cloud only, so Local Cloud operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943.

What the account so far does not say is how the attackers first got in, or whether any of the credentials they may have reached were actually taken. An outside digital forensics and incident response team has been brought in, and the company says a formal root cause analysis is due within two weeks of yesterday's update. Separate restoration times for quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization, which were being brought back in phases, have not been given.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw Exploited in Attacks
articles.context: “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands
articles.full_text:
Federal agencies have until Monday, November 23 to patch a critical flaw in Cisco Expressway, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has said.

CISA added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on 20 November after reports emerged that the flaw was being used in active attacks.

“Cisco Expressway Series contains a use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service,” CISA explained.

Cisco Expressway products are described as “advanced collaboration gateways” which operate in a pair: Expressway-C sits inside the corporate network and connects with internal collaboration systems, while Expressway-E sits in the DMZ to handle external traffic.

Read more on Cisco Expressway: Cisco Releases 10 Security Patches For Expressway Series and TelePresence VCS Products

The vulnerability has a CVSS score of 9.8, indicating a high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability, with low attack complexity and no user interaction required.

“This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies. Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated,” Cisco explained in an October 21 advisory.

“An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.”

First Cisco Expressway Exploit Observed

Moscow-based cybersecurity firm F6 claimed to have investigated the first observed case of exploitation of CVE-2026-76466.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices. Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network,” specialists from the Cyber Defense Center at F6 explained.

“After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure. They used custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and explore GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information.”

The security vendor urged Cisco Expressway customers not only to patch the flaw but also deploy network segmentation and monitoring to mitigate the risk of compromise.

It recommended organizations to:

Update Cisco Expressway to the current version containing the fix for CVE-2026-76466, or if not possible, to restrict connections to ports TCP/4371–4372 at the firewall layer and allow access only from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes

Implement external attack surface monitoring to identify vulnerable digital assets before they can be exploited

Ensure continuous monitoring and incident response to detect compromise fast, rapidly “localize and investigate,” isolate compromised systems, determine scope, and block lateral movement

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical ASP.NET Anti-CSRF Library Flaw Allowing Unauthenticated RCE
articles.context: dll") following the discovery of a critical vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have urged users to discontinue using a legacy ASP.NET anti-CSRF library named Idunno.AntiCsrf ("Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll") following the discovery of a critical vulnerability that has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-131914, carries a CVSS score of 9.3 out of 10.0. The issue affects versions 0.9.1.0 and 0.9.1 Beta, and relates to an insecure deserialization vulnerability in the Idunno.AntiCsrf.AntiCsrfModule HTTP module.

Idunno.AntiCsrf is a third-party ASP.NET IHttpModule designed to provide double-submit cookie Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection for ASP.NET WebForms applications. The open-source project is currently defunct and has not been updated since December 2008.

At its core, the problem stems from the fact that the module deserializes untrusted CSRF form token data using an unkeyed .NET System.Web.UI.ObjectStateFormatter instance without cryptographic MAC or signature verification when handling incoming HTTP POST requests to ASP.NET WebForms (System.Web.UI.Page) endpoints.

This behavior, in turn, can allow a remote attacker to achieve arbitrary remote code execution (RCE). Google's Mandiant division has given the vulnerability a "High" exploitability assessment, adding that exploitation hinges only on a single HTTP POST request with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token.

LDB, Genwei Jiang, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, Brian Bahtiarian, and Lucas Kossack of Google Cloud and Mandiant Incident Response have been credited with discovering the flaw earlier this month.

"A remote attacker can supply any non-empty value in the configured CSRF cookie alongside a Base64-encoded .NET ObjectStateFormatter gadget chain in the configured CSRF form field to execute arbitrary code in the context of the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe), resulting in complete compromise of the web application server," Google-owned Mandiant said in an alert issued last week.

"Active exploitation in the wild has been observed."

Google's threat intelligence team did not disclose any further details related to the activity. The Hacker News has contacted Google, and we will update the story if we hear back.

In the absence of an official patch, organizations still using the library are advised to discontinue its use and replace it with an actively supported anti-CSRF alternative such as follows -

System.Web.Helpers.AntiForgery

ASP.NET WebForms Page.ViewStateUserKey combined with MAC-verified/encrypted ViewState on postback forms

ASP.NET Core Anti-Request Forgery (IAntiforgery)

"Audit all ASP.NET Web.config files and bin/ directories for references to Idunno.AntiCsrf or AntiCsrfModule, and review IIS logs for anomalous POST requests to .aspx endpoints returning HTTP 302 or HTTP 500 with elevated cs-bytes (where logged)," Google said.

"Environments with evidence of exploitation should rotate all secrets stored in Web.config and applicationHost.config (including <machineKey> keys, encryption keys, and database credentials) and inspect webroots for unauthorized files."

articles.title: Hackers Exploited GL.iNet Cloud Flaw to Install Malware on Routers and KVM Devices
articles.context: Hackers exploited a vulnerability in GL
articles.full_text:
Hackers exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud remote management service to install malware on some customer routers and KVM devices, the maker of travel routers and remote-access KVM hardware said in a security notice updated today.

The company identified and fixed the flaw on Friday and blocked the access the attacker used, so devices can no longer be infected through this route. The cloud-side fix does not remove malware from devices that were already infected, so owners still need to check their hardware and install the security firmware listed today.

A KVM is a small device used to control a computer remotely as if sitting in front of it. The company is still investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were affected.

It has not said how many devices were infected, when the attacks began, or how its cloud service was breached. It is emailing customers it identifies as affected, but owners do not need to wait for a message to act.

A model missing from the firmware table below is not necessarily unaffected, the notice says, and owners should not install firmware meant for another model.

RemoteToHome Consulting, a security consultancy that examined the incident on routers it manages, says in its incident investigation that it verified a root-level reverse shell on one of its GL-AXT1800 routers.

The shell started on Friday evening and connected to 170.39.226[.]219, and two more owners reported the same shell on the same model and firmware, 4.8.3, with GoodCloud switched on.

On GL-MT6000 routers, the same shell command ran but the connection never completed. On other routers the firm manages, a one-off command searched for files linked to a KVM implant and reported the result to the same address.

The shell leaves no files behind, and its traces vanish when the device restarts, per the firm's reverse-shell analysis. The process marker the vendor published was absent on the router with the verified shell.

After the researchers filed an abuse report late last week, the hosting provider told them it had suspended the server behind the address and preserved its data.

The shell arrived through the GoodCloud client software on the router itself, according to the firm's technical analysis. A handler in that client takes two values from a cloud message and runs them as root through the shell without checking them. The vendor has not confirmed that finding.

The unchecked code has been in the firmware since at least December 5, 2024, when it appeared in a GL-MT3000 release. It runs whether or not AstroWarp, the SD-WAN feature it belongs to, is in use, and its presence since 2024 does not mean attacks began then.

The researchers reported a second, separate weakness in the cloud client to the vendor yesterday and are withholding details until it is fixed.

One KVM owner described an infected GL-RM1 in an owner's report. Starting on Thursday, the device downloaded a script and two programs from 66.245.219[.]252, looked up the copycat domain gl-inet[.]top, and scanned the local network.

It also kept connecting to 65.20.71[.]131, which the owner suspects was a command channel. The owner did not keep the downloaded files, and the method by which the device was infected has not been confirmed.

The vendor advises checking the computer attached to an infected KVM for unfamiliar programs, accounts, startup items, and unusual network activity.

The investigation also found an unrelated, older backdoor on 49 of the routers the firm manages, installed in batches between September 2025 and May 2026 by a route that is not known. Nothing so far links it to last week's attacks.

How to Check a Device

GL.iNet's check looks for one marker: a running process whose details contain the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log. A line showing only the grep command itself is not a match.

Router, web panel: sign in to LuCI under System → Advanced Settings, open Status → Processes, and search for tmp/.log.

Router, SSH: run ps | grep tmp.

KVM: open the device's own terminal under Toolbox → Terminal → Access, then run ps -a | grep tmp on the RMQ1 or ps -aux | grep tmp on other models. Run it on the KVM, not on the attached computer.

Check before rebooting or upgrading where compromise is suspected, the researchers advise, because the shell's traces disappear at restart. The marker can also miss infected devices: it was absent on the router with the verified shell.

Before running netstat on a suspect device, check that /bin/netstat is still a link to busybox. The command itself may have been swapped, a forum warning and the researchers' indicator list say, and running a compromised copy starts the malware.

The notice also points to an unofficial community check script, with the warning that the vendor has not reviewed it and that it can run with administrative privileges. Fuller indicators are in the researchers' detailed findings.

What the Update Does and Does Not Remove

GL.iNet listed stable security firmware for its router and KVM lines in the security notice it updated today, which now says the update "removes the malware identified in this incident without requiring a factory reset," with settings kept. That replaces earlier guidance, which offered a factory reset for infected devices ahead of the firmware's release.

Model(s)

Minimum fixed version

GL-MG1300, GL-MT3000, GL-MT6000

4.11.1

GL-E5800

4.10.3

GL-BE3600, GL-BE9300

4.10.2

GL-BE14000

4.9.3

GL-BE6500, GL-MT3600BE, GL-MT5000

4.9.1

GL-BE10000

4.8.7

GL-AX1800, GL-AXT1800, GL-SFT1200, GL-X3000, GL-XE3000

4.8.4

GL-MT2500 / GL-MT2500A, GL-X2000

4.7.14

RM1, RM1V2, RM10, RM10RC, RM1PE, RM4PE (KVM)

1.10.3

RMQ1 (KVM)

1.8.7

In spot checks today, The Hacker News found the GL-MT3000 and GL-RM1 builds available at the vendor's router downloads and KVM downloads pages.

The update is not shown to cover everything a root-level attacker may have left behind. In RemoteToHome's KVM firmware analysis, upgrading an RM1 to the earlier 1.10.2 security build with settings kept carried the device's password file, SSH keys and user directory across, and that directory holds scripts that run at every boot. Whether a planted script survives the upgrade has not been tested.

For a device with signs of compromise, the researchers' advice is a firmware reinstall without keeping settings, and treating every stored secret as exposed: VPN keys, Wi-Fi and admin passwords, cloud credentials and SSH keys. The vendor's notice and that advice differ on this point.

Until a device is updated, the option the researchers describe is switching GoodCloud off, after first securing another way to reach the device. Switching it off stops the cloud client from running but does not clean a device that was already infected.

The attacker's identity, the number of affected devices, and how the cloud service itself was breached remain unknown, and The Hacker News found no CVE identifier for the flaw as of publication.

articles.context: Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug...
articles.full_text: Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September. VMware revealed several flaws on November 19. The big nasty is CVE-2026-123890, which allows unauthorized access to vCenter, the management console for hosts and guest VMs. According to seven researchers from Google’s threat intelligence group (formerly Mandiant), a crew it calls ARMORY CASTLE that it suspects of having links to the People’s Republic of China exploited CVE-2026-123890 by first compromising remote access appliances from BeyondTrust. Google’s analysis suggests the crew uses that toehold to establish access to other Linux appliances before moving deeper into victims’ networks. If the crew finds vCenter, it deploys a custom malware tool called “BONESAW” designed to slice into the VMware product. In the incident Google observed, BONESAW let attackers “forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user.” The gang put that access to work by conducting an inventory of the victim’s VMware setup, scooping up data describing the ESXi file system, attached disks, and mounted Virtual Machine File System volumes. ARMORY CASTLE also added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys, and “conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account.” Google also found evidence of BONESAW being used in July, on a server an unidentified entity had patched against CVE-2026-59309 – another authentication bypass vulnerability in vCenter. And BONESAW was just one of five tools Google thinks ARMORY CASTLE created as part of its plan to attack vCenter. It also made webshells named SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, a backdoor called BEARBONES, and a SAML utility called SAWSNAKE. “The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations,” Google’s researchers wrote. “It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets.” Few targets are as juicy as vCenter, because it can literally give attackers access to thousands of virtual machines and the hosts they run on. Google hasn't said how many attacks is saw on vCenter using BONESAW. The Register asked VMware if it was aware of the September attack, if it took any measures to defend its customers at the time, and to share a timeline for disclosure and remediation of CVE-2026-123890. A spokesperson responded by pointing to VMware’s Q&A document and stating “In today's threat environment, customers should assume any publicly disclosed critical vulnerability can and will be exploited by threat actors under the right conditions and should apply the recommended patches immediately.” VMware has tried to make that easier by adding non-disruptive patching to several of its products, and introducing a product called vDefend that offers “virtual patching” by creating compensating controls that use network micro segmentation and other techniques to block access to resources malware uses. Last month, VMware debuted another new tool, HyperArmor, to block incoming malicious traffic targeting its VCF private cloud suite. In recent discussions with The Register, VMware execs told us the Broadcom business unit will emphasize security improvements in future product releases. “Our teams have integrated frontier AI security model testing directly into our engineering workflows, strengthened our software supply chain to reduce third-party dependencies and speed up upstream responses, and built VCF 9.1 specifically for high-velocity security,” a spokesperson said in response to questions about the Mandiant report. Freebie patches hard to find One security offering VMware won’t continue is free access to patches for zero-day flaws in supported versions of products sold under its old perpetual licenses – even to users who don’t have an ongoing support deal or software subscription. VMware last year stopped making those patches available for download and promised it would establish “a separate patch delivery cycle.” Readers have pointed out that information about the new cycle isn’t easy to find, and The Register noticed that the blog post in which Broadcom CEO Hock Tan promised the free patches no longer contains references to the offer. Removing the promise seems to be a recent edit as an Internet Archive snapshot of the page from October 20 does mention the zero-day patch freebies. A VMware spokesperson told us the free zero-day patch policy remains in place despite changes to the post. “Broadcom’s policy to provide access to zero-day critical security patches to customers who, at their own risk, continue to run perpetual VMware vSphere 8 software without an active support agreement, remains in place,” the spokesperson wrote. “Those customers can get these patches by contacting Broadcom. This policy covers vSphere 8 patches only and is expected to remain in effect through the end of general support on October 11, 2027.” ®

articles.title: Proof-of-concept exploit code available for Ghostscript ‘Upload2Shell’ vulnerability (CVE-2026-125396)
articles.context: Sophos countermeasures SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available
articles.full_text:
On November 21, 2026, pwn.ai described a proof of concept for exploiting a high-severity (CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5) vulnerability in Ghostscript, which is used to convert PostScript and PDF files into other formats. This use-after-free vulnerability (CVE-2026-125396) has been dubbed ‘Upload2Shell’. Attackers could exploit this flaw by sending custom PostScript or PDF documents that bypass the -dSAFER sandbox, gaining the ability to execute arbitrary code.

Artifex patched the issue in September, and affected distributions are being updated. There are no reports of active exploitation.

Recommended actions

Organizations should upgrade to the latest Ghostscript release as appropriate and can monitor the status of vulnerable distributions listed in the pwn.ai article. Until updates are available, organizations can reduce the risk by preventing Ghostscript from processing untrusted files.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this threat and will deliver detections and protections as available.

The Sophos MDR team is actively monitoring for exploitation and post-exploitation activity related to this threat and will investigate and respond to suspicious activity.

An internal investigation is also underway to determine if Sophos products or services are affected.

articles.title: Introducing Mitigeddon: Real-world exploitation and prevalence data for impactful CVEs
articles.context: The median time from disclosure to exploitation was 33 days, down from 60 days in 2025 and 163 days in 2024 (these numbers exclude KEV entries released prior to the...
articles.full_text:
Over 27 years ago, CVE-1999-0001 was reserved as the first vulnerability in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database. Since then, this catalog has grown quickly, especially in recent years with the advent of AI-assisted security research. In this post, we introduce Mitigeddon, a new public website that security practitioners and leaders can use to stay on top of the latest impactful vulnerabilities, and better estimate the risk that specific exposures cause to the industry.

The number of CVEs keeps growing faster than real risk

In 2026 so far, well over 100k CVEs have been published. For comparison, this number was 50k in 2025 and 40k in 2024.

However, not all CVEs are created equal. Most CVEs don't appear widely in real-world environments, and only a tiny fraction are exploitable. Of 34k CVEs applicable to software applications, 38% are present in the sample of environments Datadog monitors, 12% are exploitable, and only 0.8% are known to be exploited in the wild according to VulnCheck and CISA. These numbers are similar for CVEs applicable to OS packages and container images: of 113k CVEs, 56% are present in environments, 10% are exploitable, and 0.6% are exploited in the wild.

This evolution means that to keep up, practitioners increasingly need to cut through the noise.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild get weaponized faster

To understand how fast attackers move once a vulnerability is disclosed, we measured the time between a vulnerability's release date and when it was added to the CISA or VulnCheck Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs. In 2026 so far, 17% of vulnerabilities reported as exploited in the wild were exploited on the same day the vulnerability was released, and another 20% within a week. The median time from disclosure to exploitation was 33 days, down from 60 days in 2025 and 163 days in 2024 (these numbers exclude KEV entries released prior to the vulnerability itself, which are indicative of zero-day exploitation rather than weaponization of a freshly released vulnerability).

Mitigeddon: a new project to browse impactful vulnerabilities and visualize their industry impact

Today, we're proud to release Mitigeddon, a website that aggregates data from osv.dev, CISA KEV, VulnCheck KEV, and aggregated Datadog telemetry data from a sample of thousands of real-world applications.

Mitigeddon allows you to:

Quickly identify impactful vulnerabilities that are relevant to cloud environments

Visualize a timeline for each vulnerability, including when it was released, when an exploit was made publicly available, and when threat intelligence sources such as CISA or VulnCheck flagged it as exploited in the wild

Estimate the prevalence of a vulnerability in the industry

Moving forward, we'll also embed live Mitigeddon data in our posts covering Emerging Vulnerabilities. Below is an example of what this looks like for the Java4Shell vulnerability.

We'd love to hear from you

If you have any comments, feedback, or data that you feel we should add to Mitigeddon, shoot us an email at securitylabs@datadoghq.com!

Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not impacted by this vulnerability.

Recommended mitigation—The vast majority of firewalls already follow Palo Alto Networks and industry best practices. However, if you haven’t already, we strongly recommend that you secure access to your management interface according to our best practice deployment guidelines. Specifically, you should restrict access to the management interface to only trusted internal IP addresses to prevent external access from the internet.

Additionally, if you have a Threat Prevention subscription, you can block these attacks using Threat IDs 95746, 95747, 95752, 95753, 95759, and 95763 (available in Applications and Threats content version 8915-9075 and later). For these Threat IDs to protect against attacks for this vulnerability,

  • Ensure that all the listed Threat IDs are set to block mode,
  • Route incoming traffic for the MGT port through a DP port, e.g., enabling management profile on a DP interface for management access,
  • Replace the Certificate for Inbound Traffic Management,
  • Decrypt inbound traffic to the management interface so the firewall can inspect it, and
  • Enable threat prevention on the inbound traffic to management services.

Additionally, if you have a Threat Prevention subscription, you can block these attacks using Threat IDs 95746, 95747, 95752, 95753, 95759, and 95763 (available in Applications and Threats content version 8915-9075 and later). For these Threat IDs to protect against attacks for this vulnerability, * Ensure that all the listed Threat IDs are set to block mode, * Route incoming traffic for the MGT port through a DP port https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/best-practices/10-1/administrative-access-best-practices/administrative-access-best-practices/deploy-administrative-access-best-practices#id59206398-3dab-4b2f-9b4b-7ea500d036ba , e.g., enabling management profile on a DP interface for management access, * Replace the Certificate for Inbound Traffic Management https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/best-practices/10-1/administrative-access-best-practices/administrative-access-best-practices/deploy-administrative-access-best-practices#id112f7714-8995-4496-bbf9-781e63dec71c , * Decrypt inbound traffic to the management interface so the firewall can inspect it https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/best-practices/10-1/administrative-access-best-practices/administrative-access-best-practices/deploy-administrative-access-best-practices#idbbd82587-17a2-42b4-9245-d3714e1e13a2 , and * Enable threat prevention on the inbound traffic to management services. articles.title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps
articles.context: ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file
articles.full_text:
A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it.

Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly.

Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks.

Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses.

The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files.

The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering.

Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor.

WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index.

Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory.

WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other.

Updating the Renderer

The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced.

Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system:

Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable

Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending

SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress

SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress

openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected

The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix.

Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell.

One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point.

The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.

articles.title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
articles.context: The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out
articles.full_text:
A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.

The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.

Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.

The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.

Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says.

The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG.

When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details.

The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier.

What to Update

The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

What to install depends on where the library sits:

Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory.

Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible.

Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch.

Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases.

GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed.

The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

articles.title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access
articles.context: They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root
articles.full_text:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.

The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.

The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.

MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.

The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.

The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.

Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.

Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.

The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.

Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.

A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.

That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.

In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.

The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.

Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.

The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw.

What to Do Now

With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach:

Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs.

Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default.

Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to.

Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched.

If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used.

The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described.

The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical VMware, Cisco, and Apache Flaws as Espionage Attacks Emerge
articles.context: The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026)

CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026)

CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025)

CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026)

Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884.

The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

articles.title: PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
articles.context: The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers
articles.full_text:
PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell, a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts.

“Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption

One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289, is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps.

If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM.

When paired with a code execution bug, it can “carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained.

Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting.

While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network.

Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority

An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data.

For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path:

The threat actor gets in through the web application.

Reads the configuration file;

Dumps the customer database;

Plants a web shell to come back later.

He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted.

RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion.

“Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said.

What enterprises should do now

Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does.

The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter:

Is session upload progress on?

Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces?

Does php-cgi face the internet?

Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside?

He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained.

“Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said.

He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project.

Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability,” Dickson noted.

In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.”

Understanding everywhere PHP runs

Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.”

Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components.

“The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

articles.title: China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day
How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
articles.context: Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score Memory corruption is usually only the first step
articles.full_text:
On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.

The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.

Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.

The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.

What we know about ruby2shell

Ruby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.

The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.

Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposed

HTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.

Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.

Who is affected

Condition

Details

Ruby version

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.

Framework

Rails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding.

Bundled software

As of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix.

Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

Six more Ruby flaws in the same release

Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws, and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

Upgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

New managed rules, on for every customer

Both rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action.

Rule description

Rule ID

Ruleset

Default action

Ruby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-132825

Block

Ruby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-132825

1afa543a1ed84893b01df04c34402c88

Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)

Block

Ruby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px

8660e37e86444f9f9267ba22e9855f05

Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)

Ruby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px

Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)
