articles.title: Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts
articles.context: The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2
articles.full_text:
A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years.

In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities.

What to Do

The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted.

Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range.

Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected.

Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change.

Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it:

Check the setting with cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested. A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on.

If the host cannot be updated yet, add options kvm_amd nested=0 to the host's module configuration.

Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with uname -r and by reading the nested setting again.

The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

articles.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability

CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in
articles.context: Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2
articles.full_text: A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2. The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again." Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored." Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID. Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected. An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets. Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

articles.title: SonicWall Warns Gen 6 Firewalls Won't Get Security Patches, Even for Critical Flaws
articles.context: "Attackers now use automation and AI to find and exploit unsupported edge devices faster than ever," SonicWall said
articles.full_text:
SonicWall has urged all customers still running Generation 6 firewalls to retire and replace them immediately and stop exposing the devices on the internet edge, citing security risks fueled by AI-assisted attacks.

"Attackers now use automation and AI to find and exploit unsupported edge devices faster than ever," SonicWall said. "We expect internet-facing Gen 6 firewalls to be actively targeted. Treat any Gen 6 firewall still in service as a high-risk exposure, and migrate to a supported Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8."

The affected products running SonicOS 6.x include -

TZ350, TZ350W, TZ500, TZ500W, SOHO 250, SOHO 250W

NSA 4600, NSA 5600, NSA 6600

NSa 4650, NSa 5650, NSa 6650

TZ400, TZ400W, TZ600, TZ600P, NSA 3600

NSa 3650

NSa 2650

SOHO, SOHO W, TZ300P, NSa 9250, NSa 9450, NSa 9650

NSv 10 to NSv 1600 (Gen 6 virtual)

SuperMassive 9200, 9400, 9600, 9800

NSsp 12800, NSsp 12400

TZ300, TZ300W

NSA 2600

In recent years, threat actors have increasingly targeted edge devices as a launch point to obtain initial access, even as the window between disclosure and confirmed exploitation has collapsed significantly, in part driven by threat actors' use of automation and AI to scan the internet for unsupported devices, analyze patches and vulnerability disclosure announcements, and build working exploits faster.

According to Google Mandiant's M-Trends report published in March 2026, the mean time to exploit vulnerabilities has turned negative, reaching an estimated -7 days, meaning exploitation, on average, begins before a patch is available, down from 63 days in 2018 and -1 day in 2024.

"This trend is compounded by threat actors' evolving interest in security appliances and networking infrastructure," Google said. "Because these assets provide critical inspection of data ingress and egress points, they grant significant visibility and permissions to those who gain access to them."

Cisco Talos' 2025 Year in Review report has also found that 23% of CVEs discovered in the year directly impact network devices like VPN appliances, next-generation firewalls (NGFWs), load balancers, routers, and others.

"Since these systems sit at the perimeter of enterprise environments, compromise may lead to direct access to the critical networks," Talos said. "This aligns with real-world trends from CISA'sKnown Exploitation Vulnerability (KEV) catalog, where exploitation consistently favors edge devices because they are internetfacing, often lag in patching, and provide direct operational leverage once compromised."

With Gen 6 no longer being actively supported and receiving patches, even for critical flaws, users are recommended to follow the steps below without any delay -

Inventory every Gen 6 firewall in the production environment and retire them.

Prioritize units that are exposed to the internet or provide remote access.

Replace them with a Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8

Contact an authorized SonicWall partner to plan the migration

Until the firewall is replaced, it's advised to take the below actions to minimize exposure -

Disable WAN management (HTTPS, SSH, and SNMP on WAN interfaces).

Disable SSL VPN, or restrict it to known source addresses.

Enforce multi-factor authentication on every remaining remote-access and admin account, and reset local passwords.

Disable services and interfaces not in use.

Monitor logs closely for unusual logins, configuration changes and traffic.

"The risk to an unsupported firewall grows every day it stays online," SonicWall said. "One breach reaches everything. A compromised perimeter firewall gives attackers a foothold for credential theft, lateral movement and ransomware deployment."

articles.title: SonicWall Warns Gen 6 Firewalls Won't Get Security Patches, Even for Critical Flaws
Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw, Breach Four Devices and Reach Internal Network
articles.context: Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization shortly after the public release of...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization shortly after the public release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit.

The activity involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.

"This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies," Cisco said in an advisory released late last month. "Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated."

"An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device."

Patches for the flaw were released in the following versions on October 21, 2026 -

Cisco Expressway Series Release X14 and earlier - Migrate to a fixed release

Cisco Expressway Series Release X15.5.3 and earlier - X15.5.20

In a report published Thursday, Russian cybersecurity company F6 said it observed what appears to be the first case of in-the-wild exploitation of the flaw to gain remote command execution on compromised Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices with root privileges after a PoC exploit became publicly available.

"The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices," F6 said. "Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization's internal network."

Following root access, the attackers are said to have undertaken efforts to move laterally across the network and use custom Python scripts to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and access GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive data.

Analysis of the scripts indicates that they were possibly developed with assistance from artificial intelligence (AI) tools, given the presence of comments and descriptions of fixes.

The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the activity -

IP addresses geolocated: 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116

Presence of "wombat@127.0.0.1" in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices

Python scripts staged in "/mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py"

The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Users are advised to update to the latest supported version of Cisco Expressway, audit environments for signs of compromise, isolate affected systems, determine the scope of the attack, and block potential lateral movement vectors.

"This incident demonstrates that compromise of a perimeter device can open a path for an attacker to an organization's critical systems," F6 said. "That means protection should therefore include not only timely vulnerability remediation but also properly configured segmentation and infrastructure monitoring."

articles.title: China-Linked Hackers Exploit Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day to Gain Admin Access and Steal Data
articles.context: The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware...
articles.full_text:
The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system.

It has been addressed as part of patches released on November 19, 2026, in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.1.0200

VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0200

VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m

VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)

VMware Cloud Foundation - Fixed in 5.2.5

VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

"CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC)," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said.

"Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local."

An attacker can exploit the vulnerability to obtain an authenticated administrator session, execute arbitrary commands, and acquire files, such as the data.mdb database, by using the Directory Service ("vmdird"). The tech giant's threat intelligence and incident response teams said it observed the Chinese hacking group weaponizing the flaw using a utility dubbed BONESAW.

"BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang, which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account," Google said.

The activity is part of the same campaign that also involved the exploitation of a then zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to conduct reconnaissance, obtain administrative control, establish persistence, and deploy a bespoke proxy tunneler called BARECLAW.

From the Remote Support device, the threat actor is said to have moved laterally to an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and deployed additional payloads to broaden their access, map the environment, conduct data theft, and move into the virtualized environment.

"The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012," Google said. "Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of Armory Castle's remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW."

Deployed as part of the attack are six identified malware families and utilities -

SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, JSP web shells designed to run arbitrary commands, stage payloads, and establish a foothold on the Linux appliance.

BONESAW, the Golang-based remote exploitation utility for CVE-2026-123890 used to target an internal vCenter Server.

SAWSNAKE, a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, thereby making it possible to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW and allowing the attacker to forge authentication tokens, bypass multi-factor authentication(MFA), and impersonate any user. It's a Go-based port of an open-source Python script named "vcenter_saml_login.py."

BEARBONES, a C backdoor based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server that's capable of bypassing system password authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from the temporary directory.

LAZYBONES, a lightweight Go backdoor that uses Slack for command-and-control (C2) communications and has been previously deployed in a separate intrusion in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of a critical flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2025-22457, CVSS score: 9.0).

It's suspected that Armory Castle had knowledge of the flaw prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026, with the recovered BONESAW binary containing a build timestamp of July 13, 2026. However, it's worth noting that build metadata can be modified before compilation.

"After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, Armory Castle moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-<REDACTED>@vsphere.local," Google said.

"Notably, Armory Castle enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. After enabling SSH, Armory Castle connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account."

In the final stage of the attack, the adversary was found enumerating the ESXi file system, mounting Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and adding an SSH public key to the root account's authorized keys. It also conducted additional reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi file system, which were then archived and downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance for subsequent exfiltration.

Furthermore, the attackers have been observed dropping LAZYBONES to a separate Linux appliance, which periodically checks for commands from a designated Slack channel, allowing it to perform command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment.

CVE-2026-123890 is the second vulnerability in a VMware product to be exploited by Armory Castle as a zero-day this year alone. Late last month, CrowdStrike revealed it identified incidents where the hacking crew abused CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an insufficient logging flaw in VMware ESX, to reduce audit trail visibility.

"BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days," Google said. "The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each."

"The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting Armory Castle operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor's operational commitment to compromise high-priority targets."

articles.title: New Unpatched Windows 0-Day FastUnlock Lets Someone Holding a Locked PC Run Programs on It
articles.context: The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker tested it the same day and...
articles.full_text:
A newly disclosed unpatched zero-day technique called FastUnlock lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows computer start programs without signing in. Whoever uses it gets only a limited account, not administrator control of the machine.

The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker tested it the same day and found it works.

There is no fix from Microsoft yet, and nothing shows the method has been used in a real attack.

The technique does not work on every machine. It requires physical access to the computer and a Microsoft account accessible through the lock screen's recovery options, and it uses Windows' built-in screen reader, Narrator, to navigate the locked screen.

In its test, the firm reached a point where it could run a program from the lock screen in a limited account that ThreatLocker identified as WSIAccount and said is "not an administrator account."

The researcher's GitHub disclosure is a short post with a video and little written detail, so the clearest account of what the flaw does comes from the firm's independent test.

Many Windows computers encrypt their drives with BitLocker, but in a common setup, that does not make them immune to this technique. A chip called the TPM unlocks the drive automatically when the computer starts, so by the time the lock screen appears, the files are already readable, and the bypass runs at that point. Microsoft's own TPM documentation describes this mode, in which the drive unlocks "without having to enter a PIN."

FastUnlock does not break that encryption or recover the key. It runs on a computer that has already unlocked its own drive in the normal way, which is a smaller problem than cracking an encrypted disk, though still a real one for a machine someone else is holding.

The conditions above, physical access and a reachable Microsoft account, are what put a machine at risk. No official list of affected Windows versions has been published, so treat any machine that meets those conditions as possibly affected until one is.

What You Can Do Now

With no patch available, the useful steps are about physical control and startup protection.

Keep machines that can go missing out of the wrong hands. Lock away or closely manage laptops, shared desks, and front-counter computers that a stranger could reach.

On sensitive machines, add a startup PIN to BitLocker instead of letting the drive unlock on its own.

Shut down or hibernate devices when they leave someone's control. A startup PIN protects only a machine that has not yet started, not one already on the lock screen.

Do not treat a locked screen on its own as enough.

Microsoft's countermeasures guidance recommends using a startup PIN, along with shutting down or hibernating machines when faced with determined, hands-on attackers. Until an official fix or advisory appears, watch for one and apply it when it comes.

articles.title: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
articles.context: But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection...
articles.full_text:
On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633.

nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers.

Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work.

The short version

Cloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out globally before the vulnerabilities were published. The same releases fix five other nginx CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3.

Origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. For proxied hostnames, Cloudflare terminates every client HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection at our edge and opens a separate connection to your origin. The attacker's frames never reach your nginx.

The resolver and mail proxy vulnerabilities depend on specific configuration. Many configurations of nginx will not be vulnerable, but the safest way to be sure is to update your install or disable features.

You should still patch. Update to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or your vendor's fixed build) and restart. Some configurations, covered below, are not protected by the proxy.

What was disclosed

nginx2root is five independent bugs. Each one works on its own and each one needs a different configuration.

CVE

Bug class

Affected configuration

First affected release

CVE-2026-123007

Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/write

HTTP/2 enabled

1.9.5 (2015)

CVE-2026-123633

Use-after-free

HTTP/2 with proxy_pass to a backend, worker low on worker_connections

1.19.7

CVE-2026-121810

Use-after-free

HTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass to a backend

1.25.0

CVE-2026-123634

Use-after-free

resolver + proxy_pass with variables + a subrequest (mirror or SSI)

0.6.18

CVE-2026-113425

Use-after-free

Mail proxy with proxy on and auth_http

0.5.33

F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2), and notes that code execution requires disabling or bypassing ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization). For CVE-2026-123007, Xint's write-up shows how it leaked memory addresses to do exactly that.

CVE-2026-123007 is the one to worry about most. It only needs HTTP/2 turned on, which is commonly enabled on TLS deployments, and it has been in every nginx release since HTTP/2 support shipped in 1.9.5. Xint ran the exploit over the public Internet against servers on AWS, GCP and Azure. Xint searched Shodan on November 10, before the disclosure, and found 56.7 million hosts matching product:nginx. Of the 11.94 million that reported a version, 98.9% fell in the affected range. As of November 19, Censys's nginx2root exposure tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. Version strings don't prove a host is vulnerable, since distributions backport fixes, but the exposure is large.

The same nginx releases also fix five other bugs. The most serious, CVE-2026-118899, is an infinite loop when reading a request body over TLS 1.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker stall a worker, in nginx 1.13.0 and later.

The Linux kernel bug is the sixth part of nginx2root. Xint found a use-after-free in the kernel's SCTP send path, present since Linux 4.15 (2018): while a send operation waits, its SCTP association can be moved to another socket, and the waiting send can then free it. An attacker who already runs code as the nginx worker can use it to gain root on the host, and Xint did this from an nginx running inside a Docker container. Many distributions load the SCTP module automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of November 18, no kernel fix was available and Xint was withholding the details until there is one.

As of November 19, none of the five nginx2root CVEs is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and we have not seen reports of exploitation in the wild. Xint and Wiz Research have not released their exploits. Rapid7 has published a proof of concept, which it describes as suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started local container. Fake 'exploits' are also circulating on GitHub.

Why Cloudflare's proxy protects your origin

nginx2root's most dangerous bugs live in how nginx parses and manages HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections. To trigger them, an attacker has to send a carefully ordered stream of protocol frames directly to the nginx process: billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames, a SETTINGS frame that holds response data back, PING frames that fill the send buffers, partial HEADERS frames, RST_STREAM at exactly the right moment.

When your DNS record is proxied through Cloudflare, that connection ends at our edge.

Cloudflare reads the client's HTTP request, applies your security and caching rules, and then makes its own request to your origin over a connection Cloudflare controls. The flow-control frames, pings, settings, and stream resets that the attacker sends are consumed by our edge. They are not forwarded. Your nginx only ever sees the requests Cloudflare chooses to send, framed the way Cloudflare frames them. This also holds when Cloudflare connects to your origin over HTTP/2: Cloudflare runs its own flow control on that connection and sends WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM frames only as its own traffic needs, so a client can't make it relay the billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames the attack requires.

Rapid7 makes the same point in its analysis of CVE-2026-123007: if the HTTP/2 connection is proxied, the attacker's frames "will likely not be retransmitted" in a way that allows exploitation. This breaks each of the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks.

CVE

What the attacker needs

Behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy

CVE-2026-123007

Direct control over HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, SETTINGS, PING and RST_STREAM on one connection to nginx

Protected. Control frames terminate at Cloudflare's edge.

CVE-2026-123633

The first part of a HEADERS frame on a direct HTTP/2 connection, plus the ability to exhaust nginx connection slots and reset the TCP connection

Protected. The client's HTTP/2 connection terminates at Cloudflare.

CVE-2026-121810

A direct QUIC/HTTP/3 connection to nginx

Protected. HTTP/3 terminates at Cloudflare's edge. We do not communicate to origins over HTTP/3

CVE-2026-123634

A request and its mirror or SSI subrequest waiting on the same DNS lookup, and the main request ending while the answer is processed. In Xint's exploit, nginx's resolver had to reach the attacker's DNS server.

Not fully protected. Depends on how your config builds proxy_pass. Patch.

CVE-2026-113425

A direct IMAP/POP3/SMTP connection to the nginx mail proxy

Not protected. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry mail traffic.

There is one condition to be protected by Cloudflare here: your origin must not be reachable directly. If an attacker can find your origin's IP and connect to it directly (TCP 443 or 80 for HTTP/2, UDP 443 for HTTP/3, or the mail ports), Cloudflare isn't in the path and the protection doesn't apply. You should ensure that your origin servers can only be accessed through Cloudflare’s proxies, using one of the following approaches:

Cloudflare Tunnel. Your origin makes an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare and exposes no inbound ports.

Firewall to Cloudflare IP ranges. Accept inbound HTTP/HTTPS only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges. This must be done using an IP firewall, not based on configuration in your nginx server.

Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS). Your origin rejects any TLS connection that doesn't present Cloudflare's client certificate.

Xint's own exposure check makes the same point: "If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front of nginx, the test only reaches the proxy, so also run it directly against the nginx server."

Where the protection does not apply

There are several situations in which Cloudflare’s HTTP proxy does not provide protection.

Spectrum TCP/UDP applications. For these configurations, traffic from the Internet is passed unmodified through to your origin. If your origin is running nginx, patch or disable the affected features.

nginx mail proxy. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry IMAP, POP3 or SMTP. Restrict mail listeners to trusted networks until patched.

CVE-2026-123634 (resolver). This depends on how your configuration builds the proxy_pass target from the request, combined with a carefully timed cancellation of an HTTP request. Passing your traffic through Cloudflare’s proxy makes it harder to exploit this, but does not provide full protection. Update regardless.

DNS-only (grey-cloud), internal or non-proxied nginx. Any nginx server an attacker can reach without going through Cloudflare, including internal services behind a compromised host, needs to be patched.

Cloudflare’s WAF rules are not relevant to these vulnerabilities. These are protocol-level bugs. Because Cloudflare’s proxy handles parsing the HTTP protocol messages, and creates new messages to fetch information from origin servers, origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are protected from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 bugs without needing a rule. We have therefore not released a managed rule. The protection comes from connection termination, not from pattern matching.

What to do now

Find every nginx server. Include nginx Plus, distribution packages, container images and appliances. Run nginx -V and nginx -T on each and note HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC listeners, proxy_pass with variables plus SSI or mirror, and any mail block.

Patch. Update nginx Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distribution's fixed package. F5 lists nginx Plus R34 to R36 as affected with no fixed build, so move those to a fixed 37.x release. Then restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade. A config reload does not replace the running binary.

Check backport versions carefully. Distributions often patch without changing the version nginx -v reports. Compare the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

Make sure your origin is only reachable through Cloudflare. Use Tunnel, IP allowlisting or Authenticated Origin Pulls.

If you can't patch yet, disable what you don't need. http2 off; (nginx 1.25.1 and later; on older versions, remove http2 from the listen directive) blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Removing QUIC listeners and setting http3 off; blocks CVE-2026-121810. Point proxy_pass at fixed upstream groups for CVE-2026-123634. Don't rely on mirror_request_body alone: Xint's tested setup set it to off, and the default on stopped that exploit, but SSI and other subrequests can still reach the bug. Bind mail listeners to trusted networks for CVE-2026-113425. Restart so old connections close.

Block SCTP if you don't use it. Add install sctp /bin/false to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ to stop the kernel module from loading. This doesn't unload an already-loaded module or disable SCTP built into the kernel. When your distribution ships a kernel update for the SCTP bug, install it and reboot. Blocking the module is a stopgap until then.

The Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire entry for nginx2root has the full checklist, a prompt you can give an agent to run a read-only assessment of your fleet, and links to every vendor advisory.

Technical deep dive

Let’s dig into the details of the five bugs by looking through the code. We’re looking at nginx 1.31.8 (commit 140aa94) which was the most recent code published before the fixes, and comparing this to the fixes in 1.31.9 (which were also included in release 1.30.7 on the stable branch).

A note on methodology: we based our analysis on the public advisories, and to verify our reading of the code, we built the public 1.31.8 and 1.31.9 releases with AddressSanitizer and ran tests for four of the five bugs (flow control, HTTP/2 use-after-free, resolver and mail proxy). Each one faults on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. We did not reproduce the HTTP/3 bug; that section is based on the fix commit and the published analysis.

One pattern, in four places

Four of the five bugs are use-after-free bugs. This is a common issue with programs that manually manage memory without language support: one part of the code frees an object that another part is still using.

nginx is event driven. A handler runs, calls other code, and that code returns to the handler. Three of the bugs occur when the called code tears down the connection or request the handler is working on. In the fourth, a second connection still holds a pointer to the object.

CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810. A request needs a connection slot to reach its upstream. nginx is low on slots, so it closes an idle connection to free one. The connection it chooses is the one the request belongs to.

CVE-2026-123634. A resolver callback ends a request. Cleanup of that request frees a second resolver context that the resolver is about to call next.

CVE-2026-113425. When a write to a mail client fails, the client connection is closed while the connection to the authentication service still points at its session.

F5 rates all four as potential code execution if address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed, and in its tests Xint reports code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker.

The fifth bug, CVE-2026-123007, is of a different kind: an accounting error that becomes a length error.

CVE-2026-123007: two flow-control pieces that each look correct

HTTP/2 flow control limits the amount of response data a server may send. nginx tracks a send window for each stream and one for the connection, h2c->send_window. The client enlarges a window with a WINDOW_UPDATE frame, and the protocol caps every window at 2^31 − 1.

nginx enforces that cap when a WINDOW_UPDATE arrives (ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()):

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { /* logs "client violated connection flow control" */ return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR); }

On its own, this check is correct. But the connection window also grows in a second place. When nginx queues DATA frames for a stream, it subtracts their length from the window. If the stream is canceled before those frames go out, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() takes them off the queue and returns the credit:

h2c->send_window += window;

Nothing caps this line. As the fix commit describes, if the client enlarges the connection window after the frames are queued and before the stream is terminated, the refund pushes the window past 2^31 − 1.

From that point the first check no longer works. h2c->send_window is an unsigned size_t, so NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window wraps around to a very large number and every subsequent WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. The client can then raise the window as far as it wants.

The window is unsigned, but the code that sizes DATA frames compares it as a signed value (ngx_http_v2_send_chain()):

if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) { limit = h2c->send_window; } ... if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) { frame_size = (size_t) limit; }

After the window passes 2^63, it is negative as an off_t. The frame size becomes the window value itself, a number between 2^63 and 2^64, and nginx builds a buffer whose last pointer lies before its pos pointer.

Over TLS, that buffer reaches a memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain() with that length. Our TLS test stops at that point under AddressSanitizer. Xint's write-up explains how, with the window pushed close to 2^64, this turns into a controlled out-of-bounds write and an address leak, and Xint, Rapid7, and Wiz each report code execution from it. This post goes no further than the fault.

Over cleartext HTTP/2, the same invalid buffer follows a different output path. Our cleartext test also faults under AddressSanitizer on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. The public write-ups address the TLS case.

How much traffic the known attacks require

The biggest step a WINDOW_UPDATE can take is 2^31 − 1, and a WINDOW_UPDATE frame is 13 bytes. Bringing a 64-bit window near its top therefore requires about 2^33 frames: roughly 8.6 billion frames, or about 112 GB (104 GiB).

Rapid7, which published a proof of concept, gives the same figure and adds that nginx limits control-frame traffic relative to other traffic on the connection, so its run also sends about 15 GiB of other request traffic. Its total comes to approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: about two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s link and about seventeen minutes at 1 Gbit/s. Rapid7 estimates the WINDOW_UPDATE traffic needed to reach 2^63 at about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB, half of the 104 GiB figure. It also notes that these figures describe its route and are not a proven minimum.

For defenders, this is the useful fact about the bug. At this volume, the known attacks are hard to hide: nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a single client over one long-lived connection and sends little back, much more than the requests in the access log account for.

Why it was difficult to find

The refund line has existed in nginx since HTTP/2 support arrived in 1.9.5 in 2015. Two things made it difficult to notice.

First, each piece looks correct on its own. The check on WINDOW_UPDATE is the right check. The refund is the right refund. The bug is that the check relies on an assumption the refund does not preserve.

Second, testing that waits for a crash is very unlikely to reach it, because a crash requires tens of gigabytes of input. The bad state itself can be reached with very little traffic: Censys published a cleartext test that reaches what it calls the corrupted flow-control state with a 5.69 MB capture. A test that asserts "the send window never exceeds its protocol maximum" after every frame would flag the bad state as soon as a test sequence got there. A test that waits for memory corruption would not.

The fix

The fix (6 lines added) introduces a counter, h2c->send_queued, for DATA that is queued but not yet sent. The WINDOW_UPDATE check now includes those bytes in the window:

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window - h2c->send_queued) {

From the client's perspective, queued frames still count toward the window, so the client can no longer refill credit that nginx is about to refund. On a fixed version the attempt is rejected with a flow-control error.

CVE-2026-123633: where two protections interact

An nginx worker has a fixed number of connection slots (worker_connections), which the client and upstream connections share. Since 1.19.2, when free slots run low (1/16 of the total or fewer), ngx_get_connection() calls ngx_drain_connections(), which closes connections marked "reusable": connections with nothing in progress, such as idle keep-alive connections.

This works only if a reusable connection truly has nothing in progress. For HTTP/2 that was not always the case. Two commits landed on the same day in February 2021 and were released together in 1.19.7:

"HTTP/2: fixed reusing connections with active requests" fixed a case in which a cleartext HTTP/2 connection could remain reusable while it had a request.

"HTTP/2: reuse of connections with incomplete frames" registered a connection as reusable while it waits for the remainder of a partly received frame, so that a client cannot hold slots with partial frames.

The second change is the relevant one here. As the fix commit explains, if the remainder of that frame is a HEADERS frame, a stream is created, but the reusable status was not reset until the connection next went idle. The connection then has a request and remains in the reusable queue.

If that request is proxied, nginx requests a slot for the upstream connection. If slots are short, the drain runs inside that call and can choose this same connection. The drain instructs the connection to close and nginx attempts to send GOAWAY. If that send fails, nginx frees the connection and every stream on it. Control then goes back to the upstream code, which continues to use the request it was called for.

Each change made sense on its own. The interaction between them was subtle and stayed unnoticed until this year. F5's advisory credits Albert Ebb of Metnir, Nir Ohfeld at Wiz Research, Xint.io and memN0ps of Palo Alto Networks Unit 42; nginx.org's changelog credits Albert of Vexera AI.

The fix

Two lines added: ngx_http_v2_create_stream() now calls ngx_reusable_connection(h2c->connection, 0). A connection that has a stream is never reusable, regardless of the state it was in before.

CVE-2026-121810: the same idea, in QUIC

According to the fix commit and Xint's analysis, the HTTP/3 bug reaches the same result by a different route.

In nginx's QUIC code, each QUIC connection uses one connection slot and each stream uses another. A QUIC connection may be drained only when every stream remaining in its tree can be cancelled, and nginx determines this by walking the connection's tree of streams.

ngx_quic_create_stream() removes the QUIC connection from the reusable queue and then requests a slot for the new stream. Before the fix, the new stream was added to the tree only after that. If the slot request triggered a drain that closed another, idle stream of the same QUIC connection, the code handling the closed stream walked the tree, did not find the stream being created, concluded the connection was idle, and made it reusable again. A later drain, for example when the new request connects to its upstream, could then close the QUIC connection while that request was running.

F5's advisory states that exploitation "also depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control". Xint writes that the bug "is triggered by a slightly different mechanism" from the HTTP/2 one.

The fix

Four lines added: the stream goes into the tree before the slot is requested, and is taken out again on the error paths.

CVE-2026-123634: freeing the next item of a list during the walk

When proxy_pass contains a variable, nginx resolves the host name while handling the request. If a lookup for the same name is already in progress, the new request waits on the same resolver node. When the answer arrives, nginx detaches the list of waiting contexts and calls each in turn:

next = rn->waiting; rn->waiting = NULL; while (next) { ctx = next; ... next = ctx->next; ctx->handler(ctx); }

The loop stores next before the handler call, so a handler may free its own context. The trouble starts when a handler frees a different context in the same list. This happens when two contexts belong to one request, as with a request and its mirror subrequest resolving the same name (the case Xint tested; F5 also lists SSI subrequests). If the first handler ends the request, the request's cleanup calls ngx_resolve_name_done() for the second context. That function searches the node's waiting list for the context, does not find it because the list has been detached, and frees the context regardless. The loop then advances to the freed context.

Usually nginx logs this. On vulnerable versions, when the search fails, it writes

could not cancel <name> resolving

to the error log at alert level. This line is worth searching for. It is not proof either way: the fix commit notes that one variant, while following a CNAME, produced no alert.

The fix

A context cancelled while it sits in a detached list is no longer freed immediately. Its handler is swapped for one that frees it when the loop gets to it (31 lines added). The fix also downgrades the alert to a debug message, so the line above shows up at alert level only on unpatched versions.

CVE-2026-113425: two connections, one session

With auth_http, the mail proxy asks an HTTP service to verify each login. During the wait, it holds two connections for one session: the client connection and the connection to the authentication service. The second points at the session and uses the memory pool of the client connection.

Before the fix, the reply the protocol handler had prepared for the client remained queued while the authentication request was in progress, and the client's write handler was still ngx_mail_send(). If that handler ran and the write failed because the client had reset the connection, it closed the client connection and destroyed the session. The authentication connection still pointed at the session, and the next event on that connection used freed memory.

Xint describes two conditions for this: the client's write event must already be registered (for example, because the client stopped reading replies), and the login command and the reset must be handled in the same pass of the event loop. Valid credentials are not needed, because this happens before the login is checked.

The fix

Two added lines discard the queued reply when the authentication request begins. The same release contains three further commits that block client writes while the proxy waits for the authentication response, while it connects to the upstream and reads its greeting, and while it resolves an SMTP client's address and name.

What the fixes share

The five fixes each involve minor corrections to the code. They add between 2 and 31 lines each, and the mail proxy fix came with three further commits. There is no design change needed. Each fix restores an invariant that the rest of the code already depended on:

a send window never goes above the protocol maximum

a connection with a request in progress is never reusable

an object that other code is about to use is not freed out from under it

In every case, one code path failed to keep a rule that the rest of the code relied on, and the fix makes that path keep it. As code is modified over time, it is very easy for these kinds of rules to become broken.

What to watch for

Attempts to exploit this will typically trigger some characteristic log messages. Three of these messages (the two at info and the one at warn) fall below nginx's default error_log level of error and appear only if a lower level is set. The alert messages are logged by default.

Bug

Log messages or other signals

CVE-2026-123007

A single long-lived HTTP/2 connection on which nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a client and sends little back, much more than its logged requests account for. On fixed versions a rejected attempt logs client violated connection flow control: received WINDOW_UPDATE frame with window increment ... not allowed for window ... (level info; older versions have the same message for ordinary violations). http2 flood detected (level info) on such a connection can be a failed attempt, but nginx also logs that message for several other limits.

CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810

worker process <pid> exited on signal 11 (level alert) on servers that accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and proxy to an upstream, along with worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections (level warn). A use-after-free does not always crash.

CVE-2026-123634

could not cancel <name> resolving (level alert, unpatched versions only). The absence of this message does not rule the bug out.

CVE-2026-113425

Worker crashes in a mail proxy using auth_http, with client connections reset during login.

All five

Unexpected programs launched by an nginx worker process, for example from an auditd rule on execve for the worker's user. Xint recommends this check, and it is the strongest sign of a successful attack.

Timeline

Date (UTC)

Event

Oct 11, 2026

Xint discovers the vulnerabilities

Oct 16, 2026

Reported to F5 via HackerOne

Oct 27, 2026

Reports delivered to the nginx development team

Nov 10, 2026

Xint completes patch validation

Nov 18, 2026

Public disclosure; nginx 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 released

Closing

CVE-2026-123007 sat in nginx for more than ten years. The SCTP bug has been in the Linux kernel since 2018. Xint says one of its researchers found CVE-2026-123007 by hand and an automated Xint scan found the other four nginx bugs. Several other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently. Meanwhile, nginx's advisory list has gone from two entries in 2025 to 36 so far this year. AI-assisted research is finding bugs in heavily reviewed code faster than before, and more disclosures like this one are coming.

That's a large part of why it's worth putting Cloudflare in front of your origin. A protocol bug in your web server becomes much less of a risk when the attacker can't speak that protocol to your server directly. Our edge is not affected, and the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks against your nginx end at our network. Patch anyway, lock down your origin so Cloudflare is the only way in, and use the Radar Zero Wire page to check your fleet.

articles.title: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else
articles.context: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by...
articles.full_text: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories. VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. VMSA-2026-0009 also details four more CVEs, some of them high-severity. VMware’s second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618). A KVM curiosity Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours. This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host. It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses. This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5. Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs. Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18. Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours. The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment. Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE. The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

articles.title: phpAfterShell and Critical PHP RCE Vulnerabilities: Everything You Need To Know
articles.context: phpAfterShell: File-Based Session Handling (CVE-2026-126714) Reported by depthfirst, this vulnerability exists in PHP’s default file-based session handler (session
articles.full_text:
On November 19, 2026, the PHP group published security updates addressing 17 vulnerabilities across all actively supported branches (PHP 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5). Seven of these flaws are rated Critical (CVSS 9.2) and present direct pathways to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Security teams are advised to identify and patch exposed PHP deployments, as earlier mitigation efforts implemented during October's response to "PHP2Shell" do not provide protection against all of these new exploit vectors. As of yet, no exploitation in the wild has been observed by Wiz or mentioned in public reporting.

What are these vulnerabilities?

phpAfterShell: File-Based Session Handling (CVE-2026-126714)

Reported by depthfirst, this vulnerability exists in PHP’s default file-based session handler (session.save_handler = files). When PHP writes session update progress (such as during unauthenticated file uploads), the file-write process is not atomic. If a PHP worker process is abruptly stopped during this write, due to memory limits or timeout settings, it can leave behind a partially written, malformed session file.

When a subsequent request calls session_start(), PHP attempts to deserialize this file. If the file's contents are carefully structured, this deserialization process can be manipulated to trigger an object deserialization primitive. This behavior bypasses the initial parameters set during October's PHP2Shell patches, making a fresh update necessary to secure file-based session pipelines.

PHP-FPM Request Smuggling (CVE-2026-129289)

This issue centers on how PHP-FPM processes unread request-body bytes before reusing a persistent connection. In environments where the front-end web server (such as Nginx or Apache) is configured to keep FastCGI connections open to the FPM backend, an unauthenticated user can structure a request to append a secondary, hidden FastCGI request within the request body.

Because the backend does not discard the leftover bytes, the subsequent request handled over that same connection executes the smuggled instructions. This allows a request to bypass front-end routing rules and execute with the privileges of the active FPM worker.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

The overall risk depends largely on your environment's configuration. PHP remains widely used, powering approximately 70% of websites with known server-side languages. While the technical severity of these bugs is high, executing them successfully requires specific conditions. For instance, phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) requires file-based sessions (the PHP default) and relies on finding an exploitable gadget chain in the application's code (which isn’t guaranteed to exist in every application) to achieve code execution.

Importantly, the vast majority of the other critical vulnerabilities in this release require non-default configurations or uncommon setups, such as enabling runtime-mixed session serializers, enabling PHP 8.5 exception arguments (zend.exception_ignore_args = 0), or writing startup warnings to a file-based error log on non-thread-safe builds. This ultimately means that default installations are naturally insulated from many of these vectors.

Which products are affected?

No Official Fix

Which actions should security teams take?

A. Plan a Routine Upgrade

Plan to update your PHP installations to 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, or 8.2.36 (or 8.6.0).

Rebuild affected container images and restart the PHP-FPM master service or web server process to ensure the newly patched binaries are active in memory.

B. Temporary Configuration Adjustments (If patching is delayed)

Disable Session Upload Progress: If your application does not require tracking upload progress, disabling this feature in php.ini mitigates the primary attack path for phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) in particular: session.upload_progress.enabled = 0

Disable FastCGI Connection Reuse: Block the PHP-FPM request smuggling vector by configuring Nginx (fastcgi_keep_conn off) or Apache (enablereuse=off) to close backend connections immediately.

Configure Exception Arguments (PHP 8.5): Ensure exception arguments are omitted to mitigate CVE-2026-129474: zend.exception_ignore_args = 1

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.title: Four flaws, no time to stall.
articles.context: Attackers start probing for critical Java4Shell bugs, and major vendors rush out urgent web infrastructure patches
articles.full_text:
CISA flags four actively exploited flaws, while widespread tech outages spark scrutiny over national security cuts. Attackers start probing for critical Java4Shell bugs, and major vendors rush out urgent web infrastructure patches. Plus, Ukraine arrests four suspects in a $40 million ransomware ring, Microsoft tests Lockdown Mode for Edge, and thousands of exposed AI servers show signs of tampering. Our guest is Russel Van Tuyl, Vice President of Services at SpecterOps, exploring how AI can assist offensive-security work through the Mythic control plane. A computer scientist argues the AI superintelligence race is flawed and reckless.

Remember to leave us a 5-star rating and review in your favorite podcast app.

articles.title: Critical flaw in VMware vCenter allows authentication bypass
articles.context: Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9
articles.full_text:
Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9.8 out of 10 in severity.

The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. It advises immediate patching.

Broadcom has provided fixed vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m; customers running v7.0 will only get a patch if they have an extended support contract. The patched version of VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is 5.2.5.

Customers using the VMware Telco Cloud Platform and Infrastructure, also affected, should consult KB463116 for remediation instructions.

The remaining four issues are: SDDC Manager SQL-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123891), rated 8.1 (Important) in severity; SDDC Manager authenticated command-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123892), rated 7.2 (Important); SDDC Manager local privilege-escalation vulnerability (CVE-2026-123893), rated 6.7 (Moderate), and VMware Tools SAML Token Signature Bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-123894), also rated 6.7. There are no workarounds for any of them.

Broadcom has released a supplementary FAQ providing addition information on all five bugs, in which it said, “You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as “fixed” in the [advisory]. This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines.”

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.

articles.title: CVE-2026-123890: Critical Authentication Bypass in VMware vCenter
articles.context: Broadcom assigned the vulnerability a critical CVSSv3 score of 9
articles.full_text:
Overview

On November 19, 2026, Broadcom published VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0009, addressing five vulnerabilities in VMware products. The most severe of these, CVE-2026-123890, is an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel (CWE-288) in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned the vulnerability a critical CVSSv3 score of 9.8.

A malicious actor with network access to an affected vCenter deployment may exploit CVE-2026-123890 without credentials to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system as the Administrator user. Mandiant privately reported the issue to Broadcom. Also, Mandiant/Google Threat Intelligence confirmed in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by Chinese state-linked threat actor ARMORY CASTLE as early as September 2026.

CVE-2026-123890 is distinct from the vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-59309 that Broadcom addressed earlier in 2026. The vendor FAQ states that all vCenter systems below the versions fixed by VMSA-2026-0009 require the new update, including systems that already received the earlier fix. Broadcom characterizes the vCenter update as an emergency change requiring prompt action.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-provided updates are available for CVE-2026-123890. Broadcom lists no workaround, and the patches cannot be applied using vCenter Quick Patch. Organizations should prioritize upgrading vCenter on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for their deployment.
