articles.title: AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites
articles.context: “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats
articles.full_text: Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX. These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services. As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years. Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently. Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.” “We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.” NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version. On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible. CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5. “Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.” Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8. Xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.” The AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers. AI-powered bug hunting for the win? "While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company said in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance." All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation . “AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.” There is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.” But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities. “Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz said.®

articles.title: 10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers
articles.context: Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker...
articles.full_text:
A flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in.

The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today.

F5, the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port.

Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg.

In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container.

Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today.

Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.

Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories. That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6.

Wiz PoC

NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory.

Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0.

Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup:

Flaw

What it needs

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 turned on

CVE-2026-123633

HTTP/2, with requests passed to a backend server while the worker is running low on worker_connections

CVE-2026-123634

A proxied server name built from variables, plus a server-side include (SSI) or mirror subrequest to a location that looks up the same name

CVE-2026-121810

HTTP/3 turned on

CVE-2026-113425

NGINX used as a mail proxy

HTTP/2 is on where a listen directive includes http2, or where http2 on is set. Running openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads ALPN protocol: h2 if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2.

Fixes, Workarounds and Signs of Attack

These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5:

NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 to 1.31.8 (mainline): fixed in 1.31.9

NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6, including older branches such as 1.28: fixed in 1.30.7

NGINX Plus 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1: fixed in 37.3.0.1

NGINX Plus 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1: fixed in 37.0.8.1

NGINX Plus R34 to R36: no fix listed

Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes. On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1.

After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes.

The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants.

Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that nginx -v reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory.

Xint PoC

The vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and mirror directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks.

CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs.

On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from its listen directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from the listen directive, so listen 443 ssl http2; becomes listen 443 ssl;. Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the openssl check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2.

Until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/. That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel.

For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own.

Rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis. The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail.

The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the avx512f and avx512vl features.

Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post.

Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report.

articles.title: F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCE
articles.context: Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts
articles.full_text:
Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts.

Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent.

F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround.

The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company.

None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself.

Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition.

Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server:

CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only.

CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.

CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.

CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.

CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.

CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected.

F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX.

For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed.

The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work.

A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team.

BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285.

The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe.

Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day.

That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings.

Six Other BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Flaws

Today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1:

CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8): A user with network access and at least the Guest role can send an unauthorized management request. The company says this may allow them to run system commands, create or delete files, or disable services. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6, and in BIG-IQ 8.4.2.3. Until then, the SOAP advisory explains how to limit iControl SOAP access to trusted networks and warns that blocking it on self-IP addresses may break high-availability setups.

CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST, 8.1): iControl REST tokens may not expire as expected. An attacker who already holds a token may be able to extend how long it stays valid unless its owner deletes it. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.2, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6. As a workaround, scripts that create tokens can be changed to delete them when they are no longer needed.

CVE-2026-125272 (APM, 7.5): When an APM access profile on a virtual server has a per-request policy with a form-based Logon Page, an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes as the six critical flaws.

CVE-2026-126822 (APM SAML, 7.5): When an access profile is set up as a SAML Service Provider (SP), an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes. Until then, the company suggests removing the SAML Auth agent if SAML SP is not needed, and limiting access to that virtual server to trusted client networks.

CVE-2026-126336 (APM SAML, 7.5): A SAML SP agent with encrypted assertions turned on lets an attacker crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6, and the company recommends a high-availability setup to reduce the impact.

CVE-2026-121812 (APM and SSL Orchestrator, 7.5): A per-request policy with the tmm.access.policytrace database key turned on lets an attacker crash TMM. The key is off by default. APM is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes, and for SSL Orchestrator the advisory lists fixes on the 21.1 and 17.1 branches only.

articles.title: Hostile Inference: Exploiting Docker Model Runner for Container Escapes
articles.context: Examining the llama-server logging paths, we found multiple unsanitized sinks that let an attacker place arbitrary content into the logs: • GGUF metadata key names
articles.full_text:
Local LLM inference is seeing adoption in default developer workflows, and the tooling that serves those models now ships inside products developers already trust. One of those is Docker Model Runner (DMR), the feature in Docker Desktop that pulls, runs, and serves models locally. In November 2025, we reported ZDI-26-150 / CVE-2026-28400, a denial-of-service (on macOS) stemming from an unauthenticated argument-injection vulnerability in DMR. A container created with the default set of privileges could overwrite and corrupt the Docker Desktop VM’s data disk. Further analysis, under non-default configurations, turned the same primitive into arbitrary code execution on the host, on both macOS and Windows.

In this post, we walk through the full chain: the argument-injection primitive, the host file read/write foothold it grants, how we take partial control of what gets written, and the payoff that turns a constrained file write into arbitrary code execution on the host through Docker Extensions. We then cover two further escapes we found along the way: one from an overly permissive Seatbelt sandbox configuration on macOS, and one that pivots the WSL2 VM-to-host boundary through Docker Extensions.

Background: Docker Model Runner and the host boundary

Docker Desktop helps run Docker containers on macOS, Windows, and Linux. Docker Desktop for Windows with Windows containers and Docker Desktop for Linux are out of scope for this blog. Since macOS and Windows don’t come with a Linux kernel to run Linux containers, Docker Desktop ships a LinuxKit VM that hosts the container runtime; on macOS the VM runs using the Apple Virtualization Framework, while on Windows it runs under WSL2 by default.

Linux containers and the Docker Engine components (runc, containerd, dockerd) run in the Linux VM. Bridging the gap between the host OS and the VM is a daemon called Docker Backend: com.docker.backend (macOS) or com.docker.backend.exe (Windows). This process is responsible for managing the execution environment and brokering all inter-process communication (IPC) across the VM–OS boundary.

DMR lets users pull, run, and serve models over OpenAI-compatible APIs using the same idioms as running containers (docker model pull, docker model run). Models are distributed as OCI artifacts through OCI-compliant registries and stored on the host. At the time of our research, DMR would create an instance of llama.cpp’s llama-server for inference tasks. DMR is compiled into the Docker Backend. The detail that makes this interesting: on macOS and Windows the inference process does not run inside the VM; it runs on the host, as a child of the Docker Backend, with the privileges of the user running Docker Desktop. Because models are, correctly, treated as untrusted input, the inference process is wrapped in an OS-native sandbox using Seatbelt on macOS and Job Objects on Windows. These are not equivalent boundaries, and that difference carries much of the weight on Windows, as we will see in a bit.

The DMR REST API is unauthenticated and reachable from any container at the container-internal DNS name model-runner.docker.internal over HTTP. The question we set out to answer was whether a stock container, created with no additional capabilities, flags, mounts, or privileges, could lead to a container-to-host compromise.

The Primitive: Argument Injection in _configure

We refer throughout to the DMR repository at docker/model-runner@38a800. The API is split by two prefixes, both served over model-runner.docker.internal:

Backed by the ConfigureRequest struct, the _configure endpoint accepts two JSON properties whose values are appended as command-line arguments for llama-server. It calls the “Configure” method of the scheduler.

[1] - The body of the incoming /engines/_configure request is unmarshalled.

[2.1 & 2.2] - If the body of the POST request has runtime-flags populated, the value is saved to runtimeFlags as-is. If the body has raw-runtime-flags populated, the value is tokenized through shellwords.Parse().

[3 & 4] - runnerConfig stores the inference server`s backend configuration.

[5] - The POST request's model property is used to fetch the model ID for which the config will be modified.

[6] - setRunnerConfig persists the modified configuration per model and mode (embedding or non-embedding). At this point, the altered configuration will be applied to the runner's next spawn.

Using the chat-completions endpoint /v1/chat/completions, we can load the model that would run the inference server with the altered configuration. Let's see how the arguments propagate.

[1] - The backend mode is deduced from the URL path suffix /v1/chat/completions or /v1/completions for completion mode; /v1/embeddings for embedding mode.

[2] - The chat completion request's model property contains the model for which chat completion is being invoked.

[3] - The scheduler asks the loader using load to execute the request.

[4] - If an existing runner for {backend, modelID, mode} is alive, it is reused as-is. Altered configuration is ignored if a runner already exists.

[5] - Otherwise, the persisted flags from _configure endpoint are retrieved into runnerConfig.

[6] - The runner is created via the package-level run(...) in pkg/scheduling/runner.go, passing the retrieved configuration.

[7] - run() calls backend.Run() inside a goroutine, populated with the slot's Unix socket path, the model ID, the request-deduced mode, and the attacker-controlled runnerConfig retrieved from _configure. backend.Run() invokes the inference.Backend interface; the registered and default implementation is llama.cpp`s llama-server.

[8, 8.1] - GetArgs constructs llama-server’s final command line: hardcoded performance flags, model path, socket host, mode, context-size arguments, followed by the caller-supplied runtime flags appended as-is.

[9] - The final set of arguments is supplied to sandbox.Create [10], which starts com.docker.llama-server in a macOS Seatbelt sandbox (sandbox-exec -p <profile>) with the attacker-controlled flags passed through as-is.

Using /engines/_configure or /engines/llama.cpp/_configure, a container created with default privileges can supply arbitrary command-line arguments to the llama-server process that runs on the host.

This sounds quite promising – a container created with default privileges can modify arguments of a process that runs on the host. There have been memory-corruption bugs in llama.cpp that could be triggered by malicious GGUF models. Using the DMR REST API, we can pull and load arbitrary GGUF models. So, an obvious next step would be to examine the llama-server codebase for exploitable bugs that result in arbitrary code execution, – either through malicious GGUF models or through the argument injection primitive we already have. llama-server offers no flag that executes code on its own. The useful arguments are the ones that touch the filesystem, and whether they are really useful at all depends on what the OS sandbox around llama-server permits. So, we examine the llama-server flags that result in file operations.

The Foothold: Reading and Writing Host Files

Three llama-server flags are file-operation sinks, and llama-server is the same binary on both platforms, so they behave identically. What differs is which paths the surrounding sandbox leaves reachable.

• --grammar-file: reads a file as a GBNF (GGML Backus-Naur Form) grammar; parsing errors log the file’s contents.

• --chat-template-file: reads a file as a Jinja2 chat template; its content can be logged by combining it with --verbose.

• --log-file: writes inference logs to the specified path.

macOS: Seatbelt profile

Since Docker Desktop 4.46.0, llama-server on macOS is launched via sandbox-exec using a Seatbelt profile. The profile opens with (allow default), a deliberate choice that requires enumerating the DYLD, Mach, IOKit, and Darwin surfaces llama-server depends on, and then denying known-dangerous operations.

From a process standpoint, the profile is heavily locked down, so we focused on the file operations it permits, which are:

• Reads under ~/.docker/models, ~/Library/Containers/com.docker.docker/Data, and WORKDIR (which resolves to that same Data directory).

• Writes to /dev/null, and under /private/var/, ~/Library/Containers/com.docker.docker/Data, and WORKDIR.

The directory ~/Library/Containers/com.docker.docker/Data is where Docker Desktop stores its logs, the Unix sockets for VM-host IPC, Docker Extension assets, and the data disk at vms/0/data/Docker.raw. Since the Seatbelt profile allows file reads and writes in paths under the Data tree, we can point the file read flags (--grammar-file, --chat-template-file) to read Docker Desktop logs, which have many times been found to contain credentials. This is one interesting find.

Another possibility is to point --log-file to the path of the disk located at vms/0/data/Docker.raw to overwrite it with llama-server logs. This disk contains every container, image, volume, and image build cache for the current user running Docker Desktop. The following requests from a Docker container result in the data disk being overwritten:

Windows: Job Objects

On Windows, DMR sandboxes llama-server using a Windows Job Object, built on go-winjob, with a configuration that blocks clipboard read and write, disables outgoing network traffic, prevents desktop switching and system-parameter changes, and terminates the process on unhandled exceptions.

Job Objects are used to constrain memory, CPU, process count, and process lifetime. They impose no filesystem restrictions at all, other than what's allowed by the user's privileges. The sandboxed llama-server runs with the same filesystem access as the Docker Desktop user, so the file-operation flags give arbitrary read and write access, bounded only by the user's DACL.

Using --grammar-file flag to read files from the host

Using --log-file flag to write files on the host

One will immediately notice that the username is required to construct paths of interest. DMR decides where llama-server runs by comparing the digest of its bundled binary with the Docker Hub image docker/docker-model-backend-llamacpp:latest. On a mismatch, the image from Docker Hub is pulled and the binary and DLLs are extracted to %USERPROFILE%\.docker\bin\; otherwise llama-server runs from %PROGRAMFILES%\Docker\Docker\resources\model-runner\bin. The working directory is therefore not deterministic, and path traversal into the user’s data directories is unstable. To write to %APPDATA%, %LOCALAPPDATA%, or %USERPROFILE% reliably, we need the username. We found two ways to leak it from a container without any user interaction.

The first is a UNC path. The --log-file flag accepts a UNC path, and the SMB session-setup negotiation against an attacker-controlled SMB server discloses the Docker Desktop user’s username in cleartext (and yields a capturable Net-NTLMv2 value as a bonus, which could be relayed or cracked, though the chain only needs the username). During enumeration we found the following flags also accept UNC paths: --lora, --control-vector, --model, --grammar-file, --json-schema-file, --mmproj, --api-key-file, --chat-template-file, and --model-draft.

Leaking Windows username using UNC path in --lora flag

The second is simpler and entirely local. Passing an invalid argument or value makes llama-server exit with an error, and the username appears in the error log along with the host paths it prints.

llama-server error log leaking the host username after a rejected argument value

With the username in hand, the Windows write becomes deterministic; anywhere the Docker Desktop user can read and write, from a container created with default capabilities. At this point we have, from a stock container on either platform, host file read and a write whose destination we control. We do not yet control the file’s contents, and we do not have arbitrary code execution. Both come next.

The Payload: Controlling Log Contents

--log-file writes llama-server’s own log output, not arbitrary bytes of our choosing, so the write is only as useful as our control over what llama-server logs. When llama-server loads a GGUF model, it serializes server info, the model path, and then the model metadata. GGUF models store hyperparameters, names, descriptions, and chat templates as key-value pairs inside a single file. Examining the llama-server logging paths, we found multiple unsanitized sinks that let an attacker place arbitrary content into the logs:

• GGUF metadata key names.

• GGUF metadata values, for example general.name.

• The chat template stored in the metadata key tokenizer.chat_template.

This list is not exhaustive, and using it requires the content to be in a GGUF model, which we can pull via /models/create. Two llama-server arguments make log pollution independent of a crafted model: --verbose, which logs system and user prompts along with responses (and the chat-completions endpoint is reachable from a container, so we simply send our content in the prompt and let llama-server log it for us), and --override-kv, which injects or overwrites GGUF metadata key-value pairs at runtime. Chained with the argument-injection primitive, --override-kv is a direct path to writing attacker-crafted metadata into the inference logs.

These sinks are a property of llama-server, not the host OS, so the technique carries across platforms unchanged. After this step, we control the destination path (within each platform’s cap), the file name, and, deterministically, a meaningful portion of the content. The remaining question is where a partially-controlled file write becomes arbitrary code execution. The answer is Docker Extensions.

The Payoff: Arbitrary Code Execution via Docker Extensions

Docker Extensions let third-party tools plug into Docker Desktop. They consist of a renderer that runs inside Docker Desktop’s Electron UI, an optional container backend, and executables that can be run on the host (as required by the Docker Extension). For a deeper treatment of the extension attack surface, we recommend Orange Cyberdefense’s write-up, “An Offensive Look at Docker Desktop Extensions,” by Leon Jacobs. Docker Desktop’s UI runs Electron with Node.js integration disabled and with context isolation and sandboxing enabled. Extensions have been leveraged before as a route to arbitrary code execution (e.g., CVE-2024-8695, CVE-2024-8696, ZDI-24-1019).

The renderer exposes the Docker Extensions SDK. A ddClient object offers methods for listing containers and images, navigating the Docker Desktop UI, and more. Two are relevant to this chain:

• ddClient.docker.cli.exec(cmd, [args...]): runs the Docker CLI on the host with arbitrary arguments, including powerful flags such as --privileged, volume mounts, --cap-add, --pid, --ipc, --net, and --device

• ddClient.extension.host.cli.exec(cmd, [args...]): invokes an executable located in the extension’s dedicated host/ directory on the host, unsandboxed.

Because extensions can trigger privileged host operations by design, their assets (web resources and host executables) are valuable. Furthermore, they are stored on the host at predictable paths. On macOS, those paths sit inside the Seatbelt-permitted Data subtree, which makes them writable via the --log-file primitive. On Windows they live under %APPDATA%\Docker\extensions\, which is why the username leak above matters.

To drop an executable rather than only overwrite a renderer, we also need the host filesystem to be reachable from an additional helper container that is launched by the Extension frontend. By default, Docker Desktop shares host directories into the VM with the privileges of the user running Docker Desktop: on macOS over VirtioFS (/Users, /Volumes, /private, /tmp, /var/folders), and on Windows over WSL2’s 9P protocol, with host drives mounted under /mnt.

In both cases, a container with the VM filesystem bind-mounted can write directly into the Extensions assets directory. This design choice is also why a container that has escaped to the Docker Desktop VM can reach the host filesystem as the current user running Docker Desktop.

Proof of Concept

The PoC has the following prerequisites:

1. A Docker Extension is installed

2. The user runs a malicious image or a container gets compromised

3. The user opens the extension`s UI after running it

Here’s the GGUF Payload:

We create an OCI artifact with a GGUF model with the general.name metadata key's value set to a JS block that invokes two ddClient calls that result in arbitrary code execution on the host. The vm_escape image drops the executable calc.sh on macOS and calc.bat on Windows. The chain runs as follows and is identical on macOS and Windows except for the one Windows-only username-leak step and the platform-specific paths.

1. Stage 0, from the container: on Windows, first leak the Docker Desktop username, either by pointing a UNC --log-file at an attacker-controlled SMB server or by forcing llama-server to exit on a rejected argument and then reading the username from its error log. In either event, the next step is to use the file-read primitive to read the Docker Desktop logs and enumerate the names of installed extensions; on Windows this read requires the leaked username, while on macOS all logs can be found within the Data subtree.

2. Stage 1, from the container: pull the crafted GGUF whose general.name is a JS payload that will be rendered in the extension UI. On Windows, use the username from Stage 0 to construct the %APPDATA% extension path. Point --log-file at each installed extension’s index.html and trigger inference. When the chat completion runs, llama-server logs the metadata value, overwriting the extension’s index.html on the host with the inference log containing the JS payload.

3. Stage 2, from the host: when the user opens the extension, the renderer parses the overwritten index.html and executes the injected JS. It calls ddClient.docker.cli.exec to create a helper container that mounts the VM root at /hostOS and, through the VirtioFS or 9P mount, writes an executable into the extension’s host/ directory (calc.sh on macOS, calc.bat on Windows). It then calls ddClient.extension.host.cli.exec to run the dropped executable on the host, with the Docker Desktop user’s privileges. No sandbox profile gates arbitrary code execution through the extension UI.

Here’s the PoC in action on macOS

And here it is on Windows OS

Going Further: Escaping the macOS Seatbelt Sandbox (ZDI-26-451)

In Stage 2 of the above chain, we use two ddClient calls – one to drop an executable to the host directory, and a second to invoke it. We found that it was possible to achieve arbitrary code execution on the host using a single ddClient call that uses only the Docker CLI.

The llama-server executable is generally run from the user's home directory, as DMR ships an update mechanism that downloads the latest binaries from Docker Hub into ~/.docker/bin/inference/. Our question is: what happens if the binary itself is replaced with an executable script and then invoked through the chat-completions API?

The weakness lies in the Seatbelt profile: com.docker.llama-server’s profile does not deny access to the launchservicesd Mach service. Seatbelt profiles are inherited across standard fork/exec, but macOS offers an alternate execution path through LaunchServices via the /usr/bin/open executable.

When a sandboxed process invokes open, execution is delegated to launchd, and because launchd becomes the parent, the target spawns as a new process, free of the caller’s sandbox restrictions.

Proof of Concept

Simulating a container with access to the Docker Desktop VM via a bind mount (the same VirtioFS sharing described above), we overwrite ~/.docker/bin/inference/com.docker.llama-server with a shell script. The container then calls the chat-completions API, which triggers the Docker Backend to launch our script under the Seatbelt profile.

The script creates an application bundle under /private/var/tmp (a location the profile permits writing to), containing an app that spawns a reverse shell, and then runs open -a /private/var/tmp/poc.app followed by open -a Calculator. Both calls are delegated to LaunchServices and forwarded to launchd, which spawns the apps unsandboxed. The Seatbelt profile is not inherited across that boundary, although the standard macOS protections such as TCC and Gatekeeper still hold.

Going Further: Escaping the WSL2 VM via Docker Extensions (ZDI-26-258)

On Windows, Docker Desktop uses WSL2 as the default backend. For readers interested in WSL2 VM-escape techniques that are structurally independent of DMR, our companion write-up documents several; here we share the first Docker Desktop WSL2 VM-to-host technique we found that pivots on Docker Extensions.

At Pwn2Own Vancouver 2024, STAR Labs researchers demonstrated a Docker Desktop container escape on Ubuntu (ZDI-24-1019 / CVE-2024-6222, fixed in 4.29.0), using an io_uring use-after-free to escape from the container into the VM and Docker Extensions to pivot from the VM to the host.

They installed an arbitrary extension via the extension-manager socket and navigated the UI via a socket named backend.sock to invoke a host binary. In response, Docker disabled io_uring and later enabled a flag in version 4.31.0 to only allow installation of extensions distributed through the Docker Marketplace.

In April 2025 we found that if the Docker Desktop VM is compromised, the “Allow only extensions distributed through the Docker Marketplace” flag could be toggled from the VM itself through the same backend socket. The backend socket is located at /run/host-services/backend.sock in the VM. It exposes an /app/settings API that answers both GET and POST, where GET returns the current settings and POST modifies them.

Flipping onlyMarketPlaceExtensions re-enabled arbitrary extension installation, which in turn leads to arbitrary code execution on the host. We reported our findings as ZDI-26-258 to Docker, to which Docker responded that the attack scenario falls outside of their threat model since the container-to-VM escape prerequisite is privileged in the first place. Hence, if you have a container-to-VM escape for WSL2 or an exposed Docker API (e.g., CVE-2025-9074) or a way to mount Docker sockets, you can use such VM-to-host escapes to achieve arbitrary code execution on the host.

Vendor Response and Patches

For ZDI-26-150, the fix came in three stages.

1. 0699420a (#482, 2025-12-05) removed runtime flags from POST /engines/_configure entirely, replacing them with structured backend-specific configuration.

2. 41dd3f13 (#518, 2025-12-16) reintroduced runtime flags but added validatePathSafety, which rejects any flag or value containing `/` or `\` - fixing the path operations.

3. 9acf1ed9 (#601, 2026-02-09) layered on a strict per-backend allowlist, so only safe flags such as --threads or --ctx-size pass validation.

All three shipped in DMR v1.0.16 with a follow-up hardening commit 78504107 (#667) removing --trust-remote-code, an allowlisted flag that could allow models in vLLM to escape the container. Docker Desktop users received the fixed DMR via version 4.61.0 and later.

For ZDI-26-451, commit 98038869 modified the Seatbelt profile to deny Mach service lookups for com.apple.launchservicesd and com.apple.coreservices.launchservicesd, blocking the LaunchServices path.

Disclosure Timeline

ZDI-26-150 (Docker Desktop for Mac Docker Model Runner Exposed Dangerous Function Denial-of-Service Vulnerability):

• 2025-11-05: Reported to the vendor.

• 2026-03-03: Docker confirmed the fix (CVE-2026-28400, GHSA-m456-c56c-hh5c).

• 2026-03-03: Coordinated public release of the advisory.

ZDI-26-451 (Docker Desktop for macOS Inference Server Permissive Allow List Sandbox Escape Vulnerability):

• 2026-02-25: Reported to the vendor.

• 2026-02-27: Docker merged the tightened Seatbelt profile.

• 2026-07-23: Coordinated public release of the advisory.

Conclusion

Local inference is only going to become more common in developer environments as open-weight models and the hardware to run them improve. The boundaries developers tend to trust (container isolation, sandboxed inference, and marketplace-only extensions) do not automatically extend to the attack paths that arrive with a local-AI stack. A careful audit of deliberate design choices is essential to identify potential vulnerabilities before the most critical components of the supply chain are compromised.

You can find me on Twitter at @_niteshsurana, and follow the team on Twitter, Mastodon, LinkedIn, or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

articles.title: Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw Under Active Exploitation, No Authentication Required
articles.context: A critical security flaw in Apache Roller, an open-source, Java-based blogging platform, has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to the Apache Software...
articles.full_text:
A critical security flaw in Apache Roller, an open-source, Java-based blogging platform, has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF)

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of unauthenticated deserialization in the XML-RPC endpoint that could lead to remote code execution.

"Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code," project maintainers said. "The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester."

ASF also noted that the vulnerability is the same as CVE-2026-82384 (CVSS score: 9.8), which was patched in September 2026 and listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected.

"This issue is being actively exploited," it added. ASF did not share any details on how the vulnerability is being exploited, or who is being targeted as part of these efforts.

A security researcher named n0mi1k has been credited with finding the flaw, and Matt Raible has been acknowledged for reporting it.

Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

If immediate patching is not an option, it's recommended to set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and then restart Roller.

"Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting," ASF noted.

articles.title: Two Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.context: The vulnerabilities were discovered independently by several research teams and reported to F5, which released fixed versions on November 18, 2026
articles.full_text:
F5 has disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both in the HTTP/2 module (ngx_http_v2_module). Both are rated 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 (8.1 under CVSS 3.1) and can be triggered remotely without authentication on NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled. Successful exploitation can crash NGINX worker processes, corrupt memory and potentially lead to remote code execution on the server.

NGINX is one of the most widely deployed web servers and reverse proxies, often sitting in front of multiple websites and APIs. Because the flaws are in NGINX itself, applications behind an affected NGINX instance can be exposed even when their own code is secure. One of the flaws, CVE-2026-123007, dates back to NGINX 1.9.5, released in 2015. The vulnerabilities were discovered independently by several research teams and reported to F5, which released fixed versions on November 18, 2026.

NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities: key facts

Fact

Detail

CVEs

CVE-2026-123633 (use-after-free, CWE-416); CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow leading to heap buffer overflow, CWE-191 / CWE-787)

Severity

CVSS 4.0: 9.2 (Critical); CVSS 3.1: 8.1 (High) for both

Component

NGINX HTTP/2 module (ngx_http_v2_module)

Attack

Remote, unauthenticated, no user interaction

Required configuration

HTTP/2 enabled. CVE-2026-123633 additionally requires NGINX to proxy requests to a backend and the worker process to be running low on worker_connections

Affected NGINX Open Source

CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 and later; CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 and later (up to the fixed releases below)

Fixed NGINX Open Source

1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline)

Affected / fixed NGINX Plus

R33 and later; fixed in 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 (see version table below)

Workaround

Disable HTTP/2 until patched

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; public proof-of-concept code for CVE-2026-123007 is available

What are CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007?

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety flaws in how NGINX processes HTTP/2 traffic.

CVE-2026-123633 (HTTP/2 connection use-after-free). NGINX keeps a list of idle connections that it may close when it runs out of free connection slots. An HTTP/2 connection could remain on this “reusable” list even after a new request stream started on it. When NGINX is proxying the request to a backend and is running low on worker_connections, it can close and free that connection while the request is still using it, resulting in a use-after-free in the worker process. The fix resets the connection’s reusable status when a new stream is created.

CVE-2026-123007 (HTTP/2 flow-control integer underflow). When an HTTP/2 stream is terminated, its unsent data is credited back to the connection’s flow-control window. A client could cause this window to exceed its allowed maximum, which breaks NGINX’s buffer size accounting and leads to an out-of-bounds memory write (heap buffer overflow), typically followed by a worker crash. Unlike CVE-2026-123633, this flaw does not require a backend: according to the researchers, it can also affect NGINX instances that only serve static content over HTTP/2. The fix accounts for queued frames when validating the client’s WINDOW_UPDATE.

According to F5, both flaws can lead to denial of service and memory corruption, and code execution is possible on systems where Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is disabled or can be bypassed. Researchers who reported the issues state that they were able to achieve code execution, including bypassing ASLR, on standard 64-bit systems. Both issues affect the data plane only; F5 reports no control-plane exposure.

Which NGINX versions are affected?

Any NGINX deployment with HTTP/2 enabled that runs an affected version should be considered vulnerable. Versions on branches that have reached End of Technical Support are not evaluated by F5; they should be upgraded to a supported fixed release.

Product

CVE

To address both vulnerabilities, NGINX Open Source users should move to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, and NGINX Plus users to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. Products and container images that bundle NGINX may also be affected; check the relevant vendor’s advisory for their fixed builds.

Additional NGINX vulnerabilities fixed in the same release

The same F5 security release also fixes three other critical NGINX vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. They do not involve HTTP/2, so disabling HTTP/2 does not mitigate them. Upgrading to NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or to NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, fixes all five vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-123634: a use-after-free when NGINX is configured as a proxy, the proxied server name includes variables, and a Server Side Includes (SSI) or mirror subrequest is sent to a location that resolves the same server name. Affects NGINX Open Source 0.6.18 and later.

CVE-2026-121810: a use-after-free in configurations that use HTTP/3. Affects NGINX Open Source 1.25.0 and later.

CVE-2026-113425: a use-after-free when NGINX is configured as a mail proxy. Affects NGINX Open Source 0.5.33 and later.

Is there a patch for the NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities?

Yes. F5 released fixes on November 18, 2026: NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline), and NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 (37.0.7.1 and 37.2.0.1 address CVE-2026-123633 only). Linux distributions and other vendors that package NGINX release updates on their own schedules, so organizations using distribution packages or bundled NGINX should track their vendor’s advisory.

How to mitigate the NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities before patching

If upgrading is not immediately possible, disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances, which blocks both vulnerabilities:

On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in the affected server blocks.

On all versions, remove the http2 parameter from listen directives.

Reload NGINX, confirm that old worker processes have exited, and test application compatibility. Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Additional recommended steps:

Inventory all NGINX deployments, including reverse proxies, load balancers, ingress layers and container images, and identify which have HTTP/2 enabled.

Prioritize internet-facing instances, and those that proxy traffic to backends.

Monitor for unexpected NGINX worker crashes or processes launched by NGINX, which can be general signs of exploitation attempts.

Are the NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, there are no reports of in-the-wild exploitation. However, public proof-of-concept code for CVE-2026-123007 has been released, including a script that triggers the flaw and an exploit demonstrating unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable NGINX server in a lab environment. Together with the detailed technical write-ups published alongside the disclosure, this significantly shortens the time to working exploits. Given how widely NGINX is exposed to the internet, organizations should treat these vulnerabilities as urgent.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable NGINX versions, including NGINX installed from OS packages and NGINX bundled in container images, and to understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, so they can prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone. Orca’s runtime sensor can also help detect post-exploitation activity on affected hosts.

articles.title: Five Critical Vulnerabilities Found in World's Most Widely Used Open-Source Web Server
articles.context: It can allow attackers to exploit memory-handling flaws in the request-processing path CVE-2026-121810: a vulnerability affecting NGINX servers using HTTP/3 (QUIC) with upstream...
articles.full_text:
Several security research teams have independently discovered five new critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, the world's most widely used open-source web server that powers more than 225 million websites worldwide.

The flaws could lead to attackers remotely taking control of NGINX-based websites without being authenticated.

On November 18, security researchers at Google Cloud-owned Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7 and Xint all disclosed several vulnerabilities in NGINX 1.31.8, the current release.

The set of vulnerabilities includes CVE-2026-113425, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123634 – all with a critical severity rating of 9.2 (CVSS 4.0).

However, the number of flaws reported differs between their disclosures. Ikotas Labs has highlighted one vulnerability, which it calls ‘NGINX2Shell,’ while Wiz researchers have detailed two vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Xint, meanwhile, has documented five vulnerabilities under the collective name ‘NGINX2Root.’

Some of these research teams have publicly disclosed they used AI models and collaborated with OpenAI to find these vulnerabilities.

Wiz Report: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free vulnerability that can cause memory corruption, while CVE-2026-123007 involves an integer underflow in HTTP/2 flow control. Both could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely on vulnerable servers.

According to Wiz, both vulnerabilities affect a wide range of NGINX versions, with one dating back to 2015 and the other to 2020. Exploitation requires HTTP/2 to be enabled.

Wiz said it reported the flaws to F5, the maintainer of NGINX, which has since addressed both flaws in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline).

Administrators unable to upgrade immediately are advised to disable HTTP/2 until the patches can be applied.

Xint’s Added Details for CVE-2026-113425, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-123634

In addition to the two HTTP/2 vulnerabilities identified by Wiz, Xint disclosed three further NGINX vulnerabilities as part of its NGINX2Root research:

CVE-2026-123634: a vulnerability affecting NGINX configurations using the resolver, proxy_pass and mirror directives together with mirror_request_body off. It can allow attackers to exploit memory-handling flaws in the request-processing path

CVE-2026-121810: a vulnerability affecting NGINX servers using HTTP/3 (QUIC) with upstream proxy connections, including configurations using proxy_pass, fastcgi_pass or grpc_pass. It creates another potential route to remote code execution

CVE-2026-113425: a vulnerability affecting NGINX Mail Proxy deployments using the proxy and auth_http directives. It exposes servers using this functionality to a separate attack path

All three additional vulnerabilities are addressed by the NGINX 1.31.9 release, but administrators and operators are advised to consult the individual advisories for configuration-specific mitigations.

Xint said each of the five NGINX vulnerabilities has a proven exploit, although the precise configuration requirements and affected versions differ.

The security company also said that, while it had no evidence of exploitation in the wild at the time of publication, the age of some vulnerabilities means exploitation cannot be ruled out.

The CVEs are listed on a number of CVE databases including OpenCVE and CVE.org.

articles.title: Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem
Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007
articles.context: This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.

NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server, it powers more than 225 million websites.

Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.

We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

Responsible disclosure timeline

October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.

November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.

November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.

November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.

November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.

Overview

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.

Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.

What is NGINX?

NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.

NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

The Vulnerabilities

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Tracking ID

The bug

What an attacker can achieve

CVE-2026-123633

HTTP/2 connection use-after-free

Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow

Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication.

Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

Impact

On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.

An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.

Coordinated disclosure

We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.

Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release

F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table):

Mitigation and detection

Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.

37.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1
