In this article

Java4Shell can cause memory corruption and, in some applications, remote code execution

Exploitation depends on the Java runtime, processor and application

Most home users are unlikely to be affected, but organizations should patch promptly

A critical-sounding Java flaw is making headlines. Most consumers are unlikely to be affected, but companies running Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and similar tools have work to do.

On November 17, Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption bug in Java’s Base64 decoder. Security firm Calif discovered the flaw and named it Java4Shell. CISA urged organizations to patch immediately.

After a run of high-profile computer problems and security scares, it’s understandable that another vulnerability with a catchy name would set alarm bells ringing. But it’s important to separate the potential damage from the likelihood of being affected. This is a serious issue for organizations running vulnerable applications, not a reason for every home user to assume their computer is at risk.

It doesn’t help that organizations give out different CVSS scores for the same vulnerability.

Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 and describes it as “difficult to exploit.”

Calif rates it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

Meanwhile, there are currently no reports of abuse in the wild. Calif demonstrated remote code execution without logging in on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It also demonstrated post-login code execution on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Technical details

Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. It’s used in login protocols, file uploads and network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 CPU instructions.

The bug is in hand-written assembly code for that fast path. A short, malformed input can write 62 bytes past the end of a memory buffer.

For remote code execution, several conditions have to line up:

The right processor. The flaw only affects x86-64 CPUs that support the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set. Examples include Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 chips aren’t affected.

A recent OpenJDK-based Java. The flaw affects OpenJDK from 17.0.6 onward, and the distributions built on it.

An exposed Java service. The attacker has to feed crafted data to a Java application that decodes it. Oracle notes it can only be exploited by supplying data to the affected APIs, such as through a web service. It can’t be exploited through untrusted Java Web Start applications or applets.

A target-specific exploit. Calif says there is no universal exploit. Each chain needs a decoder route, a feedback path, a heap layout, and an application-specific action. The attack also works best with low, stable network latency, and Calif rented a VM in the same region as its target.

An ordinary home PC rarely runs a Java server that accepts Base64 input from the internet. Organizations running affected Java applications on vulnerable processors should patch promptly, since attackers may find narrow, application-specific paths to remote code execution.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: Java4Shell: Critical OpenJDK Flaw Allows Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.context: 2 (Critical), according to Calif, which discovered the flaw, and 8
articles.full_text:
Key findings

CVE-2026-114938, which has been dubbed Java4Shell, is a critical heap overflow in the Base64 decoder of the OpenJDK HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM) on x86-64. It has a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), according to Calif, which discovered the flaw, and 8.1 (High) on CVSS 3.1 per OpenJDK's advisory.

A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can deliver crafted Base64 input to a vulnerable Java process can corrupt heap memory and achieve remote code execution (RCE). No user interaction is required for server-side attacks.

Only hosts with AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) are exposed. That means Intel Ice Lake or newer, or AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 hosts, Java 11 and standard OpenJDK 8 are not affected.

Security company Calif demonstrated pre-authentication RCE in test configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026. Fixed builds end in ".1", and the same version number without the suffix remains vulnerable.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of publication, but a proof-of-concept trigger is public. Symantec and Carbon Black Security Response is investigating, and up-to-date protection information will be added to our Protection Bulletin.

Overview

A critical vulnerability in OpenJDK, CVE-2026-114938 (aka Java4Shell), was disclosed on November 17, 2026. The flaw sits in the optimized Base64 decoder that the HotSpot JVM uses on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support. Oracle and OpenJDK have released patches, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged immediate patching. At time of writing on November 18 there has been no evidence found of in-the-wild exploitation of this bug.

Java4Shell is significant because Base64 decoding is routine in server software. Authentication headers, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertions, file uploads and API fields are all Base64 encoded, so internet-facing login and API services decode attacker-controlled data by design. Calif, the security firm that first reported the flaw, published a standalone trigger and said product-specific exploit chains would be held back until upgrades are more widespread. Details about the flaw became public before patches were available.

How the vulnerability works

The store mask used by the decoder is wrong when the Base64 input ends in padding. As a result, the calculated output length underflows, and the decoder writes a full 64 bytes into a buffer that is smaller than that. According to Calif, a 65-byte input overflows the heap by 62 bytes, which corrupts adjacent Java objects, allowing an actor to gain heap read and write primitives, which makes the bug remotely exploitable.

Exploitation of the heap overflow depends on the layout of the target application, and a failed attempt can crash the JVM. A crash would result in denial of service, but Calif reported that retries often succeed. Heap memory disclosure is also possible. A client-side variant exists: a Java application that connects over Transport Layer Security (TLS) to a malicious server can be compromised.

Who is affected?

Affected versions are OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (including 17.0.6 to 17.0.21), Java 21 before 21.0.13.1, Java 25 before 25.0.5.1 and Java 27. Oracle also lists Java SE 8 8u511b33-perf. Builds from Oracle, Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat and GraalVM are affected. Hosts must also run on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Ice Lake and newer and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Java 11, standard OpenJDK 8, ARM64 hosts and x86 processors without AVX-512 VBMI are not affected.

Enterprise and server deployments carry the most risk, particularly identity, application lifecycle, build pipeline, artifact and data platforms. Popular Java-based applications such as Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, Kafka and Elasticsearch could be affected. Many of these products ship their own bundled Java runtime, so organizations should check each vendor for updated releases and should not rely on the host's Java version alone. Consumers are mainly exposed through Java client applications.

Exploitation status

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of November 18, 2026. However, Calif published a trigger that reproduces the overflow. It also showed pre-authentication RCE in Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory and PingFederate, as well as post-authentication RCE in Apache Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Fake proof-of-concept repositories are likely to appear, and unpatched internet-facing Java services on AVX-512 hardware should be treated as potentially exposed.

Patching

Oracle released fixes in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update, alongside an OpenJDK advisory of the same date. Fixed builds are:

Java 17: 17.0.21.1

Java 21: 21.0.13.1

Java 25: 25.0.5.1

Java 27: 27.0.1.1

Java SE 8 (-perf builds): see the Oracle advisory

A running JVM keeps the vulnerable code until it is restarted, so every Java process must be restarted after upgrading. Containers should be rebuilt on patched base images. Downstream vendors are rolling out their own fixes, and fixed builds for several of them were not yet published at time of writing. CISA also advised identifying all Java installations, including those bundled in third-party applications, containers and appliances, and prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Interim mitigations

Where patching is not immediately possible, Calif lists two JVM options. Both require a restart and neither replaces patching.

Add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the Base64 intrinsics. This may slow Base64-heavy workloads.

Add -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512. Use this on x86-64 hosts only, because the JVM will not start with it on ARM.

Do not set -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own. It breaks JVM startup and can cause an outage if pushed fleet-wide.

CISA also recommended compensating controls such as validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Defenders can look for Base64 tokens that contain an equals sign and whose length is not a multiple of four, decoder exceptions such as “Input byte array has wrong 4-byte ending unit” in application logs, and unexpected JVM crashes or new hs_err_pid log files. The exception is thrown after the overflow, so it indicates an attempt and not a blocked attack.

Protection

Symantec and Carbon Black Security Response is investigating this vulnerability, guidance and reproduction steps. Full protection information is in the Symantec Protection Bulletin for Java4Shell. The bulletin will be updated continuously as new information becomes available.

articles.title: Three AI Models Agree on Just One of 121 Potential Code Flaws
articles.context: " If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit
articles.full_text:
Three frontier AI models given the same open source code to audit have produced vulnerability findings that barely overlap, according to new frontier AI research. Of 121 distinct potential issues, Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Z.ai's GLM-5.3 all flagged just one, software security firm Echo found.

Echo published the comparison in its November 18 research. Each model worked through two Maven libraries and one npm package with Echo's own hunting framework and the same validation process. Echo reached GPT-5.6 Sol through Daybreak, the program OpenAI runs for vetted security teams.

Of the 121 issues, 83% (100), came from a single model and 20 from the other two.

Read more on AI vulnerability discovery: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

Where the AI Models Disagreed

Claude Mythos logged the most validation passes overall, with 25, against nine for GLM-5.3 and eight for GPT-5.6 Sol. But GPT-5.6 Sol accounted for six of the seven passes on one Maven library, and GLM-5.3 found six validated issues on the other that its rivals missed.

Severity ratings split too. GLM-5.3 rated one flaw in an npm package with more than 350 million monthly downloads as Critical, Claude Mythos put it at High and GPT-5.6 Sol treated it as documented behavior rather than a bug. Automated validation rated it Low.

GPT-5.6 Sol finished its hunts in about 24 minutes, against roughly 198 for Claude Mythos and 174 for GLM-5.3. GLM-5.3 was the cheapest overall, with its three hunts costing about $22, against $303 for Claude Mythos and $30 for GPT-5.6 Sol, though Echo said the costs reflected its own access terms.

How Many AI Findings Held Up

The nine runs produced 446 initial findings, cut to 152 after cleanup. Of those, 74 were rated High or Critical, and 55 went through automated proof-of-concept testing after duplicates were set aside. Forty-two passed.

Echo cautioned that the 42 were not necessarily distinct bugs, since an issue found by more than one model could be credited to each. Findings rated Medium or Low were never tested, so a previously known flaw that Claude Mythos rated Medium never reached validation.

Echo security researcher Yuval Saggie said the race to find the best model was "the wrong question." If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit."

Each model ran only once, and Echo called the exercise "a controlled comparison rather than a comprehensive benchmark." It said automated validation did not amount to confirmation from the projects' maintainers.

Echo said the projects would stay unnamed, and technical details unpublished, until their maintainers had been notified.

articles.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Check Your Java Services Now
articles.context: Check Point IPS protection for the public PoC is available now, but patching is still the only complete fix
articles.full_text:
Bottom line: A single malformed Base64 string can give an attacker code execution on unpatched Java runtimes, often without logging in. Fixes were released on November 17, 2026. Inventory your Java runtimes, patch identity providers first, and use a startup flag where you cannot patch today. Check Point IPS protection for the public PoC is available now, but patching is still the only complete fix. Our full advisory has every detail.

What we see

The flaw: On recent Intel and AMD x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI, Java’s hand-tuned Base64 decoder miscalculates the output length for the padded tail of a short malformed input. The result is a write of 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its buffer, depending on the padding. Java rejects the input, but only after the write.

The impact: The bytes written are fixed, so on its own the overflow usually crashes Java. Calif, the firm that found the flaw, reports shaping server memory so the overflow enlarges a neighboring array, which gives read and write access and then code execution. It demonstrated this without authentication against default installations of Keycloak, self-managed Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login against Apache Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. The same corruption can also expose heap memory, including private keys, session tokens, and credentials, without any code execution.

Why login is often not needed: Applications decode Base64 before authentication, in HTTP Basic authentication headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and file uploads.

Side effects: Failed attempts often crash the Java process, and an attacker can often retry. Calif also reports that a Java client can be compromised by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Exploitation status (as of November 18, 2026):We are not aware of confirmed exploitation. However, the root cause is public, and a triggering input has been visible since September 9, 2026. Several independent teams have reproduced crashes and the memory leak in lab conditions, though not code execution as of November 18.

Important Note : There is no universal exploit, because each product needs its own memory layout and timing. That slows mass exploitation but does not protect a specific, high-value target such as an identity provider.

Are you affected?

A system is vulnerable only when all three conditions are true: an unpatched runtime, a specific processor, and attacker-controlled Base64 that reaches Java’s standard decoder.

Condition

Affected

Not affected

Java runtime

Unpatched OpenJDK-based builds from 17.0.6 onward on Java 17, and all Java 21, 25, and 27 builds before the fix, from any vendor. Oracle also lists its Java 8 performance build.

Java 17 releases before 17.0.6, standard Java 8 and Java 11, and fixed builds (Oracle: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1)

Processor

x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI, including Intel Xeon Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 and newer. The CPU must expose avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2

ARM64, and x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI

Reachability

Attacker-controlled Base64 reaches Java’s standard decoder (login headers, tokens, uploads)

No path for external input to reach the standard Base64 decoder

How to check

Runtime: Build an inventory of the runtime each application actually uses. Bundled runtimes do not get OS updates, so check the one each application ships with.

Processor: Run the Linux command in the advisory. A host is affected only if avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2 all appear in its CPU flags (/proc/cpuinfo). Use the result to prioritize, not to dismiss a finding, because a cloud resize can silently move a workload onto an affected processor.

Reachability: This is the hardest to settle from the inside, because it depends on how each application is deployed and what sits in front of it.

What else is in scope

Self-managed Jira and Confluence: The risk applies to self-managed Data Center deployments. Atlassian manages the Java runtime for Atlassian Cloud. Atlassian installers typically ship their own bundled runtime, so operating system patches alone do not fix a self-managed instance.

Spring Boot: Treat every Spring Boot service on an affected runtime as in scope. Researchers reached code execution in sample Spring Boot applications, where login handling, tokens, and file uploads often decode Base64 before a user is authenticated.

Apache Tomcat: It was not tested and no advisory links it to this CVE. It runs a large share of Java web applications and is embedded in Spring Boot by default, so include every Tomcat server in your inventory.

Anything else: If you cannot rule out that attacker input reaches Java’s built-in Base64 decoder, assume it does. Vendor advisories cover only Java 17, 21, 25, and 27, so move any other release to a fixed build rather than assuming it is safe.

What to do: patch first

Updating the Java runtime is the only complete fix.

Fix availability (as of November 18, 2026)

Fixed builds shipped: Oracle, Amazon (Corretto), Azul (Zulu). For Oracle, only builds ending in .1 are patched.

Not yet released: Red Hat and Eclipse Temurin

Status unconfirmed: Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, BellSoft Liberica. Check each vendor’s page.

Bundled runtimes: Products that ship their own Java runtime need an update from the product vendor.

Patch in this order

Identity providers: Keycloak and PingFederate

Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and Artifactory (for Jira and Confluence, apply Atlassian’s update or the startup flag)

Other internet-facing Java services that handle logins, tokens, or uploads

Internal systems and Java clients

If you cannot patch today

Add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the Java startup options and restart the service. This turns off only the accelerated Base64 decoder. Applications that decode large volumes of Base64 may slow down, so test first.

Alternatively, use -XX:UseAVX=2. It turns off AVX-512 entirely, at a broader performance cost. Java on ARM64 rejects this option and will not start.

Remove either option after you have patched.

Avoid: -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own. It can stop Java from starting.

Verify: A patch or a flag takes effect only after Java restarts. Confirm on the running process:

jcmd <pid> VM.version

jcmd <pid> VM.flags

VM.version should show a fixed build. For Oracle that is a version ending in .1, such as 17.0.21.1, and other vendors use their own version strings. If you set the startup flag, VM.flags should list -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics.

Elasticsearch

Elasticsearch ships with a bundled Java runtime, and Calif demonstrated code execution against it after login. Some attacks depend on a request arriving in pieces, so a reverse proxy that waits for complete requests (nginx does by default) blocks those. This attack works in a single complete request, so request buffering does not stop it. Treat clusters with anonymous access or weak credentials as exposed without a login. Apply Elastic’s update, or add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics in a new .options file under config/jvm.options.d/ (/etc/elasticsearch/jvm.options.d/ for DEB and RPM installs) and restart each node. Do not edit the root jvm.options file.

Block known exploit attempts at the gateway

Check Point has released an IPS protection, [protection name / ID], that detects and blocks the public proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-114938. Make sure it is set to Prevent on your Quantum gateways, especially for traffic going to internet-facing Java services. This reduces exposure while you patch. It does not replace the runtime update, because it targets the known triggering input and not every possible variant

How to spot attempts

Failed attempts often crash Java, so watch for unexpected service restarts and new hs_err_pid<pid>.log files, which the JVM writes on a fatal crash. Crashes during garbage collection are also a known sign of this corruption. Then list every place where attacker-controlled Base64 reaches Java before login: HTTP Basic headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and file uploads.

Find the Java services you expose to the internet

Check Point Exposure Management can identify internet-facing assets that appear to run Java, including the version, so you know where to start. This is a passive check of technologies and versions. It does not exploit anything or send attack traffic to your services.

A technology check shows where Java is present. It cannot confirm the processor or whether attacker-controlled input reaches Java’s Base64 decoder, so use the results to prioritize and still run the runtime and processor checks above.

Beyond this flaw, Exposure Management helps you find, prioritize, validate, and fix the exposures that matter most across your environment:

Threat Intelligence: Know which threats and vulnerabilities attackers are targeting.

CAASM: Get a continuously updated view of your assets and where they are exposed.

Vulnerability Prioritization: Focus on the exposures with real risk, not the longest list.

Agentic Exposure Validation (AEV): Test whether an exposure is exploitable.

Safe Remediation: Fix confirmed exposures without disrupting the business.

articles.title: ZDI-26-1037: (0Day) (Pwn2Own) United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP Backend Configuration Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP backend configuration requests. The issue results from the lack of authentication prior to allowing access to functionality. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device.

Additional Details

Since 04/14/26, ZDI has made multiple attempts to contact United Chargers to establish a vendor disclosure channel for the vulnerabilities identified in the Grizzl-E Smart 40A during Pwn2Own Automotive 2026. Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Disclosure Timeline

2026-11-06 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-18 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-18 - Advisory Updated

Credit

Cyrill Bannwart, Emanuele Barbeno, Yves Bieri, Lukasz D., Urs Mueller of Compass Security

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of FTP URL paths during firmware updates. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device.

Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

articles.title: ZDI-26-1031: (0Day) LiteLLM MCP Command Injection Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LiteLLM
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LiteLLM. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of MCP stdio configurations. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to execute a system call. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.

Additional Details

06/17/26 - ZDI reported the vulnerability to the vendor07/03/26 - ZDI asked for updates08/28/26 - ZDI asked for updates09/15/26 - the vendor closed the report as a false positive10/26/26 - ZDI disputed the vendor's closure as the existing fix was incomplete10/29/26 - the vendor reopened the report agreeing the mitigation wasn't enough10/30/26 - ZDI asked for the fix plan11/04/26 - ZDI notified the vendor of the intention to publish the case as a 0-day advisory on 11/18/2611/13/26 - the vendor stated it planned to ship a fix and issue a GHSA before the 11/18 deadline11/16/26 - ZDI asked the vendor to confirm whether the fix/GHSA had shipped11/17/26 - the vendor clarified no separate patch is coming, and disputed that the report describes a vulnerability11/17/26 - ZDI confirmed the zero-day advisory would publish on 11/18/26

-- Mitigation: The vendor recommends the following mitigation: Stdio MCP servers run admin-chosen host commands; only proxy admins can create or test them. The CVE-2026-42271 allowlist doesn’t limit what admins can run, isn’t a security control, and will be removed. From v1.104.0, stdio servers are disabled unless LITELLM_ENABLE_MCP_STDIO=true is set in env (not via API/config/DB); to stay safe, upgrade to 1.104.0+ and leave unset. Always replace any default/example master key with a strong random value; v1.104.0+ blocks startup if unset, empty, or sk-1234.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of ASL files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an integer overflow before allocating a buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

articles.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
articles.context: ” Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet
articles.full_text: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November, which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938, which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning. The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw, says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. Akamai’s Chief Information Security Architect Jan Schaumann, writing on the Openwall project’s mailing list, expressed a little discomfort with Calif’s work. “Calif.io set their priorities on publicity-maxxing, it seems,” he wrote, pointing out that the flaw-finding firm’s announcement of Java4Shell opens by stating “After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.” Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.” That second sentence perhaps supports Calif’s assertion that news of the flaw leaked before disclosure. The rest of Big Red’s flaws Java4Shell deserves a place high up on patch priority lists. So do the six 10.10 flaws Oracle reported, three in its Access Manager product, one in the Oracle Platform Security for Java, another in the WebLogic Server, and one in Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition. Big Red also repaired five 9.9-rated bugs, in Oracle Text, Hyperion, RDBMS, and Autovue. The November patch dump also includes 28 flaws rated 9.8/10. By Tenable Security’s count, 249 of the patches are for high severity bugs. Oracle’s Hyperion enterprise performance management accounts for 267 of the bugs. Such is life in the age of AI-powered flaw finders – which Calif says burned through just $200 worth of tokens to find Java4Shell. ®

articles.title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Frequently asked questions about OpenJDK remote code execution vulnerability
articles.context: Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory
articles.full_text:
Java4Shell is a flaw in how Java decodes Base64 data. Calif, which found it, says it can let attackers run code on widely used Java applications without logging in. Oracle released fixed Java builds on November 17, and Calif is withholding its exploits for individual applications for now.

Key takeaways

CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell, is an OpenJDK memory corruption vulnerability that Oracle scores 8.1 on CVSS 3.1, and Calif says its testing showed attackers could run code without logging in on applications such as Atlassian Jira and Jenkins.

As of November 17, Tenable is not aware of any reports that attackers have exploited this flaw, though Calif has published a PoC that triggers the bug without taking control of the system and a second researcher reports building a working exploit.

Oracle released fixed builds on November 17, and according to Calif, only systems running an affected Java version on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI can be affected.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Java4Shell, a vulnerability in OpenJDK that was patched on November 17, 2026.

FAQ

When was Java4Shell first disclosed?

On November 17, security firm Calif said on X that it had found and reported the flaw, and that details of Java4Shell, as Calif named it, had leaked ahead of a fix. Later that day, Oracle released its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU), and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group published its own advisory. Calif then published its technical write-up. Oracle credits Quang Luong of Calif.io and Albert Yang for reporting the vulnerability.

Since the vulnerability has leaked: Calif discovered and reported Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).We're publishing technical details by 1 PM Pacific today, after Oracle releases a patch.Stay tuned! https://t.co/No5hJXK1Zx

— Calif (@calif_io) November 17, 2026

What is CVE-2026-114938?

CVE

Description

CVSSv3.1

CVE-2026-114938

OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Memory Corruption Vulnerability (Java4Shell)

8.1

CVE-2026-114938 is a memory corruption vulnerability in the part of Java that decodes Base64, a common format that applications use to send data such as login details and file uploads. Oracle assigned it a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and rates its attack complexity as high. Calif says it scores 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. An attacker does not need to log in to exploit it remotely. According to Oracle, the flaw can only be exploited when an application passes untrusted data to the affected Java APIs, such as through a web service.

Is CVE-2026-114938 among the Java fixes in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU?

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 is addressed by one of the 11 Java SE security patches in Oracle's November 2026 CSPU, released November 17. For a breakdown of all the patches in this release, see our blog post on Oracle's November 2026 CSPU.

What is known about CVE-2026-114938?

The flaw is in a performance shortcut that Java uses to decode Base64 data faster on certain Intel and AMD processors. When the shortcut receives a specially crafted Base64 string, it writes data beyond the memory it set aside. That can corrupt other information the application is holding in memory.

According to Calif, an attacker can use this flaw in two ways. The first, which Calif calls "JavaBleed," lets an attacker read the application's memory. That memory may hold secrets such as keys and tokens. The second lets an attacker run their own code on the server. Calif also says that each application needs its own exploit, and that a failed attempt can crash the application, though an attacker can often try again.

Exposure depends on the processor as well as the Java version. According to Calif, Java uses the affected code only on x86-64 processors that support a feature called AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon processors from the Granite Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Sapphire Rapids and Ice Lake families, as well as AMD processors based on Zen 4 or newer. Calif says systems with ARM64 processors are not affected. On Linux, a system meets this requirement when its processor reports all four of the avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2 flags.

Which versions of Java are affected?

The OpenJDK Vulnerability Group lists the Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 release lines as affected by CVE-2026-114938. Calif says OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer are affected. Oracle lists the following Oracle builds as affected:

Product

Affected versions (and likely earlier)

Oracle Java SE

8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3

Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition

21.3.20.0.3

Oracle lists only builds it supports and says earlier versions are likely also affected. The Java 8 build on Oracle's list is its Enterprise Performance Pack. The OpenJDK advisory does not list standard Java 8 or Java 11 as affected by this vulnerability.

I don't use Oracle's Java builds. Am I affected?

Possibly. The flaw is in OpenJDK code, and according to Calif, the following Java distributions built from OpenJDK are also vulnerable:

Amazon Corretto

Eclipse Temurin

Microsoft Build of OpenJDK

Azul Zulu

BellSoft Liberica

SAP SapMachine

Red Hat OpenJDK

Oracle OpenJDK

Each vendor releases fixed builds on its own schedule, so check with your distribution's vendor for its fixed versions.

Which applications are known to be affected?

Calif says its initial testing showed that an attacker could run their own code on the following applications in their default configurations, when they run on an affected version of Java on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI. The list is not exhaustive, according to Calif.

Application

Calif's result

Keycloak

Exploitable before login

Atlassian Jira

Exploitable before login

Atlassian Confluence

Exploitable before login

JFrog Artifactory

Exploitable before login

Jenkins

Exploitable before login

PingFederate

Exploitable before login

Apache Kafka Broker

Exploitable after login

Apache Solr

Exploitable after login

Elasticsearch

Exploitable after login

Gerrit

Exploitable after login

Spinnaker

Exploitable after login

Calif also said it ran its own code on sample applications built on frameworks including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Calif adds that everyday functions, including authentication and file uploads, can lead to the vulnerable code, so more applications than the ones Calif tested may be exposed. Calif says researcher samczsun gave it a client-side exploit, and that a Java program can be compromised when it connects over TLS to a server an attacker controls, even if the program offers no service of its own. Calif says it will publish its exploits for individual products at a later date.

Has Java4Shell been exploited in the wild?

As of November 17, we are not aware of any reports of exploitation of CVE-2026-114938, and it is not listed in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Yes. Calif published a PoC alongside its write-up that triggers the flaw without taking control of the system. It shows whether a given Java version and processor reproduce the bug. It does not show whether a particular application is exposed.

On November 17, Kevin Breen of Immersive said on X that they had developed a working exploit for CVE-2026-114938. According to Breen, the exploit has to be adapted to each application. It works only on a vulnerable version of Java running on a processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, and only against applications that decode Base64 data. Breen also said that Apache Tomcat's Basic authentication and the java-jwt library provide ways to exploit the flaw before a user logs in. The post does not say that the exploit has been released.

Have a functional exploit POC for CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell. This is not a generic exploit and will need to be application specific, you need a CPU with AVX-512 VBMI support, vulnerable JDK Version, and the app needs to use Base64, note that tomcats basic auth and java-jwt…

— KevTheHermit (@KevTheHermit) November 17, 2026

Are patches available?

Yes. On November 17, Oracle released the following fixed builds:

Java line

Affected Oracle build

Fixed Oracle build

Java 8 Enterprise Performance Pack

8u511b33-perf

8u513-perf

Java 17

17.0.21.0.3

17.0.21.1

Java 21

21.0.13.0.3

21.0.13.1

Java 25

25.0.5.0.3

25.0.5.1

Java 27

27.0.1.0.3

27.0.1.1

For Oracle GraalVM, see Oracle's advisory. For other Java distributions, see each vendor's advisory.

Are there any mitigations?

Calif identified two Java startup options that keep the vulnerable code from running. The first, -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, turns off the Base64 shortcut. The second, -XX:UseAVX=2, turns off AVX-512 instructions. According to Calif, the second option applies only to x86-64 systems, and Java on ARM processors fails to start with it. Neither Oracle nor the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group mentions these options in its advisory.

Has Java been targeted historically?

Yes. CISA's KEV catalog includes 13 vulnerabilities in Oracle Java SE and the Java Runtime Environment (JRE), six of which are known to have been used in ransomware campaigns. Those six are:

CVE

KEV name

Added to KEV

CVE-2013-0431

Oracle JRE Sandbox Bypass Vulnerability

May 25, 2022

CVE-2013-0422

Oracle JRE Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

May 25, 2022

CVE-2013-2465

Oracle Java SE Unspecified Vulnerability

March 28, 2022

CVE-2012-4681

Oracle Java SE Runtime Environment (JRE) Arbitrary Code Execution Vulnerability

March 3, 2022

CVE-2012-1723

Oracle Java SE Runtime Environment (JRE) Arbitrary Code Execution Vulnerability

March 3, 2022

CVE-2012-0507

Oracle Java SE Runtime Environment (JRE) Arbitrary Code Execution Vulnerability

March 3, 2022

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-114938 has been classified as a "Vulnerability of Interest" as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Are Tenable products affected by this vulnerability?

Tenable is aware of this vulnerability and is investigating whether it affects any Tenable products.

Has Tenable released any product coverage for this vulnerability?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-114938 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

How can Tenable customers find affected assets?

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can go to Explore > Software to view installed software across their assets, then filter by product name and version to look for Java installations to compare against the affected versions above. Exposure also depends on the processor, as described above. Software data comes from credentialed and agent scans. For details, see Use the Software Page.

Tenable One Vulnerability Management customers can also use the Java Visibility and Exposures report, which lists Java installations and the hosts where they were detected.

Tenable One Attack Surface Management customers can find internet-facing assets running Java with the filter Programming Languages contains Java. Those assets can then be scanned with other Tenable sensors to check whether they are affected by CVE-2026-114938.

Get more information

Calif: Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere

articles.title: CVE-2026-114938: Critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java
articles.context: This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a...
articles.full_text:
Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK Java (CVE-2026-114938), dubbed “Java4Shell,” with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 that may lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). This vulnerability can be triggered by sending a malformed Base64 input to affected JVMs, which can result in RCE.

Details

This vulnerability affects OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed.

This vulnerability does require a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI; these include commonly deployed processors from both Intel and AMD, resulting in a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems, including both on-premise and cloud environments.

Cisco Talos would like to thank Calif.io for sharing the details of the vulnerability in advance of public disclosure.

Observed exploitation

Talos has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure. Talos will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and will provide updates accordingly.

Recommendations and guidance

Talos recommends applying the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, other mitigations can be implemented in the interim. The primary mitigation is starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled. This can be done by starting the application with “=XX:UseAVX=2”. Note that this is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command, likely resulting in failure to start.

Cisco is following its well-established process to evaluate its products and will provide updates shortly. Customers should reach out to their sales teams with specific questions

Coverage

SNORT® SIDs covering this vulnerability for subscribers:

Snort2: 1:67502 - 1:67513

Snort3: 1:301754, 1:67502 - 1:67513

Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset.

These rules detect malformed base64 data in specific HTTP request fields associated with the vulnerability. This vulnerability is implementation specific. Talos made every effort to identify as many common vulnerable applications as possible and cover potential attack vectors in those applications.

Splunk customers can refer to Splunk’s ES Content Updates (ESCU) pre-packaged security content for detections against high-profile vulnerabilities. Existing detections from Splunk cover suspicious indicators such as heavily encoded content, and post-exploitation scenarios such as arbitrary command execution or processes and web or application servers spawning shells.

articles.title: Patches released for critical ‘NGINX2Root’ vulnerabilities
articles.context: Sophos countermeasures SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this vulnerability and will deliver detections and protections as available
articles.full_text:
On November 18, 2026, F5 published security advisories for five critical (CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2) vulnerabilities that Xint has collectively dubbed ‘NGINX2Root’: (K000163925, K000163926, K000163927, K000163928, and K000163931). The issues affect NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus configurations. Exploitation could lead to crashes, denial of service, memory corruption, or code execution. According to F5, code execution requires ASLR to be disabled or bypassed.

Two of the vulnerabilities relate to NGINX HTTP/2 handling, and Wiz Research reports that they can be used to bypass Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR):

CVE-2026-123007 is an integer underflow issue in HTTP/2 flow control

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free issue affecting HTTP/2 connections that are proxied to a backend

The other three issues are use-after-free flaws that require specific configurations:

CVE-2026-123634 affects the NGINX resolver in some NGINX Open Source versions when NGINX proxies to a server name that contains variables and an SSI or mirror directive sends a subrequest that resolves the same name

CVE-2026-121810 affects HTTP/3 configurations in some NGINX Open Source versions

CVE-2026-113425 affects some NGINX Open Source versions when configured as a mail proxy server

Xint reports that each vulnerability can be chained with a separate Linux kernel SCTP vulnerability to obtain root privileges on the host, including when NGINX runs in a Docker container.

Recommended actions

Organizations should review the F5 advisories and upgrade vulnerable versions as appropriate. Updated source code and Linux packages for NGINX Open Source are also available from the NGINX website. Packages may not be immediately available for older, unsupported distributions. Xint notes that nginx -s reload does not load the new binary, so NGINX must be restarted or its binary upgraded after updating. If immediate upgrades are not possible, F5 advises avoiding SSI or mirror directives and proxied server names with variables (CVE-2026-123634), and restricting mail proxy listeners to trusted networks (CVE-2026-113425). For the HTTP/2 flaws, Wiz and Xint recommend disabling HTTP/2 on affected listeners but note that there may be implications for that action.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this vulnerability and will deliver detections and protections as available.

An internal investigation is also underway to determine if Sophos products or services are affected.
