The median number of high or critical vulnerabilities in cloud workloads increased fourfold between May and November this year, due to the impact of frontier AI, Datadog has claimed.

The cloud observability and security specialist revealed the findings in its State of Cloud Security 2026 published on November 10. It’s based on analysis of the cloud security posture of thousands of customer organizations around the world.

Datadog claimed that the median number of high/critical severity flaws in cloud workloads surged from four in May, when Anthropic’s Mythos model was released, to 14 in June and 16 in November.

The data was sourced from analysis of vulnerabilities in third-party libraries used by applications monitored through Datadog Code Security’s Software Composition Analysis (SCA) feature, the report noted.

“This data reveals that the increased number of vulnerabilities in the CVE database isn't a theoretical risk,” it added. “It affects an increasing number of real-world applications running in cloud environments, reinforcing the need for cloud security foundations that limit the blast radius of compromised applications.”

Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds.

The report also highlighted the challenge of long-lived credentials; specifically related to cloud-hosted AI inference services and CI/CD pipelines.

Datadog warned that such credentials are consistently ranked as one of the most common causes of cloud breaches, with automated tools continuously scanning the web for weaknesses.

“Red-team frameworks like Pacu and Datadog’s own Pathrunner along with secret scanners like TruffleHog reliably find over-permissioned credentials and exposed keys at scale,” it said. “That same tooling is available to autonomous attackers, who enumerate for long-lived credentials first because they’re the highest-value, longest-lived prize in the environment.”

The report revealed that nearly half of organizations using Gemini use long-lived Gemini API keys, while the percentage of cloud users with access keys older than three years has reached nearly 30% for AWS IAM and Google Cloud Service Account users.

“Rather than static Bedrock or Gemini API keys, you should access AI inference services through the calling workload’s short-lived identity when supported (IAM role, managed identity, or service account) so the model is reached with the same federated credentials as other cloud resources and not a separate long-lived key,” Datadog explained.

Cloud Dependencies Expose Users to Machine-Speed Attacks

Supply-chain attacks are increasingly run autonomously and at machine speed, with hijacked dependencies one of the most popular routes to compromise, Datadog claimed.

Part of the challenge is the speed with which new dependency versions are adopted by users. If adopted automatically without proper vetting, they can result in the rapid compromise of cloud credentials and services.

Some 60% of organizations Datadog analyzed run versions that were released less than 24 hours earlier, with these versions appearing in more than a fifth (21%) of cloud applications.

The risk is amplified the more dependencies there are, and Datadog found that app workloads running in the cloud have on average 149 software dependencies. The figure across the average organization is 568.

“Organizations should implement dependency cooldowns to lower the risk of malicious dependencies reaching their cloud environments, because the community usually identifies and contains hijacked libraries within a few hours,” the report recommended.

articles.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability

CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Security Flaws Across UK Government Sites Exposed ‘God-Tier’ Information
articles.context: A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene
articles.full_text:
A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene.

The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities.

But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.”

In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub. The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.”

The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says.

A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED.

The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.”

In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues.

Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models.

Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues would be the “worst case scenario,” according to Nesbitt-Smith, as it prevents researchers like him from finding them, and it’s likely that an adversary has already mirrored these repositories and so will maintain access to them. “Unless you’re going to go and fix all of the problems, if anything, you’re probably drawing more attention to it by closing it,” says Nesbitt-Smith, “because you’re like, ‘Here be dragons over this space. Don’t look here though, please.’”

articles.title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 1,252 CVEs Include One Zero-Day and 68 Critical Vulnerabilities
articles.context: November 2026 Attack Surface Analysis Preview-pane-triggered exploitation remains a dominant attack surface pattern for the third consecutive month, with eight Critical RCE...
articles.full_text:
November 2026 Attack Surface Analysis

Preview-pane-triggered exploitation remains a dominant attack surface pattern for the third consecutive month, with eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities across Microsoft Office applications including Outlook and Word. CVE-2026-110043 and CVE-2026-110068 in Outlook exemplify the risk: Merely selecting a malicious message in the Reading Pane or previewing an attachment in File Explorer triggers code execution without any click or macro prompt. This attack pattern continues to be attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document or message delivery into reliable code execution, bypassing the user-action barrier that many enterprises treat as a training backstop.

Identity platform components face elevated risk this month with Critical flaws in both Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). CVE-2026-119958 enables RCE against LDAP, while CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 target AD DS with RCE and elevation-of-privilege attack paths, respectively. These protocols underpin domain authentication and authorization for every joined workstation and server; successful exploitation of either can cascade to domain-wide compromise. Similar identity fabric vulnerabilities have historically been targeted by advanced adversaries seeking persistent access to enterprise environments.

Windows Hyper-V sees an unusually high concentration of privilege escalation vulnerabilities this month, with eight CVEs spanning multiple flaw classes. CVE-2026-113753, CVE-2026-113856, and CVE-2026-113860 all enable elevation of privilege within the hypervisor boundary. Hyper-V underpins Azure compute infrastructure and endpoint features such as Windows Sandbox, Credential Guard, and other Virtualization-Based Security capabilities, so the exposure extends beyond dedicated virtualization hosts to ordinary Windows endpoints with these features enabled.

Legacy network services including Server Message Block (SMB) and Print Spooler continue to draw Critical-severity RCE findings, reinforcing the persistent risk these widely deployed components carry. The unauthenticated network-reachable RCE cluster spans 14 CVEs this month, with Windows Message Queuing (MSMQ) vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-109459 and CVE-2026-116710 representing exposure on any system with MSMQ enabled. These services listen on the network by design and often lack authentication requirements for initial protocol negotiation, making any exposed instance an immediate target for opportunistic scanning. This class of legacy network service has historically been targeted in wormable exploitation scenarios.

Exploited Zero-Day Spoofing Vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook

CVE-2026-124194 is a Moderate spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook with a CVSS score of 6.5, and Microsoft confirms it is being exploited in the wild. The flaw stems from the product UI failing to warn users of unsafe actions: A specially crafted message file can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, disclosing the victim's NTLMv2 hash.

Outlook is the default mail client across most enterprise Windows deployments, making any flaw that bypasses user safety prompts a direct initial access vector at scale. Exploitation requires the victim to open a malicious file delivered via email or another channel. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector for this particular CVE. Once the victim opens the file, Outlook silently initiates an outbound connection, and the captured NTLMv2 hash can be relayed or cracked offline to impersonate the user against other services that accept NTLM authentication.

The Moderate severity rating reflects the user interaction requirement, but the real-world exposure is broader than the score suggests. Credential disclosure flaws that require only a file open, bypass visible warnings, and yield reusable authentication material are a well-established technique in targeted intrusion campaigns. Similar spoofing primitives in Outlook have historically drawn attention from both commodity phishing operators and advanced adversaries seeking footholds in enterprise environments.

Critical RCE Vulnerabilities in Windows Services

CVE-2026-112967 and CVE-2026-116928 are Critical RCE vulnerabilities in Windows services, each carrying a CVSS score of 9.8. Both allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code over the network, though they affect distinct components with different deployment realities.

CVE-2026-112967 is a heap-based buffer overflow in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service. An in-network attacker can call arbitrary endpoints on the service to trigger the flaw. Enterprise exposure depends on whether the service is present and running. Consumer-oriented Windows SKUs and gaming-enabled configurations are the primary population, making this lower priority for most corporate fleets.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component. The attack path is notable: An unauthenticated attacker can send an email with a specially crafted attachment to an Exchange Server, and the search indexer processes the attachment automatically for indexing. The recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation grants code execution with the permissions of the indexing service. Windows Search is broadly deployed and tightly integrated with Exchange for mailbox indexing, which places this flaw on an email delivery attack surface that reaches internet-facing mail infrastructure. The Windows Search path is the more significant exposure for enterprise environments. Email-delivered payloads that trigger without user interaction have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they bypass the phishing-click dependency that slows most initial access campaigns.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)

CVE-2026-119958 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows LDAP with a CVSS score of 9.8. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code by sending specially crafted LDAP calls to a listening server. No authentication or user interaction is required.

LDAP is the directory access protocol that underpins Active Directory. Every domain controller exposes LDAP on TCP/389 (and TCP/636 for LDAPS) by design, and the service cannot be disabled without breaking domain operations. Member servers, workstations, and applications query LDAP continuously for authentication, group policy retrieval, and object lookups, making it one of the most heavily trafficked protocols inside any AD environment.

The scope-of-impact concern is substantial. Code execution within the LDAP service on a domain controller places the attacker inside the trust boundary that every other domain resource relies on. From that position, credential extraction, replication abuse, and lateral movement to additional DCs become straightforward follow-on actions. Because LDAP is network-reachable from any domain-joined host by default, any internal foothold that can route to a DC can attempt exploitation.

Unauthenticated RCE flaws in core AD infrastructure have historically drawn rapid attention from ransomware operators and targeted intrusion actors because they collapse the gap between initial access and domain-wide compromise.

Preview Pane-Triggered RCE Vulnerabilities Across Microsoft Office

Eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities this month share a common attack vector: the Preview Pane in Outlook and Word. All carry CVSS scores of 7.5 to 8.8, with seven of the eight scoring 8.8. The underlying flaw classes are use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (two CVEs), release of invalid pointer (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). Despite the variation in memory-corruption primitives, the exploitation pattern is uniform: An attacker delivers a malicious document or email, and merely selecting it for preview triggers code execution with the user's privileges.

The Outlook vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110043, CVE-2026-110068, CVE-2026-111309) are the highest-exposure items in this group. Email is the delivery mechanism, and the Preview Pane is enabled by default in most enterprise Outlook deployments. An external attacker who can send mail to a target organization can reach the vulnerable code path without any authentication or prior foothold. The Word vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-110067, CVE-2026-111285, CVE-2026-124185) require document delivery, which typically means a phishing attachment or a link to a malicious file, but still fire on preview rather than open.

The remaining two CVEs (CVE-2026-111289, CVE-2026-120003) affect the broader Office suite and follow the same preview-triggered pattern. CVE-2026-124185 has a lower score (7.5) due to high attack complexity, but the others require no special conditions beyond user receipt of the malicious content.

Preview Pane vulnerabilities have historically been attractive to phishing operators and initial-access brokers because delivery converts directly to execution, with no need to persuade a user to open an attachment.

Critical Vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)

CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 are Critical vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services that both stem from incorrect authorization flaws. The two CVEs share a flaw class but differ in outcome and attack complexity.

CVE-2026-118146 carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and enables RCE. An authenticated attacker with low-level access to an affected server can send a specially crafted request and execute code without any user interaction. The authorization flaw means the server fails to properly validate that the authenticated principal should be permitted to perform the requested operation, turning a low-privilege foothold into code execution on a domain controller.

CVE-2026-118148 has a CVSS score of 7.5 and results in elevation of privilege to SYSTEM. This vulnerability has high attack complexity because successful exploitation requires the attacker to win a race condition. An authenticated attacker who can trigger the race gains SYSTEM privileges on the domain controller.

Active Directory Domain Services provides directory and authentication services for Windows enterprise domains. Domain controllers running AD DS issue Kerberos tickets, store the directory database, and process authentication and authorization decisions for every domain-joined resource. Compromise of a domain controller typically means compromise of the entire domain, since the attacker gains access to credential material and can issue arbitrary authentication assertions.

The attack surface for both vulnerabilities is any domain controller reachable from an authenticated low-privileged foothold. In most enterprise deployments, that includes every writable DC in the forest. Incorrect authorization flaws in identity platform components have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they convert commodity initial access into domain-wide compromise without requiring credential theft or additional tooling.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange Server

CVE-2026-118207 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange Server with a CVSS score of 8.8. The flaw stems from use of an incorrectly resolved name or reference, allowing an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send a specially crafted request and execute code on the server. No user interaction is required.

Microsoft Exchange Server provides enterprise email, calendar, and collaboration services, and is commonly deployed with internet-facing client access services for mobile and web users. The authentication requirement lowers the bar only modestly in most environments: Any compromised mailbox credential, service account, or partner federation relationship satisfies it. Once that requirement is met, the attacker reaches code execution on a server that typically holds sensitive mail content, internal address lists, and often enjoys elevated trust relationships with Active Directory.

Organizations running on-premises Exchange frequently expose Outlook Web Access, Exchange ActiveSync, and Autodiscover endpoints to the internet. Servers in this posture are reachable from any network position once the attacker obtains valid credentials, and successful exploitation yields a foothold inside the perimeter on infrastructure that processes sensitive communications.

Exchange Server vulnerabilities have historically drawn sustained attention from nation-state threat actors and ransomware operators because the combination of internet exposure, high-value data, and domain trust relationships makes compromised Exchange servers effective pivot points for broader intrusions.

Critical Elevation of Privilege Vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V

Microsoft addresses eight Critical elevation of privilege vulnerabilities in Windows Hyper-V this month, spanning five distinct flaw classes: use-after-free (four CVEs), heap-based buffer overflow (one CVE), TOCTOU race condition (one CVE), untrusted pointer dereference (one CVE), and use of uninitialized resource (one CVE). CVSS scores range from 6.4 to 8.2, with CVE-2026-113753 at the top of the range.

The exploitation outcomes fall into two categories. CVE-2026-113753 allows an attacker to gain Virtual Trust Level 1 (VTL1) privileges, which means escaping from the normal kernel (VTL0) into the secure kernel layer that underpins Virtualization-Based Security features such as Credential Guard. Five of the remaining seven CVEs enable guest-to-host escape: An attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine can execute code on the host in the security context of the virtual machine worker process.

Hyper-V is the hypervisor layer that runs Azure compute infrastructure and powers client-side Windows features including Windows Sandbox, Windows Subsystem for Linux 2, and Virtualization-Based Security. The exposure therefore reaches both datacenter server populations and ordinary endpoints where these features are enabled.

Most of the cluster carries a high attack complexity because exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk. Hypervisor escapes of this class have historically attracted attention from advanced adversaries because a successful exploit compromises the isolation boundary that separates tenants in shared infrastructure and protects credential material on endpoints.

Critical Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability in Windows Remote Desktop Services

CVE-2026-119957 is a Critical elevation of privilege vulnerability in Windows Remote Desktop Services with a CVSS score of 7.8. The flaw is a double-free that requires the attacker to win a race condition. Although exploitation is local, successful exploitation allows an attacker operating inside a guest virtual machine to escape to the host and gain the privileges of the affected virtualization service.

Remote Desktop Services underpins RDP-based remote administration across Windows Server deployments and is a core component in Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) environments. The guest-to-host escape path described in Microsoft's FAQ elevates this from a local privilege escalation to a potential hypervisor boundary violation, which matters in any multi-tenant or shared-host scenario.

The attack complexity is high due to the race condition. Post-compromise scenarios where an attacker already controls a guest VM provide the dwell time needed to attempt exploitation repeatedly. RDS-based session hosts and VDI pools present the most exposure to this guest-to-host escalation path.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows SMB Server

CVE-2026-113825 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in the Windows SMB Server Network Transport Driver (srvnet.sys) with a CVSS score of 7.5. The flaw is a race condition that an authenticated attacker can trigger over the network to execute code. Microsoft notes that successful exploitation requires the attacker to win the race, which accounts for the high attack-complexity rating.

SMB is the native file-sharing protocol for Windows and is enabled by default on both client and server editions. The srvnet.sys driver handles the network transport layer for SMB traffic, sitting beneath the higher-level SMB2 and SMB3 protocol handlers. SMB listens on TCP/445 and is fundamental to domain operations such as SYSVOL replication, Group Policy delivery, and administrative shares.

The authentication requirement limits drive-by exploitation from the internet, but any attacker who has already obtained low-privileged domain credentials, or who operates from a compromised workstation, can attempt the race. Timing-based flaws in kernel-mode network drivers can be unreliable on a single attempt, yet become practical when an attacker can retry at scale across many hosts. Ransomware operators and targeted intrusion operators have historically exploited race-condition RCE flaws in legacy network services for lateral movement and wormable propagation.

Critical RCE Vulnerability in Windows Print Spooler

CVE-2026-113752 is a Critical RCE vulnerability in Windows Print Spooler with a CVSS score of 7.5. The flaw is a use-after-free that an unauthenticated attacker can trigger over an adjacent network. Successful exploitation requires winning a race condition, which raises the practical difficulty but does not eliminate the risk in contested LAN environments.

Windows Print Spooler manages print job queuing and driver loading on Windows endpoints and servers. It runs with SYSTEM privileges by default and is enabled on virtually every Windows installation, including workstations that have no physical printer attached. The adjacent-network attack vector limits exposure to attackers who already have a foothold on the same network segment, but that constraint is often satisfied during post-compromise lateral movement.

Print Spooler vulnerabilities have historically drawn sustained attacker attention because the service combines broad default deployment, high privilege, and a complex legacy codebase that has repeatedly yielded exploitable flaws.

articles.title: N-able Disables Cloud Services Following Disclosure of "Able2Shell" Exploit Chains
articles.context: During previous N-central vulnerability exploitations (such as the CVE-2026-86218 zero-day), threat actors were observed "spraying" downstream environments with unauthorized...
articles.full_text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to John Hammond, Ben Bernstein, and Andrew Brandt for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Huntress is tracking N-able's response to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in its N-central platform, a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform built for managed service providers and IT teams. On November 9, N-able took its hosted N-central environment offline while it worked to secure the environment and apply remediation.

That move came after an independent researcher published the details of 33 critical vulnerabilities to GitHub that can be chained to lead to four different exploits (dubbed "Able2Shell"). Three of those chained exploits lead to remote code execution and one leads to privilege escalation to root. The vulnerabilities impact servers running N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31 (and likely earlier versions as well).

N-able said it has not seen active exploitation of the vulnerabilities as of November 9 at 15:15:00 UTC. The company is working on a hotfix that it said will be available soon; customers should keep their N-central servers offline until N-able confirms they can be brought back online safely.

Huntress has tracked and responded to other, separate flaws in N-able's N-central this year, including five critical CVEs:

August 2026: N-able released a hotfix for CVE-2026-18556, a critical vulnerability impacting all current versions of N-central across both hosted and on‑prem deployments, giving attackers unauthenticated, "god-mode" access to the RMM console. CVE-2026-18577 was disclosed soon after as an incomplete patch to the former CVE.

September 2026: N-able issued a hotfix to address a third vulnerability, CVE-2026-86218, an actively exploited pre-auth RCE zero day with a 10.0 CVSS score. The next day Huntress produced a proof of concept (PoC) exploit of a separate, net new vulnerability chain (CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207) in N-central that allowed attackers to bypass access controls to create unauthorized administrative accounts.

What Should Potentially Impacted Organizations Do?

Potentially impacted organizations should do the following:

If you run N-central on premises, take the server offline now and keep it offline until N-able confirms it is safe to restore.

If you use N-able's hosted service, expect an outage. N-able has taken its cloud infrastructure offline; follow its status page for updates.

Review login and authentication activity from November 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access. If you find suspicious activity, involve your incident-response team and assess whether systems or client networks managed through N-central may also be affected. The document warns that exploitation could enable remote code execution or privilege escalation on the server.

Carefully examine your audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise. During previous N-central vulnerability exploitations (such as the CVE-2026-86218 zero-day), threat actors were observed "spraying" downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools. Specifically, you should monitor for anomalous remote access sessions, new scripts being deployed, or the unauthorized creation of new administrator accounts.

Apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe. The document said a hotfix was in development, with no exact ETA, so check current vendor guidance rather than relying on this dated update.

N-able does not always iterate version numbers when it pushes down live hotfixes that don't require a reboot, so it remains to be seen whether the patched version will be numbered 2026.4.0.31 or something different.

Next Steps

Huntress is actively investigating this incident and we are communicating with our potentially vulnerable customers to share updates as they become available. Please check this blog for further updates as we learn more information.

You can also get further updates from N-able at: https://uptime.n-able.com/event/202561/

articles.title: Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit
articles.context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit appeared first on Cato Networks
articles.full_text:
Executive summary

On October 21, 2026, we observed participants in underground forums seeking PHP2Shell exploits, while others shared scripts presented as exploiting CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Discussion included doubts about prerequisites and whether circulating code worked. This post examines that gap between interest, claimed capability, and verified exploitation.

Our assessment covers selected forum posts and messages collected as of October 21. The findings show what was being discussed and shared, rather than confirmed compromises.

Forum participants requested exploit material, shared code, and questioned each other’s claims. For the security industry, this is a reminder to share threat findings promptly across security teams, researchers, and vendors so defenders can assess emerging threats and coordinate their response.

Looking for an exploit they could trust

Exploit.in is a long-running, primarily Russian-language underground forum where participants discuss hacking techniques and trade tools and services. Monitoring these discussions can reveal interest in emerging vulnerabilities and questions about available exploits.

“Does anyone have it?” was the question, translated from Russian, in a discussion on Exploit.in naming both PHP2Shell CVEs. The request sought exploit material, while subsequent comments questioned the prerequisites and legitimacy of circulating PoCs. One participant wrote “Didn’t test but seems legit.” A further comment described code execution “with preconditions,” while referring to a different “real exploit.” These are participant opinions about the circulating material, not our technical conclusions.

The exchange in Figure 1 captures both demand for an exploit and doubts about whether the available code worked. It leaves open whether the requester ever obtained a working exploit.

Figure 1. PHP2Shell exploit requests and discussion observed on October 21, 2026.

What circulated on October 21

On October 21, we recorded an English-language technical writeup at 02.23 UTC whose author claimed a lab reproduction. Hebrew- and Persian-language messages recorded at 05.16 and 05.35 UTC shared security alerts about the vulnerabilities and upcoming patches. The language of a post does not tell us where its author is based. At 06.22 UTC, we recorded a separate Exploit.in post presenting scripts as exploits for both CVEs, shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2. Forum post presenting purported PHP2Shell exploits, observed on October 21, 2026.

We redacted exploit instructions and memory offsets to avoid sharing details that could help reproduce an attack. The screenshot preserves the forum context.

A separate screenshot shared in a monitored channel appeared to show command execution on a local test system. We have not independently verified the result, and its exact posting date was unavailable.

By October 21, our searches returned 68 forum posts for PHP2Shell / CVE-2026-109618 and 62 for CVE-2026-109618. Chat searches returned 81 messages for PHP2Shell and 57 for CVE-2026-109619. These figures measure discussion volume in the collected material. The searches overlap, so the counts are not a combined total.

The forum exchanges show participants openly requesting exploit material, sharing code, and questioning each other’s claims. Separately, security alerts circulated in several languages across monitored messaging channels. Together, these observations illustrate how quickly information about a vulnerability can spread. For defenders, they reinforce the value of timely information sharing across organizations and language barriers, with clear distinctions between observed activity, unverified claims, and validated findings.

Public analysis offers context on PoC reliability

Public technical discussion published on October 23 on the SANS Internet Storm Center website examined why some circulating PoCs depended on specific server settings and knowledge of the target environment. The discussion concerned the PoCs reviewed there, rather than every possible way to exploit PHP2Shell.

The public analysis suggests that the PHP version, server setup, and information available to an attacker can affect whether a PoC works. These dependencies may help explain the questions raised in the forum thread.

Connecting intelligence with observed attempts

In our separate traffic analysis, we observed exploitation attempts, scanning, and invalid-PoC attempts. The invalid-PoC attempts add context to the forum discussion about whether circulating code worked. We detail these findings in our published PHP2Shell exploitation and IPS research. We have found no evidence connecting those requests to the forum participants or scripts discussed here.

We continue to monitor PHP2Shell activity and update our protections as exploitation techniques evolve. Our cloud-delivered IPS signatures blocked exploitation attempts on inspected customer traffic without requiring a separate protection package. PHP services outside our inspection coverage require separate remediation and protection. Updating affected PHP installations remains essential.

The post Cato CTRL Threat Intel: PHP2Shell in the Underground and the Search for a Working Exploit appeared first on Cato Networks.

Buckle up Metasploit-Framework enthusiasts because we have another action packed release for you. I'm talking, unauthenticated remote code execution modules in some of the biggest names in network perimeter devices like Citrix NetScaler and Cisco Secure Email Gateway. That's not all, we have an authenticated GitLab CI/CD regular expression integer overflow RCE module that was recently making head lines among many other awesome exploit modules. Looking for auxiliary modules? We've got you covered this release with a Flowise authentication bypass and a OpenBullet2 NTLMv2 hash disclosure, because who doesn't love collecting and cracking (or in some cases relaying) NTLM hashes am I right or am I right? In our continued effort to expand the payloads supported by the framework this week we saw fetch payload support for LoongArch. Lastly, if you're ever on an engagement or at home doing some testing and you see something that's not supported in Metasploit-Framework that you'd like to see supported, either drop us suggested-features issue on GitHub or trying throwing up a Pull Request, we'd love to hear from you. Happy hacking everyone!

Description: Adds a new auxiliary module that exploits CVE-2025-58434, an unauthenticated account takeover in Flowise versions 3.0.5 and earlier. Flowise's password reset API returns a valid reset token directly in its response, so the module can reset the password of any account whose email address is known, with no credentials needed.

articles.title: Zyxel Switch Patch Missed Flaw Behind Wave of Attacks
articles.context: A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks...
articles.full_text:
A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks on 996 switches in 48 countries.

Firmware security company Binarly detailed the finding in research published on November 3, linking it to an exploit that threat intelligence firm GreyNoise had described in September. The vulnerability now carries a new identifier, CVE-2026-107441. It is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management program that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run operating system (OS) commands with root privileges.

The attacks had originally been tied to CVE-2026-7273, which Zyxel fixed on June 16 and described as a stack-based buffer overflow in the same program, rated 8.8. On September 21, GreyNoise reported that an attacker had exploited that flaw against 996 Zyxel GS1900 switches in 48 countries, taking switch configurations, hashed root credentials and networking information.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog the same day.

Read more on network device zero-days: Critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day Under Active Exploitation

June Fix Left Vulnerable Code in Place

Binarly analyzed an obfuscated Python exploit that matched the one GreyNoise described. On September 28, the researchers confirmed that all 10 firmware releases shipped as the June fix remained vulnerable to it.

Binarly said the June change added a check, but the check ran only after the unsafe copy had already occurred. The researchers wrote that the change "does not address the vulnerability."

The firm offered two explanations. Either the June patch, its description and its Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score were incorrect, or the attacks used a different flaw and CISA's link to CVE-2026-7273 would be wrong.

Either way, Binarly said, all 10 releases advertised as fixes contain the vulnerable code.

Severity Disputed as Zyxel Ships New Firmware

Zyxel rates CVE-2026-107441 at 8.8 and says an attacker must be on the local network to exploit the vulnerability, while Binarly rates it 9.8 and says exploitation requires only network access to the switch's management service.

Binarly said it notified Zyxel on September 29. Zyxel confirmed the flaw on October 11, released a fix on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models. On the GS1900-8, for example, firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier is affected and 2.90(AAHH.3)C0 contains the fix.

Zyxel told users to install the updates "for optimal protection." Its advisory lists the June releases among the affected versions, so switches last updated in June still need the new firmware.

articles.full_text: Research by: Alexey Bukhteyev Key Takeaways OpenAI recently introduced Lockdown Mode, an optional advanced security setting designed to protect sensitive user data from prompt injection-based exfiltration attacks. Check Point Research discovered a vulnerability that allowed attackers to bypass Lockdown Mode, rendering its core protections ineffective. The vulnerability exposes a wide attack surface, enabling silent exfiltration of entire chat history, credential theft via phishing, and malware delivery. In ChatGPT Classic, the attack requires zero user interaction: simply having a conversation is enough to trigger silent data exfiltration. Introduction Earlier this year, Check Point Research disclosed a security flaw in ChatGPT’s code-execution runtime that allowed sensitive conversation data to be silently exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server through DNS tunneling, a hidden outbound channel that bypassed the runtime’s network isolation. A fix for this issue was promptly deployed. Moreover, OpenAI later introduced a new security feature: Lockdown Mode. Lockdown Mode is an optional advanced security setting for logged-in ChatGPT users. Its purpose is to reduce the risk that a prompt-injection attack can exfiltrate sensitive data by causing ChatGPT or one of its tools to make outbound web, app, connector, or file-download requests. A classic example, described in OpenAI’s own write-up on URL safety, is an attacker tricking the AI into loading a link such as attacker.example/collect?data= — the private data ends up in the attacker’s server logs even though nothing suspicious ever appears in the chat. Recognizing that prompt injection remains a persistent risk regardless of implemented guardrails, Lockdown Mode mitigates it by cutting off the channels through which data could leave the conversation. When enabled, it restricts live web access to cached content, blocks the loading and display of images from the internet, disables network requests from Canvas-generated code, and turns off Deep Research, Agent Mode, live connectors, and file downloads. Figure 1 – ChatGPT Lockdown Mode notification displayed when Canvas tries to access an external resource. We found a vulnerability in ChatGPT that allowed an attacker to bypass Lockdown Mode and perform covert exfiltration of chat data to an external server. Video 1 – The entire chat history was transferred to a third-party server without any notification, bypassing Lockdown Mode. Potential attack scenarios involving this vulnerability were not limited to chat data leakage. The vulnerability allowed for manipulation of the ChatGPT Classic interface, including displaying popup windows with arbitrary content, opening the door to a wide range of phishing attacks. The attack could be carried out in several ways: through a malicious prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat. The following sections cover the technical details behind the vulnerability and walk through the possible exploitation scenarios. Technical Details On February 2026, OpenAI added the HTML page preview feature into ChatGPT code blocks. It looks like the following: Figure 2 – HTML page preview in ChatGPT. Of course, the implementation includes several safeguards around this feature, since rendering user-controlled HTML with JavaScript inside the ChatGPT interface could otherwise create a direct path for private-data exfiltration. The most obvious attack scenarios include: Embedding an external image whose URL includes data from the chat: If such images could be rendered, an attacker could trigger zero-click exfiltration of private data. Embedding an external link: Download ChatGPT update This would allow attackers to place convincing social-engineering lures directly inside the ChatGPT interface and distribute them through shared chats. Opening a popup window with an arbitrary URL, either through a link with the target="_blank" directive:Click me or through JavaScript:window.open("", "_blank", "width=380,height=260"); This scenario would be especially risky in the ChatGPT Classic client, where users may perceive the popup as part of the trusted application context. Reading cookies or localStorage data for chatgpt.com. This would create a session-compromise risk. These scenarios are effectively mitigated through several layers of isolation and runtime enforcement. The rendered HTML is placed inside a sandbox, separating user-controlled content from the main ChatGPT application context, preventing the rendered page from directly accessing the parent document, ChatGPT UI state, cookies, or localStorage associated with chatgpt.com. All attempts by the page to send data to an external resource, or load remote images, scripts, links, or open arbitrary external URLs are intercepted by the sandbox and surfaced as warnings: Figure 3 – ChatGPT displays approval dialogs when a rendered HTML page attempts to access an external resource or when a user clicks an external link. The sandbox is implemented in two nested iframes. If we look at the implementation, we see that the sandbox doesn’t restrict some actions in the iframe. For example, the allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox permissions are enabled. Figure 4 – Sandbox attribute of the HTML-preview iframes, showing the permissive popup tokens (highlighted). The popups are controlled in a different way. The sandbox scripts redefine the window.open function: window.open: h=>{if(!h)return null;const{location:f}=r;return an(o,f,h),null} Thanks to that, when the webpage displayed in the iframe tries to open a popup, ChatGPT does not allow this until the action is approved by the user. When the page tries to open a popup with empty URL or about:blank the function just returns null , and the user does not even see a notification. However, popups are not explicitly restricted by the iframe sandbox, because it has the allow-popups token. Therefore, if we could get a real window.open function, we would be able to open a popup, bypassing the HTML sandbox restrictions, and even the Lockdown Mode. In fact, we can create a one more nested iframe inside our sandboxed page, and use its contentWindow.open function: window.open("about:blank"); // blocked // creating a nested iframe var f = document.createElement('iframe'); document.body.appendChild(f); f.contentWindow.open("about:blank"); // works Further, having managed to open a pop-up window, the attacker can place arbitrary HTML code in it, which will no longer be executed in the sandbox, since the token allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox is present. Attack surface: data exfiltration, phishing and malware downloding in a trusted interface. This vulnerability opens a wide attack surface. It could enable the covert theft of entire chat history and uploaded files, the distribution of malware disguised as a legitimate update, and even credential theft. Below, we walk through several scenarios and explain how each one works. Malware Delivery Through a Spoofed Application Window Typically, default browser settings prevent JavaScript from opening pop-up windows. Opening a new window normally requires an explicit user action, such as clicking a link or a button. An attacker needs to implement a plausible decoy to trick the user into clicking on a generated preview. Since the attacker controls the content of the generated page, crafting a convincing lure is straightforward. The window that opens will retain the ChatGPT application’s icon, while the title is controlled by an attacker, creating the impression that the user is still interacting with the ChatGPT application. This, for example, can be used to trick the user to download malware disguised as an application update. The ChatGPT Classic app does not allow automatic file downloads, so to download a file, the user must additionally click on the link. Video 2 – Malware delivery through a spoofed ChatGPT window. This scenario is even easier to implement in a browser, as automatic downloads are not blocked. Furthermore, the victim doesn’t even need to have an account, and the attacker only needs to share a chat containing a malicious page, making any clicks on content in shared chats dangerous: Video 3 – Malware delivery through a shared chat. Zero-Click Exploitation in ChatGPT Classic We found that window.open in the Electron-based ChatGPT Classic application works even without a user gesture. This makes the vulnerability significantly more dangerous: an attacker could silently exfiltrate data without requiring any interaction from the user, simply having a conversation would be enough to trigger the attack. This is demonstrated in Video 1, where a malicious GPT silently leaks chat messages to an attacker-controlled server. Beyond that, we also found it was possible to reload content in the main ChatGPT application window and perform certain actions on behalf of the user, such as forcibly signing them out of their account. This could allow an attacker to craft a convincing lure and trick the user into re-authenticating on an attacker-controlled page, thereby silently stealing their credentials. Video 4 – Credential theft. Conclusion Check Point Research responsibly disclosed this vulnerability to OpenAI. On September 18, 2026, OpenAI informed us that it had deployed a fix by removing the allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox permissions from the outer HTML-preview sandbox iframe. We subsequently retested the issue and confirmed that the exploitation technique described in this article no longer works. As AI assistants evolve into full execution environments, running code in the cloud and rendering content on the client side, all while handling medical records, financial data, and other highly sensitive information, every new capability expands the attack surface, including features built purely for convenience. Guardrails and the built-in security features of AI agents and applications help mitigate threats, but they still offer no absolute guarantee of protection. That is worth remembering before entrusting AI with sensitive information or granting it full access to your computer. Securing these systems requires looking beyond individual features and considering the platform as a whole. The benefits of modern AI assistants are enormous, but adopting them safely demands careful attention to every layer, including the ones users never think about. The post ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass: Phishing, Malware Delivery, and Silent Data Exfiltration appeared first on Check Point Research.

articles.title: Gartner Report: The Attack Path is Closing Faster than Most Teams Can Patch
articles.context: Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path...
articles.full_text:
Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter.

The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery.

Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation?

Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path.

The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.”

At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively.

What should security leaders measure instead?

Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively.

Gartner advises, “Organizations must shift focus from volume and activity to speed of decision, effectiveness of response, and tangible reduction of enterprise risk in an environment where attacker reasoning scales rapidly.”

The report examines outcome-driven measures including “Attack path analysis coverage,” “Patching cadence,” “Compensating control deployment cadence,” “Mean time to remediate,” and “Technology debt.” We believe this gives leaders a stronger basis for connecting security investment with reduced exposure, faster action, and business resilience.

How can teams move from prioritization to action?

Better prioritization only creates value when teams can act on it. Gartner recommends, “Use attack path analysis to prioritize your patches, virtual patches, and compensating controls. This can scale down to a consideration of critical services mapped into critical business outcomes and exposure.”

Rapid7’s internal, practitioner-led exploration of Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing reinforces our view that faster discovery is only the beginning. A model may help identify and validate a potential vulnerability, but reducing exposure still requires teams to understand affected systems, apply business context, choose the right remediation or compensating control, verify the result, and maintain detection coverage.

Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path analysis together, helping teams identify which exposures matter most and coordinate remediation through existing workflows.

What does an outcome-led program look like?

An outcome-led program gives executives a clearer answer to a more useful question: which attacker opportunities did we reduce, and how quickly could we respond? It also supports ongoing decisions about technical debt, recovery planning, and where limited resources can deliver the greatest reduction in business risk.

Access the complimentary Gartner report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, to explore how AI-assisted vulnerability discovery may change cybersecurity priorities, metrics, and investment decisions.

⠀

articles.title: GhostMap Bug Leaves Android Phones Stuck in Reboot Loop
articles.context: Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset
articles.full_text:
Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset.

Bitdefender said it discovered the issue when an Android package (APK) it collected from the wild crashed the emulators in its labs. It found that the problem wasn’t malware, but a bug in the Android OS itself.

“The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file,” it explained in a blog post.

“We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.”

Read more on Android bugs: Google API Keys Quietly Gain Access to Gemini on Android Devices.

Bitdefender said that the crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode, meaning the only way out is a factory reset which erases all locally stored data.

The bug affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above, but Google has so far failed to address it, claiming the issue is outside the scope of a security fix, the report noted.

It was notified by the security vendor on August 20.

How Threat Actors Could Abuse GhostMap

Bitdefender warned that cybercriminals could theoretically hide the technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of GhostMap as leverage for extortion.

It shared several possible scenarios:

Brick a victim’s phone by first creating a malicious app containing a deliberately malformed resource that Android’s system service needs to read. When it does, the resource triggers a crash in system_server which renders the phone unusable. This could be used for extortion

Make a malicious app impossible to remove. In this scenario an icon contains a malformed resource which triggers a crash when Android tries to display it. The launcher, the app list in Settings, and the app's own info screen all crash when the user tries to access them to uninstall

Disable security tools. Mobile security apps, malware-analysis sandboxes and automated scanning pipelines need to use Android's resource-parsing code to examine suspect apps. By embedding a malformed resource in an APK, hackers could trigger GhostMap to crash anything inspecting it

Delivery through an app update. An app looks trusted on download but, in theory, the malformed file could be introduced later. That would mean it could pass app-store checks and security scans to infect a much larger number of potential victims at once

“This is a flaw in Android itself and, as of publication, no fix is available, so users have limited options on the device to prevent it. The most practical defense is to recognize the file before the bug is triggered,” Bitdefender concluded.

“That's possible because the malformation is visible in the file's structure, without installing or running the app. A scanner can distinguish a crafted file from a normal one by inspecting it, not by executing it.”

The vendor detects this issue as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.

articles.title: Cisco, WatchGuard Release Patches; SonicWall Won’t Fix GMS Flaws
How Adversaries Are Turning the Vulnerability Ecosystem Against Defenders
articles.context: Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy...
articles.full_text:
Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy Authentication Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591)

In February 2026, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations identified an open directory controlled by the Iran-nexus adversary STATIC KITTEN on IP address 157.20.182[.]49 containing 1.9 GB of data and more than 20,000 files. Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591) first released by a well-known industry source on January 27, 2025.4

Where the public POC exploit executed a single user-provided command, the modified version contained 13 hardcoded payloads designed to enumerate targets, create users, and establish persistence. The modifications reflect a systematic approach to turning a demonstration tool into a more comprehensive exploit.

Table 1. Payloads for modified CVE-2024-55591 exploit

Payload Name

Description

test

Creates the backdoor admin user FortiWiFi with password FortiWiFi123 and assigns this user the super_admin profile, granting full system access

test2

Lists all user groups in the victim system, likely to facilitate reconnaissance in order to understand the victim system’s existing group structure

test3

Displays all local user accounts, allowing the attacker to enumerate existing users

test4

Modifies the FortiWiFi admin account by assigning it the ssl-vpn-groupamoss access profile

test5

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123, adds this user to the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group, and then displays all user groups to verify the user was successfully added to the group

test6

Creates or modifies a user group named ssl-vpa-amoss and adds multiple users to this group, including the backdoor FortiWiFi account (created by test1 or test5) and users with transliterated Hebrew-language names (i.e., shachar, sigal, amos, sima, lev, and gabi)

test7

Queries the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group configuration’s help information, likely to understand available options for follow-on activities

test8

Creates the backdoor user darlen with password 1234

test9

Similar to the test payload, creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123 or updates the existing FortiWiFi user to use that password

test10

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password 1234 and adds this user (along with numerous other users, many with transliterated Hebrew-language names) to the VPN-Users group, potentially to hide the backdoor account among legitimate users

test11

Creates a system admin account named FortiSetup with super_admin privileges and an encrypted password (decrypted password is gwm1607pmw); this account provides a more sophisticated backdoor than those created by other payloads, as FortiSetup has root VDOM access

test12

Displays the FortiAdmin account’s configuration, likely to facilitate reconnaissance

test13

Creates a user named offices with an email address and an encrypted password (decrypted password is @lolo@123456); POC_ZZ_1.py‘s developer may have added this email address to make the new user appear legitimate

Whether STATIC KITTEN modified the public CVE-2024-55591 exploit themselves or obtained this modified version from another source remains unknown. However, as of this writing, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has not observed any other adversaries using this modified POC or infrastructure hosting it.

AI’s Impact on the Vulnerability Research Ecosystem

AI advancements are undoubtedly accelerating the speed and scope of how vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized.5 One only has to look at the substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities in recent Microsoft Patch Tuesdays compared to prior to the advent of frontier models earlier this year.6

Detecting and attributing adversaries’ direct use of AI for vulnerability research purposes remains hard to identify due to inherent visibility gaps and the fact there is no single identifier that distinguishes AI-generated exploit code. Complicating things further, is that the patterns suggesting AI assistance (such as well-commented code, improvements to existing POCs, or structured code organization) are also consistent with the output of someone with high technical capabilities.

Nonetheless, threat actors are leveraging AI to augment their vulnerability research. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses they will almost certainly continue to do so through at least three vectors:

Direct interaction with frontier models by trying to “jailbreak” AI safeguards and bypass any export control restrictions

Modifying open-weight proprietary models for malicious use by extracting safeguards; these are not/less monitored for abuse by frontier AI companies

Adopting AI-led/assisted public vulnerability research published by industry sources

The third point, while not a direct use, is the easiest to detect. One only has to look at the CopyFail vulnerability detailed in this blog post, whose discovery was allegedly facilitated by AI.7 Or the mass exploitation of wp2shell in July 2026, which is the first critical unauthenticated WordPress Core remote code execution (RCE) purportedly discovered in nearly a decade and was allegedly discovered using GPT5.6 Sol Ultra and $25 USD worth of tokens.8

Outlook

Adversaries will almost certainly continue using public vulnerability research as part of their offensive toolkit through the foreseeable future. As more POC exploits become routinely available within hours of disclosure, at least partially driven by AI-assisted vulnerability research, the number of threat actors using them will almost certainly increase. Over the next year, this will likely manifest itself in the rise of widespread exploitation campaigns resulting in contested environments, like the cPanel CVE-2026-41940 exploitation example covered in this blog post.

This expanding pool of adversaries leveraging public vulnerability research, combined with the rapid speed at which adversaries are operationalizing public research, reinforces three key points.

The first is that patch prioritization is harder than ever. As vulnerability disclosures continue to increase in volume, predicting which ones will attract public research (and therefore adversary attention) becomes a genuine intelligence challenge. Because adversaries have access to the same advisories and public exploits that defenders do, organizations that rely solely on CVSS scores to drive patching decisions are relying on the wrong signal. Real-world exploitability, ease of exploitation (i.e., if there is a public exploit or exploitation guidance), and adversary intent are what separate the vulnerabilities that matter from the ones that do not.

The second is that the time to patch is effectively zero. The data from the first half of 2026 shows this: 91% of vulnerabilities with POCs that CrowdStrike has seen exploited were weaponized and used in the wild within 48 hours, with the fastest observation occurring just 35 minutes after a POC became available. Adversaries treat public vulnerability research as the starting gun, and legacy patch cycles measured in weeks or days cannot compete.

Lastly, more threat actors can participate in exploitation. As the case studies show, adversaries across skill and resource levels are operationalizing public research, some using POCs with minimal modification and others refining them (as UMBRAL BISON and STATIC KITTEN both demonstrated). When motivation and intent are the only remaining barriers to exploitation, the volume of participating adversaries significantly increases.

The vulnerability research ecosystem is one of the security community's greatest assets and most significant challenges. Defenders who treat public research as a threat actor's green light, and who build the intelligence, patching timelines, and detection capabilities to match, are the ones who will keep pace.

Jaime Duque and Lacie Blythe are Senior Intelligence Analysts at CrowdStrike. This research was presented at Day Zero 2026.

Additional Resources

articles.title: APT29 Watering Holes Target Unpatched iPhones and Android Devices
articles.context: Sekoia said its analysis supported the idea that APT29 obtained the exploits from a third party
articles.full_text:
A cyberespionage campaign attributed to Russia's APT29 has served exploit chains for already-patched iPhone and Android flaws to visitors of legitimate websites, with payloads built to steal cookies, device data and Wi-Fi passwords without any user interaction.

Sekoia uncovered the activity in mid-October 2026 and detailed it in research published on November 4. It assessed with moderate to high confidence that the group behind it is APT29, also tracked as Midnight Blizzard and Cozy Bear, or at least one of its subgroups. The group is widely attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).

The campaign used three delivery routes: scripts injected into legitimate websites, lookalike domains that proxied real sites while adding scripts and a week-long compromise of Plerdy, a Ukrainian website analytics tracker.

Exposed sites included a Ukrainian gas producer, Ukrainian military and military-equipment sites, a US chemical-industry trade association, a Czech far-right movement and a Bulgarian military-related site. The lookalike domains impersonated the America250 initiative and a London hotel.

Read more on Midnight Blizzard: Midnight Blizzard Targets Travelers via Captive Portals

Plerdy Compromise Expanded the Campaign's Reach

Plerdy is loaded by thousands of mostly Ukrainian websites. Sekoia said the compromise, which ran from August 27 to September 3, exposed hundreds of them and their visitors to the exploit kit.

The researchers did not say how many devices were compromised.

The campaign also cast a wider net than an earlier APT29 operation. A 2024 Google report described a campaign on Mongolian government sites that used a hardcoded filter to target specific websites, while this one had no such filter and collected any cookies in the browser.

Visitors were fingerprinted and served exploit chains matched to their devices, and the payloads did not establish persistence.

All Exploits Had Already Been Patched

One chain targeted iOS 16.7 to steal cookies. Another, based on the DarkSword exploit kit, which Sekoia described as suspected to have been developed by a commercial surveillance vendor, targeted iOS 18.5 and collected full device data. A third targeted Chrome 139 to 145 on Android, excluding version 143, for browser cookies and Wi-Fi passwords.

The chains used n-day flaws, meaning vulnerabilities already disclosed and patched: CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2024-27834, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, CVE-2025-43520, CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038.

Sekoia said its analysis supported the idea that APT29 obtained the exploits from a third party.

That also sets the limit of the threat. In Sekoia's words, "a user running an up-to-date operating system is safe from these attacks."
